metadata.title: RemyDegenne/testing-lower-bounds (Lean blueprint)

extraction_notes.note: Lean blueprint: the \lean, \leanok and \uses macros do not survive in the prepared source, so dependencies come only from \ref and from the text; about 75 proof environments are empty (proofs exist only in Lean) and get no node.
The "Dummy lemma: ... properties" environments (no mathematical content, placeholders for the blueprint graph) get no node; leanremark environments and TODO paragraphs are also left out.

Three labelled Data-processing theorems for f-divergences state the same inequality (F315 and F342 verbatim), each with its own proof and later citations; kept as three result nodes rather than merging them as restatements.
Prose proof sketches of the DPI are proof nodes with alternative proves edges; the sketch rule asks rigor semi_formal but rigor is not allowed on proofs, so no rigor was set.
lemma or conjecture: the author writes "This is a guess, I did not check it"; kept as lemma with rigor conjectural, and the theorem relying on it (F788) is semi_formal.

This is an expository formalization of known results; only classically named results and standard divergence definitions are marked origin external (standard (uncited)), other standard facts restated in the paper\'s generality are kept as paper.
The copy-discard category claim includes its itemized data list up to the end of the list.

Defined-term edges for the foundational notions (finite/probability measure, Radon-Nikodym derivative, kernels, f-divergence) were added for every flagged use, at confidence 0.7, which makes these definitions high-degree hubs.

metadata.extraction_comment: Notation-section definitions of kernels, finite kernels and Markov kernels are restated as environments in Appendix A; the environment nodes are kept and the notation sentences are recorded in also_stated_at.

nodes.name: All measures are sigma-finite
nodes.statement: Since Radon-Nikodym derivatives don't have good properties unless the measures are sigma-finite and since those derivatives are the basic building block of all the information divergences we consider, every measure we consider will be supposed sigma-finite.

nodes.name: Countably generated sigma-algebra
nodes.statement: The countably generated assumption means that there is a countable set of sets that generates the sigma-algebra.

nodes.name: Finite measure, probability measure
nodes.statement: A measure $\mu$ is said to be finite if $\mu(\mathcal X) < \infty$, to be a probability measure if $\mu(\mathcal X) = 1$.

nodes.name: s-finite and sigma-finite measures
nodes.statement: A measure is s-finite if it can be written as a countable sum of finite measures, and is $\sigma$-finite if it can be written as a countable sum of finite measures which are pairwise mutually singular.

nodes.name: Set of measures
nodes.statement: The set of measures on $\mathcal X$ is $\mathcal M(\mathcal X)$.

nodes.name: Set of probability measures
nodes.statement: The set of probability measures is denoted by $\mathcal P(\mathcal X)$.

nodes.name: Pushforward measure
nodes.statement: For a function $g : \mathcal X \to \mathcal Y$ which is $a.e.$-measurable with respect to $\mu$, $g_* \mu$ denotes the pushforward or map of $\mu$ by $g$. This is a measure on $\mathcal Y$ such that $g_* \mu (A) = \mu(g^{-1} A)$.

nodes.name: Measure with density
nodes.statement: For $g : \mathcal X \to \mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$, $g \cdot \mu$ denotes the measure on $\mathcal X$ with density $g$ with respect to $\mu$. That is, $g \cdot \mu (A) = \int_{x \in A} g(x) \partial\mu$.

nodes.name: Radon-Nikodym derivative
nodes.statement: The Radon-Nikodym of a measure $\mu$ with respect to another measure $\mu$ is denoted by $\frac{d\mu}{d\nu}$.

nodes.name: Singular part of a measure
nodes.statement: The singular part of $\mu$ with respect to $\mu$ is $\mu_{\perp \nu}$.
also_stated_at:
For $\mu, 
u$ two measures, we denote by $\mu_{\perp 
u}$ the singular part of $\mu$ with respect to $
u$.

nodes.name: Notation P_theta
nodes.statement: We write $P_\theta$ for $P(\theta)$.

nodes.name: Quantity of interest y
nodes.statement: The goal of the estimation task is to find, given the observation of samples of $P_\theta$ for an unknown $\theta$, the value of a function $y : \Theta \to \mathcal Y$~, which maps the parameter $\theta$ to the quantity we are interested in.

nodes.name: Estimator
nodes.statement: An estimator is a Markov kernel $\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$, where most often $\mathcal Z = \mathcal Y$.

nodes.name: Loss
nodes.statement: The quality of the estimation is quantified by a loss $\ell' : \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z \to \mathbb{R}_{+, \infty}$.

nodes.name: Estimation problem
nodes.statement: In short, an estimation problem is specified by the data $(P, y, \ell')$.

nodes.name: Testing problem
nodes.statement: We say that an estimation problem is a testing problem if $\mathcal Y = \mathcal Z$ is discrete and the loss takes values in $\{0, 1\}$.

nodes.name: Binary test
nodes.statement: A test is said to be binary if $\mathcal Y$ has two elements.

nodes.name: Simple test
nodes.statement: A test is simple if $\{\theta \mid y(\theta) = y_0\}$ is a singleton for all $y_0 \in \mathcal Y$, i.e. $y$ is bijective.

nodes.name: Simple binary hypothesis testing (SBHT)
nodes.statement: In summary, in simple binary hypothesis testing, $\Theta = \mathcal Y = \mathcal Z = \{0,1\}$, $y(0) = 0$, $y(1) = 1$ (that is, $y$ is the identity). For $y_0, z \in \{0,1\}$, $\ell(y_0, z) = \mathbb{I}\{y_0 \ne z\}$.

nodes.name: Law of the estimator output
nodes.statement: Let $\hat{\mu}_\theta$ be the law of $\hat{y}(\theta)$. That is, $\hat{\mu} : \mathcal \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ is the kernel $\hat{y} \circ P$.

nodes.name: Risk
nodes.statement: The risk of an estimator $\hat{y}$ on the estimation problem $(P, y, \ell')$ at $\theta \in \Theta$ is $r^P_\theta(\hat{y}) = (\hat{y} \circ P)(\theta)\left[z \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]$~.
nodes.label: def:risk

nodes.name: Risk in SBHT
nodes.statement: \emph{Example (SBHT):} $r^P_\theta(\hat{y}) = \hat{\mu}_\theta(\hat{y}(\theta) \ne y(\theta))$.

nodes.name: Bayesian risk
nodes.statement: The Bayesian risk of an estimator $\hat{y}$ on $(P, y, \ell')$ for a prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ is $R^P_\pi(\hat{y}) = \pi\left[\theta \mapsto r^P_\theta(\hat{y})\right]$~. It can also be expanded as $R^P_\pi(\hat{y}) = (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ P))\left[ (\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z) \right]$~.
nodes.label: def:bayesianRisk

nodes.name: Bayesian risk as a mean
nodes.statement: If we write $\ell'$ and $y$ for their deterministic kernels, the Bayesian risk of $\hat{y}$ is the mean of the measure $\ell' \circ (y \parallel \hat{y}) \circ (\pi \otimes P)$~.

nodes.name: Bayes risk
nodes.statement: The Bayes risk of $(P, y, \ell')$ for prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ is $\mathcal R^P_\pi = \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} R^P_\pi(\hat{y})$~, where the infimum is over Markov kernels. The Bayes risk of $(P, y, \ell')$ is $\mathcal R^*_B = \sup_{\pi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)} \mathcal R^P_\pi \: .$
nodes.label: def:bayesRisk

nodes.name: Bayes risk in SBHT
nodes.statement: \emph{Example (SBHT):} $\mathcal R^*_B = \sup_{\gamma \in [0,1]}\inf_{\hat{y}}\left(\gamma \hat{\mu}_0(\hat{y} \ne 0) + (1 - \gamma) \hat{\mu}_1(\hat{y} \ne 1)\right)$.

nodes.name: Bayes estimator
nodes.statement: An estimator $\hat{y}$ is said to be a Bayes estimator for a prior $\pi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ if $R^P_\pi(\hat{y}) = \mathcal R^P_\pi$.
nodes.label: def:bayesEstimator

nodes.name: Minimax risk
nodes.statement: The minimax risk of $(P, y, \ell')$ is $\mathcal R^* = \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} \sup_{\theta \in \Theta} r^P_\theta(\hat{y})$~.
nodes.label: def:minimaxRisk

nodes.name: Minimax risk in SBHT
nodes.statement: \emph{Example (SBHT):} $\mathcal R^* = \inf_{\hat{y}} \max\{\hat{\mu}_0(\hat{y} \ne 0), \hat{\mu}_1(\hat{y} \ne 1)\}$.

nodes.name: Bayes risk is at most the minimax risk
nodes.statement: $\mathcal R_B^* \le \mathcal R^*$.
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_le_minimaxRisk

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: For any $\pi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and any estimator, $\pi\left[\hat{\mu}_\theta\left[\ell'(y(\theta), \hat{y}(\theta))\right]\right] \le \sup_{\theta \in \Theta}\hat{\mu}_\theta\left[\ell'(y(\theta), \hat{y}(\theta))\right]$.
nodes.statement_short: Average over the prior is bounded by the supremum over parameters.

nodes.name: Bayes risk bounded by best constant estimator
nodes.statement: The Bayes risk of a prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ on $(P, y, \ell')$ with $P$ a Markov kernel satisfies \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi \le \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} \pi\left[ \theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z) \right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
assumptions: a prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$
$P$ a Markov kernel
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_le_const

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The infimum over all Markov kernels in the definition of the Bayes risk of $\pi$ is bounded from above by the infimum restricted to constant, deterministic Markov kernels.
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
nodes.statement_short: Restrict the infimum to constant deterministic kernels.

nodes.name: Bayes risk for a constant kernel
nodes.statement: The Bayes risk of a prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ on $(P, y, \ell')$ with $P$ a constant Markov kernel is \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi = \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} \pi\left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \: . \end{align*} In particular, it does not depend on $P$.
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
assumptions: a prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$
$P$ a constant Markov kernel
conclusions: In particular, it does not depend on $P$.
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_const

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $\xi$ be the measure such that $P(\theta) = \xi$ for all $\theta$. \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi &= \inf_{\hat{y}}(\pi \times (\hat{y} \circ \xi))\left[(\theta, z)\mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \\ &= \inf_{\mu \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)} (\pi \times \mu)\left[(\theta, z)\mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \\ &= \inf_{\mu \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)} \mu\left[ z \mapsto \pi\left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right] \\ &= \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} \pi\left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the infimum over estimators as an infimum over measures, then over points.

nodes.name: Data-processing inequality for the Bayes risk
nodes.statement: For $P : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ and $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ a Markov kernel, $\mathcal R^{\kappa \circ P}_\pi \ge \mathcal R^{P}_\pi$ (where the estimation problems differ only in the kernel).
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
nodes.statement_short: Post-processing the observations by a Markov kernel cannot decrease the Bayes risk.
assumptions: $P : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$
$\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ a Markov kernel
nodes.label: thm:data_proc_bayesRisk

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The risk $\mathcal R^{\kappa \circ P}_\pi$ is \begin{align*} \mathcal R^{\kappa \circ P}_\pi &= \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X' \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ \kappa \circ P))\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \\ &\ge \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ P))\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \\ &= \mathcal R^{P}_\pi \: . \end{align*} The inequality is due to taking an infimum over a larger set: $\{\hat{y} \circ \kappa \mid \hat{y} : \mathcal X' \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z \text{ Markov}\} \subseteq \{\hat{y}' : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z \mid \hat{y} \text{ Markov}\}$~.
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
nodes.statement_short: Infimum over a larger set of estimators is smaller.

nodes.name: Bayes risk of composition-product at most that of first kernel
nodes.statement: For $P : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ and $\kappa : \Theta \times \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ a Markov kernel, $\mathcal R^{P \otimes \kappa}_\pi \le \mathcal R^{P}_\pi$~.
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
assumptions: $P : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$
$\kappa : \Theta \times \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ a Markov kernel
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_compProd_le_fst

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Use Theorem~\ref{thm:data_proc_bayesRisk}: $P$ is the composition of $P \otimes \kappa$ and the deterministic kernel $\mathcal X \times \mathcal X' \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ that forgets the second value.
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
nodes.statement_short: Apply the data-processing inequality with the projection kernel.

nodes.name: Bayes risk of composition-product at most that of its second marginal
nodes.statement: For $P : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ and $\kappa : \Theta \times \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ a Markov kernel, $\mathcal R^{P \otimes \kappa}_\pi \le \mathcal R^{(P \otimes \kappa)_{\mathcal X'}}_\pi$~, in which $(P \otimes \kappa)_{\mathcal X'} : \mathcal \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ is the kernel obtained by marginalizing over $\mathcal X$ in the output of $P \otimes \kappa$~.
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
assumptions: $P : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$
$\kappa : \Theta \times \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ a Markov kernel
conclusions: $\mathcal R^{P \otimes \kappa}_\pi \le \mathcal R^{(P \otimes \kappa)_{\mathcal X'}}_\pi$~, in which $(P \otimes \kappa)_{\mathcal X'} : \mathcal \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ is the kernel obtained by marginalizing over $\mathcal X$ in the output of $P \otimes \kappa$
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_compProd_le_snd

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Use Theorem~\ref{thm:data_proc_bayesRisk}: $(P \otimes \kappa)_{\mathcal X'}$ is the composition of $P \otimes \kappa$ and the deterministic kernel $\mathcal X \times \mathcal X' \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ that forgets the first value.
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
nodes.statement_short: Apply the data-processing inequality with the second projection.

nodes.name: Concavity of the Bayes risk
nodes.statement: The Bayes risk $\mathcal R_\pi^P$ is concave in $P : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$~.
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
conclusions: The Bayes risk $\mathcal R_\pi^P$ is concave in $P : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_concave

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The infimum of a sum is larger than the sum of the infimums: \begin{align*} \mathcal R_\pi^{\lambda P_1 + (1 - \lambda)P_2} &= \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ (\lambda P_1 + (1 - \lambda)P_2)))\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \\ &= \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} \left( \lambda (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ P_1))\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \right. \\&\qquad \left. + (1 - \lambda) (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ P_2))\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \right) \\ &\ge \lambda \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ P_1))\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \\&\qquad + (1 - \lambda) \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ P_2))\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \\ &= \lambda \mathcal R_\pi^{P_1} + (1 - \lambda)\mathcal R_\pi^{P_2} \: . \end{align*} TODO: can we build kernels such that this lemma is a consequence of one of the lemmas above?
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
nodes.statement_short: The infimum of a sum is at least the sum of infima.

nodes.name: Bayesian risk via the Bayesian inverse
nodes.statement: The Bayesian risk of a Markov kernel $\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ with respect to a prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ on $(P, y, \ell')$ satisfies \begin{align*} R^P_\pi(\hat{y}) = ((P_\pi^\dagger \times \hat{y}) \circ P \circ \pi)\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \: , \end{align*} whenever the Bayesian inverse $P_\pi^\dagger$ of $P$ with respect to $\pi$ exists (Definition~\ref{def:bayesInv}).
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
assumptions: a Markov kernel $\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$
a prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$
whenever the Bayesian inverse $P_\pi^\dagger$ of $P$ with respect to $\pi$ exists
nodes.label: lem:bayesianRisk_bayesInv

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Use the main property of the Bayesian inverse. \begin{align*} (P_\pi^\dagger \times \hat{y}) \circ P \circ \pi &= (\mathrm{id} \parallel \hat{y}) \circ (P_\pi^\dagger \times \mathrm{id}) \circ (P \circ \pi) \\ &= (\mathrm{id} \parallel \hat{y}) \circ (\mathrm{id} \times P) \circ \pi \\ &= (\mathrm{id} \times (\hat{y} \circ P)) \circ \pi \\ &= \pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ P) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the joint law using the defining property of the Bayesian inverse.

nodes.name: Bayesian risk lower bound via the Bayesian inverse
nodes.statement: The Bayesian risk of a Markov kernel $\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ with respect to a prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ on $(P, y, \ell')$ satisfies \begin{align*} R^P_\pi(\hat{y}) \ge (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} P_\pi^\dagger(x) \left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
assumptions: a Markov kernel $\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$
a prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$
nodes.label: lem:bayesianRisk_ge_inf_bayesInv

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Starting from the equality of Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesianRisk_bayesInv}, we get \begin{align*} R^P_\pi(\hat{y}) &= ((P_\pi^\dagger \times \hat{y}) \circ P \circ \pi)\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \\ &= (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto (P_\pi^\dagger(x) \times \hat{y}(x)) \left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right] \\ &= (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \hat{y}(x)\left[z \mapsto P_\pi^\dagger(x) \left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right]\right] \\ &\ge (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} P_\pi^\dagger(x) \left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
nodes.statement_short: Disintegrate via the Bayesian inverse and bound the inner integral by its infimum.

nodes.name: Generalized Bayes estimator
nodes.statement: The generalized Bayes estimator for prior $\pi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ on $(P, y, \ell')$ is the deterministic estimator $\mathcal X \to \mathcal Z$ given by \begin{align*} x \mapsto \arg\min_z P_\pi^\dagger(x)\left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \: , \end{align*} if there exists such a measurable argmin.
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
nodes.label: def:genBayesEstimator

nodes.name: Bayesian risk of the generalized Bayes estimator
nodes.statement: The Bayesian risk of the generalized Bayes estimator $\hat{y}_B$ is \begin{align*} R^P_\pi(\hat{y}_B) = (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} P_\pi^\dagger(x) \left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
nodes.label: lem:bayesianRisk_genBayesEstimator

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Start from the equality of Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesianRisk_bayesInv} and use the definition of the generalized Bayes estimator.
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
nodes.statement_short: Plug the generalized Bayes estimator into the Bayesian-inverse formula.

nodes.name: The generalized Bayes estimator is a Bayes estimator
nodes.statement: When the generalized Bayes estimator is well defined, it is a Bayes estimator. The value of the Bayes risk with respect to the prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ is then \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi = (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} P_\pi^\dagger(x) \left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
assumptions: When the generalized Bayes estimator is well defined
nodes.label: thm:isBayesEstimator_genBayesEstimator

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesianRisk_ge_inf_bayesInv}, the Bayesian risk of the generalized Bayes estimator obtained in Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesianRisk_genBayesEstimator} is a lower bound for the Bayesian risk.
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
nodes.statement_short: Its Bayesian risk matches the lower bound valid for all estimators.

nodes.name: Bayes risk via Radon-Nikodym derivatives
nodes.statement: When the generalized Bayes estimator is well defined, the Bayes risk with respect to the prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ is \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi = (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} \pi \left[\theta \mapsto \frac{d P_\theta}{d (P \circ \pi)}(x) \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
assumptions: When the generalized Bayes estimator is well defined
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_eq_rnDeriv

nodes.name: Bayes risk for 0-1 loss via the Bayesian inverse
nodes.statement: When the generalized Bayes estimator is well defined, the Bayes risk with respect to the prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ for $\mathcal Y = \mathcal Z = \Theta$, $y = \mathrm{id}$ and $\ell' = \mathbb{I}\{\theta \ne z\}$ is \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi = (P \circ \pi)[1] - (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \sup_{z \in \mathcal Z} P_\pi^\dagger(x) \{z\}\right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
assumptions: When the generalized Bayes estimator is well defined
$\mathcal Y = \mathcal Z = \Theta$, $y = \mathrm{id}$ and $\ell' = \mathbb{I}\{\theta \ne z\}$
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_binary_eq_sub_bayesInv

nodes.name: Bayes risk for 0-1 loss via Radon-Nikodym derivatives
nodes.statement: When the generalized Bayes estimator is well defined, the Bayes risk with respect to the prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ for $\mathcal Y = \mathcal Z = \Theta$, $y = \mathrm{id}$ and $\ell' = \mathbb{I}\{\theta \ne z\}$ is \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi = (P \circ \pi)[1] - (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \sup_{z \in \mathcal Z} \frac{d P_z}{d (P \circ \pi)}(x) \pi\{z\} \right] \: . \end{align*} When $\pi$ is a probability measure and $P$ is a Markov kernel, $(P \circ \pi)[1] = 1$.
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
assumptions: When the generalized Bayes estimator is well defined
$\mathcal Y = \mathcal Z = \Theta$, $y = \mathrm{id}$ and $\ell' = \mathbb{I}\{\theta \ne z\}$
conclusions: When $\pi$ is a probability measure and $P$ is a Markov kernel, $(P \circ \pi)[1] = 1$.
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_binary_eq_sub

nodes.name: Generalized Bayes estimator for 0-1 loss
nodes.statement: The generalized Bayes estimator for prior $\pi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ on the estimation problem defined by $\mathcal Y = \mathcal Z = \Theta$, $y = \mathrm{id}$ and $\ell' = \mathbb{I}\{\theta \ne z\}$ is \begin{align*} x \mapsto \arg\max_z \left( \pi\{z\} \frac{d P_z}{d (P \circ \pi)}(x) \right) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
nodes.label: lem:genBayesEstimator_binary

nodes.name: Bayes risk for 0-1 loss bounded by a weighted geometric mean
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\Theta$ is finite and let $\xi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$. The Bayes risk with respect to the prior $\pi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ for $\mathcal Y = \mathcal Z = \Theta$, $y = \mathrm{id}$, $P$ a Markov kernel and $\ell' = \mathbb{I}\{\theta \ne z\}$ satisfies \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\pi \le 1 - \left(\prod_{\theta \in \Theta} \pi_\theta^{\xi_\theta}\right) (P \circ \pi)\left[x \mapsto \prod_{\theta \in \Theta} \left(\frac{d P_\theta}{d (P \circ \pi)}(x)\right)^{\xi_\theta} \right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 1.1.1 Properties of the Bayes risk of a prior
assumptions: Suppose that $\Theta$ is finite and let $\xi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$.
$P$ a Markov kernel
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_binary_le_sub_prod

nodes.name: Bayes risk increase
nodes.statement: The Bayes risk increase $I^P_{\pi}(\kappa)$ of a kernel $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ with respect to the estimation problem $(P, y, \ell')$ and the prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ is the difference of the Bayes risk of $(\kappa \circ P, y, \ell')$ and that of $(P, y, \ell')$. That is, \begin{align*} I^P_{\pi}(\kappa) &= \mathcal R^{\kappa \circ P}_\pi - \mathcal R^P_\pi \\ &= \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X' \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ \kappa \circ P))\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] - \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z} (\pi \otimes (\hat{y} \circ P))\left[(\theta, z) \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:riskIncrease

nodes.name: Discard kernel
nodes.statement: In particular, if we take $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow *$ equal to the Markov kernel to the point space (denoted by $d_{\mathcal X}$, for ``discard'' kernel), we get $I^P_{\pi}(d_{\mathcal X}) = \mathcal R^{d_{\mathcal X} \circ P}_\pi - \mathcal R^P_\pi$, where $d_{\mathcal X} \circ P = d_\Theta$ if $P$ is a Markov kernel.
also_stated_at: The discard kernel $d_{\mathcal X}$ (TODO: conflicts with deterministic kernel notation). This is a kernel from $\mathcal X$ to $*$, the space with one point, corresponding to the constant function.

nodes.name: Bayes risk increase is nonnegative
nodes.statement: For $\kappa$ a Markov kernel, $I^P_\pi(\kappa) \ge 0$~.
assumptions: For $\kappa$ a Markov kernel
nodes.label: lem:riskIncrease_nonneg

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Use Theorem~\ref{thm:data_proc_bayesRisk}.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the data-processing inequality.

nodes.name: Chain rule for the Bayes risk increase
nodes.statement: For $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ and $\eta : \mathcal X' \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X''$ two Markov kernels, $I^P_\pi(\eta \circ \kappa) = I^P_\pi(\kappa) + I^{\kappa \circ P}_\pi(\eta)$~.
assumptions: $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$ and $\eta : \mathcal X' \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X''$ two Markov kernels
nodes.label: lem:riskIncrease_comp

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} I^P_\pi(\kappa) + I^{\kappa \circ P}_\pi(\eta) &= \mathcal R^{\kappa \circ P}_\pi - \mathcal R^{P}_\pi + \mathcal R^{\eta \circ \kappa \circ P}_\pi - \mathcal R^{\kappa \circ P}_\pi \\ &= \mathcal R^{\eta \circ \kappa \circ P}_\pi - \mathcal R^{P}_\pi \\ &= I^P_\pi(\eta \circ \kappa) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Telescoping sum of Bayes risks.

nodes.name: Data-processing inequality for the Bayes risk increase
nodes.statement: For any measurable space $\mathcal X$, let $d_{\mathcal X} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow *$ be the Markov kernel to the point space. For all Markov kernels $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$, \begin{align*} I_\pi^P(d_{\mathcal X}) \ge I_\pi^{\kappa \circ P}(d_{\mathcal X'}) \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: For all Markov kernels $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X'$
nodes.label: lem:riskIncrease_comp_del

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:riskIncrease_comp}, then Lemma~\ref{lem:riskIncrease_nonneg}, \begin{align*} I_\pi^P(d_{\mathcal X'} \circ \kappa) = I^P_\pi(\kappa) + I^{\kappa \circ P}_\pi(d_{\mathcal X'}) \ge I_\pi^{\kappa \circ P}(d_{\mathcal X'}) \: . \end{align*} Finally, $d_{\mathcal X'} \circ \kappa = d_{\mathcal X}$ since $\kappa$ is a Markov kernel.
nodes.statement_short: Chain rule for the risk increase plus nonnegativity; the discard kernel absorbs $\kappa$.

nodes.name: Weights of a measure on {0,1}
nodes.statement: In this section, for a measure $\xi$ on $\{0,1\}$, we write $\xi_0$ for $\xi(\{0\})$ and $\xi_1$ for $\xi(\{1\})$~.

nodes.name: Pair notation for measures on {0,1}
nodes.statement: We sometimes write $(a,b)$ for the measure $\xi$ on $\{0,1\}$ with $\xi_0 = a$ and $\xi_1 = b$.

nodes.name: Bayesian inverse for a binary parameter
nodes.statement: The Bayesian inverse of a kernel $P : \{0,1\} \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ with respect to a prior $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$ is $P_\xi^\dagger(x) = \left(\xi_0\frac{d P(0)}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x), \xi_1\frac{d P(1)}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)\right)$ (almost surely w.r.t. $P \circ \xi = \xi_0 P(0) + \xi_1 P(1)$).
assumptions: a kernel $P : \{0,1\} \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$
a prior $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$
conclusions: $P_\xi^\dagger(x) = \left(\xi_0\frac{d P(0)}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x), \xi_1\frac{d P(1)}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)\right)$ (almost surely w.r.t. $P \circ \xi = \xi_0 P(0) + \xi_1 P(1)$)
nodes.label: lem:bayesInv_binary

nodes.name: Bayes risk for a binary parameter
nodes.statement: For $\Theta = \{0,1\}$, the Bayes risk of a prior $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$ is \begin{align*} \mathcal R^P_\xi = (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} \left( \xi_0\frac{d P(0)}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)\ell'(y(0), z) + \xi_1\frac{d P(1)}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)\ell'(y(1), z) \right) \right] \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: For $\Theta = \{0,1\}$
a prior $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$
conclusions: \mathcal R^P_\xi = (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} \left( \xi_0\frac{d P(0)}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)\ell'(y(0), z) + \xi_1\frac{d P(1)}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)\ell'(y(1), z) \right) \right]
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_binary

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Use Theorem~\ref{thm:isBayesEstimator_genBayesEstimator}, with the value of $P_\xi^\dagger$ given by Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesInv_binary}.
nodes.statement_short: Generalized Bayes estimator formula with the explicit binary Bayesian inverse.

nodes.name: Bayes binary risk
nodes.statement:
The Bayes binary risk between measures $\mu$ and $
u$ with respect to prior $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$, denoted by $\mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u)$, is the Bayes risk $\mathcal R^P_\xi$ for $\Theta = \mathcal Y = \mathcal Z = \{0,1\}$, $\ell(y,z) = \mathbb{I}\{y 
e z\}$, $P$ the kernel sending 0 to $\mu$ and 1 to $
u$ and prior $\xi$. That is,  egin{align*} \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u) = \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \{0,1\}}\left(\xi_0 (\hat{y} \circ \mu)(\{1\}) + \xi_1 (\hat{y} \circ 
u)(\{0\})ight) \: , \end{align*} in which the infimum is over Markov kernels. If the prior is a probability measure with weights $(\pi, 1 - \pi)$, we write $B_\pi(\mu, 
u) = \mathcal B_{(\pi, 1 - \pi)}(\mu, 
u)$~.
nodes.statement_short: Bayes risk of testing $\mu$ against $\nu$ with 0-1 loss and prior $\xi$; $B_\pi$ for prior $(\pi,1-\pi)$.
nodes.label: def:bayesBinaryRisk

nodes.name: Scaling of the Bayes binary risk
nodes.statement: For all $a, b > 0$, $\mathcal B_\xi(\mu, \nu) = \mathcal B_{(a \xi_0, b \xi_1)}(a^{-1} \mu, b^{-1} \nu)$~.
assumptions: For all $a, b > 0$
nodes.label: lem:bayesBinaryRisk_mul

nodes.name: Reduction of the Bayes binary risk to prior (1,1)
nodes.statement: $\mathcal B_\xi(\mu, \nu) = \mathcal B_{(1,1)}(\xi_0\mu, \xi_1\nu)$~.
nodes.label: lem:bayesBinaryRisk_one_one

nodes.name: Data-processing inequality for the Bayes binary risk
nodes.statement:
For $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and $\kappa : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ a Markov kernel, $\mathcal B_\xi(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \ge \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u)$~.
assumptions: For $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$
$\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ a Markov kernel
nodes.label: thm:data_proc_bayesBinaryRisk

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:data_proc_bayesRisk}.
nodes.statement_short: Special case of the data-processing inequality for the Bayes risk.

nodes.name: Bayes binary risk of a measure with itself
nodes.statement: For $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$, $\mathcal B_\xi(\mu, \mu) = \min\{\xi_0, \xi_1\} \mu(\mathcal X)$~.
assumptions: For $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$
nodes.label: lem:bayesBinaryRisk_self

nodes.name: Bayes binary risk is nonnegative
nodes.statement: For all measures $\mu, \nu$, $\mathcal B_\xi(\mu, \nu) \ge 0$~.
assumptions: For all measures $\mu, \nu$
nodes.label: lem:bayesBinaryRisk_nonneg

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: It is an infimum of non-negative values.
nodes.statement_short: Infimum of nonnegative values.

nodes.name: Upper bound on the Bayes binary risk
nodes.statement:
For all measures $\mu, 
u$, $\mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u) \le \min\{\xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X), \xi_1 
u(\mathcal X)\}$~.
assumptions: For all measures $\mu, \nu$
nodes.label: lem:bayesBinaryRisk_le

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
Let $d_{\mathcal X} : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow *$ be the discard kernel and $\delta_*$ be the only probability measure over $*$, that is a Dirac delta. Then applying the DPI (Theorem~ef{thm:data_proc_bayesBinaryRisk}), followed by Lemma~ef{lem:bayesBinaryRisk_mul} and Lemma~ef{lem:bayesBinaryRisk_self}, we obtain:  egin{align*} \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u) &\le \mathcal B_\xi(d_{\mathcal X} \circ \mu, d_{\mathcal X} \circ 
u) \ &= \mathcal B_\xi(\mu(\mathcal X) \delta_*, 
u(\mathcal X) \delta_*) \ &= \mathcal B_{(\mu(\mathcal X) \xi_0, 
u(\mathcal X) \xi_1)}(\delta_*, \delta_*) \ &= \min\{\mu(\mathcal X) \xi_0, 
u(\mathcal X) \xi_1\} \delta_*(\mathcal X) \ &= \min\{\mu(\mathcal X) \xi_0, 
u(\mathcal X) \xi_1\} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: DPI with the discard kernel, then scaling and the self-risk lemma on Dirac measures.

nodes.name: Symmetry of the Bayes binary risk
nodes.statement:
For $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$, $\mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u) = \mathcal B_{\xi_{\leftrightarrow}}(
u, \mu)$ where $\xi_{\leftrightarrow} \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$ is such that $\xi_{\leftrightarrow}(\{0\}) = \xi_1$ and $\xi_{\leftrightarrow}(\{1\}) = \xi_0$. For $\pi \in [0,1]$, $B_\pi(\mu, 
u) = B_{1 - \pi}(
u, \mu)$~.
assumptions: For $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$
nodes.label: lem:bayesBinaryRisk_symm

nodes.name: Generalized Bayes estimator for the Bayes binary risk
nodes.statement: The generalized Bayes estimator for the Bayes binary risk with prior $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$ is $x \mapsto \text{if } \xi_1\frac{d \nu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) \le \xi_0\frac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) \text{ then } 0 \text{ else } 1$, i.e. it is equal to $\mathbb{I}_E$ for $E = \{x \mid \xi_1\frac{d \nu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) > \xi_0\frac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)\}$~.
conclusions: $x \mapsto \text{if } \xi_1\frac{d \nu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) \le \xi_0\frac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) \text{ then } 0 \text{ else } 1$, i.e. it is equal to $\mathbb{I}_E$ for $E = \{x \mid \xi_1\frac{d \nu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) > \xi_0\frac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)\}$
nodes.label: lem:genBayesEstimator_bayesBinaryRisk

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The generalized Bayes estimator is defined by \begin{align*} x \mapsto \arg\min_z P_\xi^\dagger(x)\left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \: . \end{align*} For the simple binary hypothesis testing problem, \begin{align*} P_\xi^\dagger(x)\left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] &= P_\xi^\dagger(x)(\theta \ne z) \: . \end{align*} For $z = 0$, this is $P_\xi^\dagger(x)(\{1\})$ and for $z = 1$, this is $P_\xi^\dagger(x)(\{0\})$. The generalized Bayes estimator is $x \mapsto \text{if } P_\xi^\dagger(x)(\{1\}) \le P_\xi^\dagger(x)(\{0\}) \text{ then } 0 \text{ else } 1$. The expression of the lemma statement is obtained by replacing $P_\xi^\dagger$ by its value (Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesInv_binary}).
nodes.statement_short: Compute the posterior 0-1 loss for each decision and compare; substitute the binary Bayesian inverse.

nodes.name: Recall the definition of the generalized Bayes estimator
nodes.statement: The generalized Bayes estimator is defined by \begin{align*} x \mapsto \arg\min_z P_\xi^\dagger(x)\left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Recall the definition of the generalized Bayes estimator.

nodes.name: Posterior loss is the posterior probability of error for each decision
nodes.statement: For the simple binary hypothesis testing problem, \begin{align*} P_\xi^\dagger(x)\left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right] &= P_\xi^\dagger(x)(\theta \ne z) \: . \end{align*} For $z = 0$, this is $P_\xi^\dagger(x)(\{1\})$ and for $z = 1$, this is $P_\xi^\dagger(x)(\{0\})$.
nodes.statement_short: Posterior loss is the posterior probability of error for each decision.

nodes.name: The estimator picks the decision with smaller posterior error
nodes.statement: The generalized Bayes estimator is $x \mapsto \text{if } P_\xi^\dagger(x)(\{1\}) \le P_\xi^\dagger(x)(\{0\}) \text{ then } 0 \text{ else } 1$.
nodes.statement_short: The estimator picks the decision with smaller posterior error.

nodes.name: Substitute the explicit binary Bayesian inverse
nodes.statement: The expression of the lemma statement is obtained by replacing $P_\xi^\dagger$ by its value (Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesInv_binary}).
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the explicit binary Bayesian inverse.

nodes.name: Bayes binary risk as infimum over events
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, \nu) = \inf_{E \text{ event}} \left( \xi_0 \mu(E) + \xi_1 \nu(E^c) \right) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:bayesBinaryRisk_eq_event

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
By definition,  egin{align*} \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u) = \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \{0,1\}}\left(\xi_0 (\hat{y} \circ \mu)(\{1\}) + \xi_1 (\hat{y} \circ 
u)(\{0\})ight) \: . \end{align*} If we restrict the infimum to deterministic kernels corresponding to functions of the form $x \mapsto \mathbb{I}\{x \in E\}$, we get that $\mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u)$ is bounded from above by the expression for which we want to show equality. Since the Bayes estimator has that shape (Lemma~ef{lem:genBayesEstimator_bayesBinaryRisk}), $\mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u)$ is also greater than the infimum and we have equality.
nodes.statement_short: Restricting to indicator tests gives one inequality; the Bayes estimator being an indicator gives the other.

nodes.name: Recall the definition of the Bayes binary risk
nodes.statement: By definition, \begin{align*} \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, \nu) = \inf_{\hat{y} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \{0,1\}}\left(\xi_0 (\hat{y} \circ \mu)(\{1\}) + \xi_1 (\hat{y} \circ \nu)(\{0\})\right) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Recall the definition of the Bayes binary risk.

nodes.name: Restricting to indicator tests gives an upper bound
nodes.statement: If we restrict the infimum to deterministic kernels corresponding to functions of the form $x \mapsto \mathbb{I}\{x \in E\}$, we get that $\mathcal B_\xi(\mu, \nu)$ is bounded from above by the expression for which we want to show equality.
nodes.statement_short: Restricting to indicator tests gives an upper bound.

nodes.name: Bayes estimator is an indicator, giving equality
nodes.statement: Since the Bayes estimator has that shape (Lemma~\ref{lem:genBayesEstimator_bayesBinaryRisk}), $\mathcal B_\xi(\mu, \nu)$ is also greater than the infimum and we have equality.
nodes.statement_short: Bayes estimator is an indicator, giving equality.

nodes.name: Bayes binary risk formula
nodes.statement: The Bayes risk of simple binary hypothesis testing for prior $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$ is \begin{align*} \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, \nu) = (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \min \left\{\xi_0\frac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x), \xi_1\frac{d \nu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)\right\}\right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bayes binary risk is the integral of the minimum of the weighted densities.
nodes.label: thm:bayesBinaryRisk_eq

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{thm:isBayesEstimator_genBayesEstimator}, the generalized Bayes estimator is a Bayes estimator, hence it suffices to compute its Bayesian risk. By Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesianRisk_genBayesEstimator}, \begin{align*} R_\xi(\hat{y}_B) &= (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} P_\xi^\dagger(x) \left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right] \\ &= (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \min \left\{P_\xi^\dagger(x)(\{0\}), P_\xi^\dagger(x)(\{1\})\right\}\right] \\ &= (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \min \left\{\xi_0\frac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x), \xi_1\frac{d \nu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)\right\}\right] \: . \end{align*} The last line is obtained by replacing $P_\xi^\dagger$ by its value (Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesInv_binary}).
nodes.statement_short: Compute the Bayesian risk of the generalized Bayes estimator using the binary Bayesian inverse.

nodes.name: Reduce to computing the risk of the generalized Bayes estimator
nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{thm:isBayesEstimator_genBayesEstimator}, the generalized Bayes estimator is a Bayes estimator, hence it suffices to compute its Bayesian risk.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to computing the risk of the generalized Bayes estimator.

nodes.name: Expand its Bayesian risk as a minimum of posterior probabilities
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesianRisk_genBayesEstimator}, \begin{align*} R_\xi(\hat{y}_B) &= (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \inf_{z \in \mathcal Z} P_\xi^\dagger(x) \left[\theta \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z)\right]\right] \\ &= (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \min \left\{P_\xi^\dagger(x)(\{0\}), P_\xi^\dagger(x)(\{1\})\right\}\right] \\ &= (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \min \left\{\xi_0\frac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x), \xi_1\frac{d \nu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)\right\}\right] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Expand its Bayesian risk as a minimum of posterior probabilities.

nodes.name: Substitute the binary Bayesian inverse
nodes.statement: The last line is obtained by replacing $P_\xi^\dagger$ by its value (Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesInv_binary}).
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the binary Bayesian inverse.

nodes.name: Bayes binary risk via absolute difference
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, \nu) = \frac{1}{2}\left((P \circ \xi)(\mathcal X) - (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \left\vert \xi_0\frac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) - \xi_1\frac{d \nu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)\right\vert\right] \right) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: cor:bayesBinaryRisk_eq_abs

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Use Theorem~\ref{thm:bayesBinaryRisk_eq} and the equality $\min\{a,b\} = \frac{1}{2}(a + b - \vert a - b \vert)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the formula with $\min\{a,b\} = \frac{1}{2}(a+b-|a-b|)$.

nodes.name: Loss of the Bayes estimator is Bernoulli
nodes.statement: Let $\hat{y}_B$ be the generalized Bayes estimator for simple binary hypothesis testing. The distribution $\ell \circ (\mathrm{id} \parallel \hat{y}_B) \circ (\pi \otimes P)$ (in which $\ell$ stands for the associated deterministic kernel) is a Bernoulli with mean $\mathcal B_\pi(\mu, \nu)$.
assumptions: Let $\hat{y}_B$ be the generalized Bayes estimator for simple binary hypothesis testing.
conclusions: The distribution $\ell \circ (\mathrm{id} \parallel \hat{y}_B) \circ (\pi \otimes P)$ (in which $\ell$ stands for the associated deterministic kernel) is a Bernoulli with mean $\mathcal B_\pi(\mu, \nu)$
nodes.label: lem:bayesBinaryRisk_bernoulli

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: $\ell$ takes values in $\{0,1\}$ so the law has to be Bernoulli. It has mean $\mathcal B_\pi(\mu, \nu)$ because the expected risk of the generalized Bayes estimator is $\mathcal B_\pi(\mu, \nu)$.
nodes.statement_short: A {0,1}-valued law is Bernoulli, with mean the Bayes risk of the Bayes estimator.

nodes.name: Sample complexity
nodes.statement: In a sequence of estimation tasks $(P^{\otimes n}, y, \ell')$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the \emph{sample complexity} is the minimal $n$ such that the risk is less than a desired value.

nodes.name: Bayes risk is monotone in the number of samples
nodes.statement: If $n \le m$ then $\mathcal R_\pi^{P^{\otimes n}} \ge \mathcal R_\pi^{P^{\otimes m}}$.
assumptions: If $n \le m$
nodes.label: lem:bayesRisk_mono_prod

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Use the data-processing inequality, Theorem~\ref{thm:data_proc_bayesRisk}, for the deterministic kernel that projects on the first $n$ coordinates.
nodes.statement_short: DPI with the projection onto the first $n$ coordinates.

nodes.name: Sample complexity of Bayesian estimation
nodes.statement: The sample complexity of Bayesian estimation with respect to a prior $\pi \in \mathcal M(\Theta)$ at risk level $\delta \in \mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$ is \begin{align*} n_\pi^P(\delta) = \min \{n \in \mathbb{N} \mid \mathcal R_\pi^{P^{\otimes n}} \le \delta\} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:priorSampleComplexity

nodes.name: Conditional divergence (joint form)
nodes.statement: Another important concept is the \emph{conditional divergence} of two kernels $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ given a measure $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$. This is the value $D(\mu \otimes \kappa, \mu \otimes \eta)$.

nodes.name: Divergence
nodes.statement: A divergence between measures is a function $D$ which for any measurable space $\mathcal X$ and any two measures $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$, returns a value $D(\mu, \nu) \in \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$.
also_stated_at: A divergence between measures is a function which maps two measures on any common space $\mathcal X$ to a value in $[-\infty, +\infty]$.
nodes.label: def:div

nodes.name: Data-processing inequality (DPI)
nodes.statement:
A divergence $D$ is said to satisfy the data-processing inequality (DPI) if for all measurable spaces $\mathcal X, \mathcal Y$, all $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and all Markov kernels $\kappa : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$,  egin{align*} D(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \le D(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*}
also_stated_at: For a Markov kernel $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$~, a fundamental property of all divergences we will consider is the \emph{data-processing inequality}, which states that $D(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ \nu) \le D(\mu, \nu)$.
nodes.label: def:dpi

nodes.name: Second marginal
nodes.statement:
Let $D$ be a divergence that satisfies the DPI. Let $\mathcal \mu, 
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$. Then  egin{align*} D(\kappa \circ \mu, \eta \circ 
u) \le D(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \eta) \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $D$ be a divergence that satisfies the DPI.
Let $\mathcal \mu, \nu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$.
nodes.label: lem:div_comp_le_div_compProd

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Use the DPI for the deterministic kernel of the function $(x,y) \mapsto y$.
nodes.statement_short: DPI for the second projection.

nodes.name: First marginal
nodes.statement:
Let $D$ be a divergence that satisfies the DPI. Let $\mathcal \mu, 
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be Markov kernels. Then  egin{align*} D(\mu, 
u) \le D(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \eta) \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $D$ be a divergence that satisfies the DPI.
Let $\mathcal \mu, \nu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be Markov kernels.
nodes.label: lem:div_le_div_compProd

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Use the DPI for the deterministic kernel of the function $(x,y) \mapsto x$.
nodes.statement_short: DPI for the first projection.

nodes.name: Divergence of composition-products with a common kernel
nodes.statement:
Let $D$ be a divergence that satisfies the DPI. Let $\mathcal \mu, 
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and let $\kappa : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be a Markov kernel. Then  egin{align*} D(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \kappa) = D(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $D$ be a divergence that satisfies the DPI.
Let $\mathcal \mu, \nu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be a Markov kernel.
nodes.label: lem:div_compProd_right

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:div_le_div_compProd} gives one inequality. The other inequality is the DPI: $\mu \otimes \kappa = (\mathrm{id} \times \kappa) \circ \mu$.
nodes.statement_short: First-marginal lemma for one inequality, DPI for the kernel $\mathrm{id}\times\kappa$ for the other.

nodes.name: Conditional divergence
nodes.statement: Let $D$ be a divergence. The conditional divergence of kernels $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ with respect to a measure $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ is $\mu[x \mapsto D(\kappa(x), \eta(x)]$. It is denoted by $D(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu)$.
nodes.label: def:condDiv

nodes.name: Conditioning increases divergence
nodes.statement: Let $D$ be a divergence that satisfies the DPI and for which $D(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu) = D(\mu \otimes \kappa, \mu \otimes \eta)$. Let $\mathcal \mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be Markov kernels. Then \begin{align*} D(\kappa \circ \mu, \eta \circ \mu) \le D(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu) \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $D$ be a divergence that satisfies the DPI and for which $D(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu) = D(\mu \otimes \kappa, \mu \otimes \eta)$.
Let $\mathcal \mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be Markov kernels.
nodes.label: lem:div_comp_le_div_compProd_right

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: This is a special case of Lemma~\ref{lem:div_comp_le_div_compProd}.
nodes.statement_short: Special case of the second-marginal lemma.

nodes.name: Statistical information
nodes.statement:
The statistical information between measures $\mu$ and $
u$ with respect to prior $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$ is $\mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) = \min\{\xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X), \xi_1 
u(\mathcal X)\} - \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u)$. This is the risk increase $I_\xi^P(d_{\mathcal X})$ in the binary hypothesis testing problem for $d_{\mathcal X} : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow *$ the Markov kernel to the point space.
nodes.label: def:statInfo

nodes.name: Statistical information of a measure with itself
nodes.statement: For $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$, $\mathcal I_\xi(\mu, \mu) = 0$~.
assumptions: For $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$
nodes.label: lem:statInfo_self

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Use Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesBinaryRisk_self}.
nodes.statement_short: From the Bayes binary risk of a measure with itself.

nodes.name: Statistical information is nonnegative
nodes.statement: For $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$, $\mathcal I_\xi(\mu, \nu) \ge 0$~.
assumptions: For $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$
nodes.label: lem:statInfo_nonneg

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Use Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesBinaryRisk_le}.
nodes.statement_short: From the upper bound on the Bayes binary risk.

nodes.name: Upper bound on the statistical information
nodes.statement:
For $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$, $\mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) \le \min\{\xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X), \xi_1 
u(\mathcal X)\}$~.
assumptions: For $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$
nodes.label: lem:statInfo_le

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Use Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesBinaryRisk_nonneg}.
nodes.statement_short: From nonnegativity of the Bayes binary risk.

nodes.name: Symmetry of the statistical information
nodes.statement:
For $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$, $\mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) = \mathcal I_{\xi_\leftrightarrow}(
u, \mu)$~.
assumptions: For $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$
nodes.label: lem:statInfo_symm

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Use Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesBinaryRisk_symm}.
nodes.statement_short: From symmetry of the Bayes binary risk.

nodes.name: Data-processing inequality for the statistical information
nodes.statement:
For $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$, $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$ and $\kappa : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ a Markov kernel, $\mathcal I_\xi(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \le \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u)$~.
assumptions: For $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$, $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$ and $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ a Markov kernel
nodes.label: thm:data_proc_statInfo

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
Since $\kappa$ is a Markov kernel,  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) &= \min\{\xi_0(\kappa \circ \mu)(\mathcal X), \xi_1(\kappa \circ 
u)(\mathcal X)\} - \mathcal B_\xi(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \ &= \min\{\xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X), \xi_1 
u(\mathcal X)\} - \mathcal B_\xi(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \end{align*} It suffices to prove $\mathcal B_\xi(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \ge \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u)$ since $\mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) = \min\{\xi_0\mu(\mathcal X), \xi_1
u(\mathcal X)\} - \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u)$. The inequality was proved in Theorem~ef{thm:data_proc_bayesBinaryRisk}. Alternatively, we can use Lemma~ef{lem:riskIncrease_comp_del}.
nodes.statement_short: Masses are preserved by a Markov kernel, so reduce to the DPI for the Bayes binary risk.

nodes.name: Markov kernels preserve total mass
nodes.statement:
Since $\kappa$ is a Markov kernel,  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) &= \min\{\xi_0(\kappa \circ \mu)(\mathcal X), \xi_1(\kappa \circ 
u)(\mathcal X)\} - \mathcal B_\xi(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \ &= \min\{\xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X), \xi_1 
u(\mathcal X)\} - \mathcal B_\xi(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Markov kernels preserve total mass.

nodes.name: Reduce to the DPI for the Bayes binary risk
nodes.statement:
It suffices to prove $\mathcal B_\xi(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \ge \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u)$ since $\mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) = \min\{\xi_0\mu(\mathcal X), \xi_1
u(\mathcal X)\} - \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u)$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the DPI for the Bayes binary risk.

nodes.name: Apply the DPI for the Bayes binary risk
nodes.statement: The inequality was proved in Theorem~\ref{thm:data_proc_bayesBinaryRisk}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the DPI for the Bayes binary risk.

nodes.name: Alternative route via the risk-increase DPI
nodes.statement: Alternatively, we can use Lemma~\ref{lem:riskIncrease_comp_del}.
nodes.statement_short: Alternative route via the risk-increase DPI.

nodes.name: Statistical information data-processing for events
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$, $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$ and let $E$ be an event on $\mathcal X$. Let $\mu_E$ and $
u_E$ be the two Bernoulli distributions with respective means $\mu(E)$ and $
u(E)$. Then $\mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) \ge \mathcal I_\xi(\mu_E, 
u_E)$.
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$, $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$ and let $E$ be an event on $\mathcal X$.
Let $\mu_E$ and $\nu_E$ be the two Bernoulli distributions with respective means $\mu(E)$ and $\nu(E)$.
nodes.label: cor:statInfo_data_proc_event

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:data_proc_statInfo} to the deterministic kernel $\mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \{0,1\}$ given by the function $x \mapsto \mathbb{I}\{x \in E\}$.
nodes.statement_short: DPI with the indicator kernel of $E$.

nodes.name: Statistical information via a dominating measure
nodes.statement:
For finite measures $\mu, 
u$ and $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$, for any measure $\zeta$ with $\mu \ll \zeta$ and $
u \ll \zeta$~,  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= \min\{\xi_0\mu(\mathcal X), \xi_1
u(\mathcal X)\} - \zeta\left[x \mapsto \min \left\{\xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d\zeta}(x), \xi_1 rac{d 
u}{d\zeta}(x)ight\}ight] \: . \end{align*} This holds in particular for $\zeta = P \circ \xi$.
assumptions: For finite measures $\mu, \nu$ and $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$
for any measure $\zeta$ with $\mu \ll \zeta$ and $\nu \ll \zeta$
nodes.label: lem:statInfo_eq_sub_min

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:bayesBinaryRisk_eq} to get that result for $\zeta = P \circ \xi$. Then for other $\zeta$ with $\mu \ll \zeta$ and $\nu \ll \zeta$~, use $\frac{d \mu}{d\zeta} = \frac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)} / \frac{d (P \circ \xi)}{d\zeta}$~.
nodes.statement_short: Bayes binary risk formula for $\zeta = P\circ\xi$, then change of dominating measure via the chain rule for densities.

nodes.name: Statistical information as integral of absolute difference
nodes.statement:
For finite measures $\mu, 
u$ and $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$, for any measure $\zeta$ with $\mu \ll \zeta$ and $
u \ll \zeta$~,  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= -  rac{1}{2} \left\vert \xi_0\mu(\mathcal X) - \xi_1
u(\mathcal X) ight\vert +  rac{1}{2} \zeta\left[x \mapsto \left\vert \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d\zeta}(x) - \xi_1 rac{d 
u}{d\zeta}(x)ight\vertight] \: . \end{align*} This holds in particular for $\zeta = P \circ \xi$.
assumptions: For finite measures $\mu, \nu$ and $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$
for any measure $\zeta$ with $\mu \ll \zeta$ and $\nu \ll \zeta$
nodes.label: lem:statInfo_eq_integral_abs_sub

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Apply Corollary~\ref{cor:bayesBinaryRisk_eq_abs} and write $\min\{\xi_0\mu(\mathcal X), \xi_1\nu(\mathcal X)\} = \frac{1}{2}\left((P \circ \xi)(\mathcal X) - \left\vert \xi_0\mu(\mathcal X) - \xi_1\nu(\mathcal X) \right\vert \right)$ to get the result for $\zeta = P \circ \xi$. The result for other $\zeta$ follows from simple manipulations of Radon-Nikodym derivatives.
nodes.statement_short: Absolute-difference form of the Bayes binary risk, rewrite the minimum of masses, change dominating measure.

nodes.name: Integral form of the statistical information
nodes.statement:
For finite measures $\mu, 
u$ and $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$,  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= 
u\left[ x \mapsto \max \left\{0 , \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d
u}(x) - \xi_1 ight\} ight] + \xi_0 \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X) & 	ext{ if } \xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X) \le \xi_1 
u(\mathcal X) \: , \ \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= 
u\left[ x \mapsto \max \left\{0 , \xi_1 - \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d
u}(x) ight\} ight] & 	ext{ if } \xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X) \ge \xi_1 
u(\mathcal X) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Statistical information as an integral of a hockey-stick function of the density ratio plus a singular term.
assumptions: For finite measures $\mu, \nu$ and $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$
\text{ if } \xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X) \le \xi_1 \nu(\mathcal X)
\text{ if } \xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X) \ge \xi_1 \nu(\mathcal X)
\text{ if } \xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X) \le \xi_1 \nu(\mathcal X)
\text{ if } \xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X) \ge \xi_1 \nu(\mathcal X)

nodes.label: thm:statInfo_eq_integral

nodes.name: Statistical information is an f-divergence for probability measures
nodes.statement: For probability measures, this theorem makes the statistical information an $f$-divergence (which is defined later in this document).

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
By Theorem~ef{thm:bayesBinaryRisk_eq},  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= \min\{\xi_0\mu(\mathcal X), \xi_1
u(\mathcal X)\} - (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \min \left\{\xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x), \xi_1 rac{d 
u}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)ight\}ight] \: . \end{align*} Suppose that $\xi_0\mu(\mathcal X) \le \xi_1
u(\mathcal X)$~. Then  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= \xi_0\mu(\mathcal X) - (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) + \min \left\{0 , \xi_1 rac{d 
u}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) - \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)ight\}ight] \ &= - (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \min \left\{0 , \xi_1 rac{d 
u}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) - \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) ight\}ight] \ &= (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \max \left\{0 , \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) - \xi_1 rac{d 
u}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) ight\}ight] \ &= 
u\left[ x \mapsto \max \left\{0 , \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d
u}(x) - \xi_1 ight\} ight] + \xi_0 \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X) \: . \end{align*} If on the other hand $\xi_0\mu(\mathcal X) \ge \xi_1
u(\mathcal X)$~, with similar computations,  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \max \left\{0 , \xi_1 rac{d 
u}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) - \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) ight\}ight] \ &= 
u\left[ x \mapsto \max \left\{0 , \xi_1 - \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d
u}(x) ight\} ight] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Start from the Bayes binary risk formula and split on which weighted mass is smaller.

nodes.name: Express the statistical information via the Bayes binary risk formula
nodes.statement:
By Theorem~ef{thm:bayesBinaryRisk_eq},  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= \min\{\xi_0\mu(\mathcal X), \xi_1
u(\mathcal X)\} - (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \min \left\{\xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x), \xi_1 rac{d 
u}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)ight\}ight] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Express the statistical information via the Bayes binary risk formula.

nodes.name: Case of smaller weighted mass of $\mu$
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $\xi_0\mu(\mathcal X) \le \xi_1
u(\mathcal X)$~. Then  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= \xi_0\mu(\mathcal X) - (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) + \min \left\{0 , \xi_1 rac{d 
u}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) - \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x)ight\}ight] \ &= - (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \min \left\{0 , \xi_1 rac{d 
u}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) - \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) ight\}ight] \ &= (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \max \left\{0 , \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) - \xi_1 rac{d 
u}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) ight\}ight] \ &= 
u\left[ x \mapsto \max \left\{0 , \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d
u}(x) - \xi_1 ight\} ight] + \xi_0 \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Case of smaller weighted mass of $\mu$.

nodes.name: Symmetric case
nodes.statement:
If on the other hand $\xi_0\mu(\mathcal X) \ge \xi_1
u(\mathcal X)$~, with similar computations,  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= (P \circ \xi)\left[x \mapsto \max \left\{0 , \xi_1 rac{d 
u}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) - \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d(P \circ \xi)}(x) ight\}ight] \ &= 
u\left[ x \mapsto \max \left\{0 , \xi_1 - \xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d
u}(x) ight\} ight] \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Symmetric case.

nodes.name: Statistical information as integral of absolute value
nodes.statement:
For finite measures $\mu, 
u$ and $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$,  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= - rac{1}{2} \left\vert\xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X) - \xi_1 
u(\mathcal X)ight\vert +  rac{1}{2}\left( 
u\left[ x \mapsto \left\vert\xi_0 rac{d \mu}{d
u}(x) - \xi_1 ight\vert ight] + \xi_0 \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X)ight) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: cor:statInfo_eq_integral_abs

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Start from Theorem~\ref{thm:statInfo_eq_integral}, then use $\max\{a,b\} = \frac{1}{2}\left( a + b + \vert a - b \vert \right)$~. The two cases of Theorem~\ref{thm:statInfo_eq_integral} lead to the same expression.
nodes.statement_short: Use $\max\{a,b\} = \frac12(a+b+|a-b|)$ in both cases of the integral form.

nodes.name: Statistical information as infimum over events
nodes.statement:
For finite measures $\mu, 
u$ and $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$,  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= \min\{\xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X), \xi_1 
u(\mathcal X)\} - \inf_{E 	ext{ event}} \left( \xi_0 \mu(E) + \xi_1 
u(E^c) ight) \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: For finite measures $\mu, \nu$ and $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$
nodes.label: lem:statInfo_eq_sub_inf_event

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: This is a direct application of Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesBinaryRisk_eq_event}.
nodes.statement_short: Direct from the event form of the Bayes binary risk.

nodes.name: Statistical information as supremum over events
nodes.statement:
For finite measures $\mu, 
u$ and $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$,  egin{align*} \mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= - \max\{0, \xi_1 
u(\mathcal X) - \xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X) \} + \sup_{E 	ext{ event}} \left( \xi_1 
u(E) - \xi_0 \mu(E) ight) \ &= - \max\{0, \xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X) - \xi_1 
u(\mathcal X) \} + \sup_{E 	ext{ event}} \left( \xi_0 \mu(E) - \xi_1 
u(E) ight) \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: For finite measures $\mu, \nu$ and $\xi \in \mathcal M(\{0,1\})$
conclusions:
\mathcal I_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= - \max\{0, \xi_1 
u(\mathcal X) - \xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X) \} + \sup_{E 	ext{ event}} \left( \xi_1 
u(E) - \xi_0 \mu(E) ight) \ &= - \max\{0, \xi_0 \mu(\mathcal X) - \xi_1 
u(\mathcal X) \} + \sup_{E 	ext{ event}} \left( \xi_0 \mu(E) - \xi_1 
u(E) ight)
nodes.label: lem:statInfo_eq_sup_event

nodes.name: DeGroot statistical information
nodes.statement:
The DeGroot statistical information between finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ for $\pi \in [0,1]$ is $I_\pi (\mu, 
u) = \mathcal I_{(\pi, 1 - \pi)}(\mu, 
u)$~.
nodes.label: def:deGrootInfo

nodes.name: E_gamma (hockey-stick) divergence
nodes.statement:
The $E_\gamma$ or hockey-stick divergence between finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ for $\gamma \in (0,+\infty)$ is $E_\gamma(\mu, 
u) = \mathcal I_{(1,\gamma)}(\mu, 
u)$~.
nodes.label: def:eGamma

nodes.name: Total variation distance
nodes.statement:
The total variation distance between finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ is $\TV(\mu, 
u) = \mathcal I_{(1,1)}(\mu, 
u)$~.
nodes.label: def:TV

nodes.name: TV equals twice DeGroot information at 1/2 and E_1
nodes.statement: This is also equal to $2 I_{1/2}(\mu, \nu)$ and to $E_1(\mu, \nu)$.

nodes.name: TV of a measure with itself
nodes.statement: For $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$, $\TV(\mu, \mu) = 0$~.
assumptions: For $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$
nodes.label: lem:tv_self

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Use Lemma~\ref{lem:statInfo_self}.
nodes.statement_short: Special case of the statistical-information lemma.

nodes.name: TV is nonnegative
nodes.statement: For $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$, $\TV(\mu, \nu) \ge 0$~.
assumptions: For $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$
nodes.label: lem:tv_nonneg

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Use Lemma~\ref{lem:statInfo_nonneg}.
nodes.statement_short: Special case of nonnegativity of the statistical information.

nodes.name: Upper bound on TV
nodes.statement:
For $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$, $\TV(\mu, 
u) \le \min\{\mu(\mathcal X), 
u(\mathcal X)\}$~.
assumptions: For $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$
nodes.label: lem:tv_le

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Use Lemma~\ref{lem:statInfo_le}.
nodes.statement_short: Special case of the statistical-information upper bound.

nodes.name: Data-processing inequality for TV
nodes.statement:
For $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and $\kappa : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ a Markov kernel, $\TV(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \le \TV(\mu, 
u)$~.
assumptions: For $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ a Markov kernel
nodes.label: thm:tv_data_proc

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:data_proc_statInfo}.
nodes.statement_short: Special case of the DPI for the statistical information.

nodes.name: TV via a dominating measure
nodes.statement:
For finite measures $\mu, 
u$, for any measure $\zeta$ with $\mu \ll \zeta$ and $
u \ll \zeta$~,  egin{align*} \TV(\mu, 
u) &= \min\{\mu(\mathcal X), 
u(\mathcal X)\} - \zeta\left[x \mapsto \min \left\{ rac{d \mu}{d\zeta}(x),  rac{d 
u}{d\zeta}(x)ight\}ight] \: . \end{align*} This holds in particular for $\zeta = P \circ \xi$.
assumptions: For finite measures $\mu, \nu$
for any measure $\zeta$ with $\mu \ll \zeta$ and $\nu \ll \zeta$
nodes.label: lem:tv_eq_sub_min

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:statInfo_eq_sub_min}.
nodes.statement_short: Special case of the statistical-information formula.

nodes.name: TV as integral of absolute difference of densities
nodes.statement:
For finite measures $\mu, 
u$, for any measure $\zeta$ with $\mu \ll \zeta$ and $
u \ll \zeta$~,  egin{align*} \TV(\mu, 
u) &= -  rac{1}{2} \left\vert \mu(\mathcal X) - 
u(\mathcal X) ight\vert +  rac{1}{2} \zeta\left[x \mapsto \left\vert  rac{d \mu}{d\zeta}(x) -  rac{d 
u}{d\zeta}(x)ight\vertight] \: . \end{align*} This holds in particular for $\zeta = P \circ \xi$.
assumptions: For finite measures $\mu, \nu$
for any measure $\zeta$ with $\mu \ll \zeta$ and $\nu \ll \zeta$
nodes.label: lem:tv_eq_integral_abs_sub

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:statInfo_eq_integral_abs_sub}.
nodes.statement_short: Special case of the statistical-information formula.

nodes.name: Integral form of the total variation distance
nodes.statement:
For finite measures $\mu, 
u$,  egin{align*} \TV(\mu, 
u) &= 
u\left[ x \mapsto \max \left\{0 ,  rac{d \mu}{d
u}(x) - 1 ight\} ight] + \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X) & 	ext{ if } \mu(\mathcal X) \le 
u(\mathcal X) \: , \ \TV(\mu, 
u) &= 
u\left[ x \mapsto \max \left\{0 , 1 -  rac{d \mu}{d
u}(x) ight\} ight] & 	ext{ if } \mu(\mathcal X) \ge 
u(\mathcal X) \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: For finite measures $\mu, \nu$
nodes.label: lem:tv_eq_integral

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:statInfo_eq_integral}.
nodes.statement_short: Special case of the integral form of the statistical information.

nodes.name: TV as integral of absolute value
nodes.statement:
For finite measures $\mu, 
u$,  egin{align*} \TV(\mu, 
u) &= - rac{1}{2} \left\vert \mu(\mathcal X) - 
u(\mathcal X)ight\vert +  rac{1}{2}\left( 
u\left[ x \mapsto \left\vert  rac{d \mu}{d
u}(x) - 1 ight\vert ight] + \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X)ight) \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: For finite measures $\mu, \nu$
nodes.label: lem:tv_eq_integral_abs

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Apply Corollary~\ref{cor:statInfo_eq_integral_abs}.
nodes.statement_short: Special case of the statistical-information corollary.

nodes.name: TV as infimum over events
nodes.statement:
For finite measures $\mu, 
u$,  egin{align*} \TV(\mu, 
u) &= \min\{\mu(\mathcal X), 
u(\mathcal X)\} - \inf_{E 	ext{ event}} \left( \mu(E) + 
u(E^c) ight) \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: For finite measures $\mu, \nu$
nodes.label: lem:tv_eq_sub_inf_event

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:statInfo_eq_sub_inf_event}.
nodes.statement_short: Special case of the statistical-information event formula.

nodes.name: TV as supremum over events
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ with $\mu(\mathcal X) \leq 
u(\mathcal X)$.\ Then $TV(\mu, 
u) = \sup_{E 	ext{ event}} \left( \mu(E) - 
u(E) ight)$.
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ with $\mu(\mathcal X) \leq \nu(\mathcal X)$.
nodes.label: thm:tv_eq_sup_sub_measure

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
Starting from Lemma~ef{lem:tv_eq_sub_inf_event},  egin{align*} \TV(\mu, 
u) &= \min\{\mu(\mathcal X), 
u(\mathcal X)\} - \inf_{E 	ext{ event}} \left( \mu(E) + 
u(E^c) ight) \ &= \mu(\mathcal X) - \inf_{E 	ext{ event}} \left( \mu(E^c) + 
u(E) ight) \ &= \mu(\mathcal X) - \mu(\mathcal X) - \inf_{E 	ext{ event}} \left( -\mu(E) + 
u(E) ight) \ &= \sup_{E 	ext{ event}} \left( \mu(E) - 
u(E) ight) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the event-infimum formula by complementing events.

nodes.name: TV bounds the supremum over bounded functions
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal F = \{f : \mathcal X 	o \mathbb{R} \mid \Vert f \Vert_\infty \le 1\}$. Then for $\mu, 
u$ finite measures with $\mu(\mathcal X) = 
u(\mathcal X)$, $ rac{1}{2} \sup_{f \in \mathcal F} \left( \mu[f] - 
u[f] ight) \le \TV(\mu, 
u)$.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal F = \{f : \mathcal X \to \mathbb{R} \mid \Vert f \Vert_\infty \le 1\}$.
for $\mu, \nu$ finite measures with $\mu(\mathcal X) = \nu(\mathcal X)$
nodes.label: lem:tv_eq_sup_aux

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
Let $p,q$ be the respective densities of $\mu, 
u$ with respect to $\xi=\mu+
u$. For any $f \in \mathcal F$,  egin{align*} \mu[f] - 
u[f] = \int_x f(x)(p(x) - q(x)) \partial\xi &\le \int_x \Vert f(x) \Vert_\infty \vert p(x) - q(x) \vert \partial\xi \ &\le \int_x \vert p(x) - q(x) \vert \partial\xi = 2 \TV(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*} The last equality is Lemma~ef{lem:tv_eq_integral_abs_sub}.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\mu[f]-\nu[f]$ by the $L^1$ distance of densities, which is twice TV.

nodes.name: Introduce densities and bound the integral of $f(p-q)$ by $\int|p-q|$
nodes.statement:
Let $p,q$ be the respective densities of $\mu, 
u$ with respect to $\xi=\mu+
u$. For any $f \in \mathcal F$,  egin{align*} \mu[f] - 
u[f] = \int_x f(x)(p(x) - q(x)) \partial\xi &\le \int_x \Vert f(x) \Vert_\infty \vert p(x) - q(x) \vert \partial\xi \ &\le \int_x \vert p(x) - q(x) \vert \partial\xi = 2 \TV(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Introduce densities and bound the integral of $f(p-q)$ by $\int|p-q|$.

nodes.name: Identify $\int|p-q|$ with $2\TV$
nodes.statement: The last equality is Lemma~\ref{lem:tv_eq_integral_abs_sub}.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $\int|p-q|$ with $2\TV$.

nodes.name: TV as supremum over bounded functions
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal F = \{f : \mathcal X 	o \mathbb{R} \mid \Vert f \Vert_\infty \le 1\}$. Then for $\mu, 
u$ finite measures with $\mu(\mathcal X) = 
u(\mathcal X)$, $\TV(\mu, 
u) =  rac{1}{2} \sup_{f \in \mathcal F} \left( \mu[f] - 
u[f] ight)$.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal F = \{f : \mathcal X \to \mathbb{R} \mid \Vert f \Vert_\infty \le 1\}$.
for $\mu, \nu$ finite measures with $\mu(\mathcal X) = \nu(\mathcal X)$
nodes.label: thm:tv_eq_sup_sub_integral

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:tv_eq_sup_aux} gives $\TV(\mu, \nu) \ge \frac{1}{2} \sup_{f \in \mathcal F} \left( \mu[f] - \nu[f] \right)$. The bayes estimator is a function of the form $x \mapsto \mathbb{I}\{x \in E\}$ for some event $E$, hence it belongs to $\mathcal F$. This gives equality.
nodes.statement_short: One inequality from the auxiliary lemma; the indicator Bayes estimator attains it.

nodes.name: Lower bound from the auxiliary lemma
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:tv_eq_sup_aux} gives $\TV(\mu, \nu) \ge \frac{1}{2} \sup_{f \in \mathcal F} \left( \mu[f] - \nu[f] \right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound from the auxiliary lemma.

nodes.name: The indicator Bayes estimator gives equality
nodes.statement: The bayes estimator is a function of the form $x \mapsto \mathbb{I}\{x \in E\}$ for some event $E$, hence it belongs to $\mathcal F$. This gives equality.
nodes.statement_short: The indicator Bayes estimator gives equality.

nodes.name: TV data-processing for events
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $E$ be an event. Let $\mu_E$ and $
u_E$ be the two Bernoulli distributions with respective means $\mu(E)$ and $
u(E)$. Then $\TV(\mu, 
u) \ge \TV(\mu_E, 
u_E)$.
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $E$ be an event.
Let $\mu_E$ and $\nu_E$ be the two Bernoulli distributions with respective means $\mu(E)$ and $\nu(E)$.
nodes.label: lem:tv_data_proc_event

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Apply Corollary~\ref{cor:statInfo_data_proc_event}.
nodes.statement_short: Special case of the statistical-information event corollary.

nodes.name: Divergence functions are measurable, continuous and convex
nodes.statement: Everywhere in this document, the functions used in divergences are assumed measurable, continuous and convex on $[0, +\infty)$.

nodes.name: Slope at infinity
nodes.statement: For such a function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, we write $f'(\infty) = \lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x)/x$ (which can be infinite).

nodes.name: f-divergence
nodes.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R} 	o \mathbb{R}$ and let $\mu, 
u$ be two measures on a measurable space $\mathcal X$. The f-divergence between $\mu$ and $
u$ is  egin{align*} D_f(\mu, 
u) = 
u\left[x \mapsto f\left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)ight)ight] + f'(\infty) \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X) \end{align*} if $x \mapsto f\left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)ight)$ is $
u$-integrable and $+\infty$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Integral of $f$ of the density ratio plus $f'(\infty)$ times the singular mass; $+\infty$ if not integrable.
nodes.label: def:fDiv

nodes.name: Finiteness criterion for f-divergences
nodes.statement:
For $\mu$ and $
u$ two finite measures, $D_f(\mu, 
u)$ is finite if and only if $x \mapsto f\left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)ight)$ is $
u$-integrable and either $f'(\infty) < \infty$ or $\mu \ll 
u$.
assumptions: For $\mu$ and $\nu$ two finite measures
conclusions:
$D_f(\mu, 
u)$ is finite if and only if $x \mapsto f\left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)ight)$ is $
u$-integrable and either $f'(\infty) < \infty$ or $\mu \ll 
u$
nodes.label: lem:fDiv_ne_top_iff

nodes.name: f-divergence of a constant function
nodes.statement:
For $
u$ a finite measure, for all $a \in \mathbb{R}$, $D_{x \mapsto a}(\mu, 
u) = a 
u(\mathcal X)$.
assumptions: For $\nu$ a finite measure
for all $a \in \mathbb{R}$
nodes.label: lem:fDiv_const

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Compute the integral.
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation of the integral.

nodes.name: f-divergence of a measure with itself
nodes.label: lem:fDiv_self

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: $\frac{d \mu}{d \mu}(x) = 1$ almost everywhere and $f(1) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: The self density is 1 a.e. and $f(1)=0$.

nodes.name: f-divergence vanishes iff measures are equal
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures. Assume that $f$ is strictly convex on $(0, +\infty)$ and $f(1) = 0$. Then $D_f(\mu, 
u) = 0$ if and only if $\mu = 
u$.
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two finite measures.
Assume that $f$ is strictly convex on $(0, +\infty)$ and $f(1) = 0$.
nodes.label: lem:fDiv_eq_zero_iff

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
If $\mu = 
u$ then $D_f(\mu, 
u) = 0$ by Lemma~ef{lem:fDiv_self}. For the other direction, since $f \ge 0$ is strictly convex with $f(1) = 0$, $f(x) = 0$ only for $x = 1$, and $f'(\infty) > 0$ (since $f(2) \le 2 f'(\infty)$ and $f(2) > 0$). $D_f(\mu, 
u) = 0$ then implies $\mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X) = 0$, hence $\mu \ll 
u$, and $f( rac{d\mu}{d
u}) = 0$ $
u$-almost everywhere, hence $ rac{d\mu}{d
u} = 1$ $
u$-almost everywhere.
nodes.statement_short: Self-divergence lemma for one direction; strict convexity forces zero singular part and density ratio 1.

nodes.name: Easy direction from the self-divergence lemma
nodes.statement: If $\mu = \nu$ then $D_f(\mu, \nu) = 0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:fDiv_self}.
nodes.statement_short: Easy direction from the self-divergence lemma.

nodes.name: Strict convexity forces zero singular part and density ratio 1 a.e
nodes.statement:
For the other direction, since $f \ge 0$ is strictly convex with $f(1) = 0$, $f(x) = 0$ only for $x = 1$, and $f'(\infty) > 0$ (since $f(2) \le 2 f'(\infty)$ and $f(2) > 0$). $D_f(\mu, 
u) = 0$ then implies $\mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X) = 0$, hence $\mu \ll 
u$, and $f( rac{d\mu}{d
u}) = 0$ $
u$-almost everywhere, hence $ rac{d\mu}{d
u} = 1$ $
u$-almost everywhere.
nodes.statement_short: Strict convexity forces zero singular part and density ratio 1 a.e.

nodes.name: f-divergence of the identity function
nodes.statement: $D_{x \mapsto x}(\mu, \nu) = \mu(\mathcal X)$.
nodes.label: lem:fDiv_id

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
Compute the integral: its value is $( rac{d\mu}{d
u}\cdot 
u)(\mathcal X)$. Then $D_{x\mapsto x}(\mu, 
u) = ( rac{d\mu}{d
u}\cdot 
u)(\mathcal X) + \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X) = \mu (\mathcal X)$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the integral and add the singular mass.
