nodes.statement_short: Convexity, the absolutely continuous case, and the decomposition lemma.

nodes.name: Nonnegativity of f-divergences
nodes.statement: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two probability measures. If $f(1) = 0$ then $D_f(\mu, \nu) \ge 0$.
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two probability measures.
nodes.label: lem:fDiv_nonneg

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:le_fDiv} and use $f(\mu(\mathcal X)) = f(1) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Jensen lower bound with $f(1)=0$.

nodes.name: Conditional f-divergence
nodes.statement: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $\mu$ a measure on $\mathcal X$ and $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ two Markov kernels from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$. The conditional f-divergence between $\kappa$ and $\eta$ with respect to $\mu$ is \begin{align*} D_f(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu) = \mu\left[x \mapsto D_f(\kappa(x), \eta(x))\right] \end{align*} if $x \mapsto D_f(\kappa(x), \eta(x))$ is $\mu$-integrable and $+\infty$ otherwise.
nodes.label: def:condFDiv

nodes.name: Conditional f-divergence is nonnegative
nodes.statement: Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\mathcal X$ and $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ two Markov kernels. If $f(1) = 0$ then $D_f(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu) \ge 0$.
assumptions: Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\mathcal X$ and $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ two Markov kernels.
nodes.label: lem:condFDiv_nonneg

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:fDiv_nonneg}.
nodes.statement_short: Pointwise nonnegativity of the f-divergence.

nodes.name: Conditional f-divergence of constant kernels
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be measures on $\mathcal X$, where $\mu$ is finite, and let $\xi$ be a finite measure on $\mathcal Y$. Then $D_f(x \mapsto \mu, x \mapsto 
u \mid \xi) = D_f(\mu, 
u) \xi (\mathcal X)$.
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be measures on $\mathcal X$, where $\mu$ is finite, and let $\xi$ be a finite measure on $\mathcal Y$.
nodes.label: lem:condFDiv_const

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
$$D_f(x \mapsto \mu, x \mapsto 
u \mid \xi) = \xi\left[x \mapsto D_f(\mu, 
u)ight] = D_f(\mu, 
u) \xi\left[1ight] = D_f(\mu, 
u) \xi (\mathcal X)$$
nodes.statement_short: Integrate a constant.

nodes.name: Integrability of f of the composition-product density
nodes.statement: Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\mathcal X$ and $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two finite kernels from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$. Then $p \mapsto f \left(\frac{d(\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d(\mu \otimes \eta)}(p)\right)$ is $(\mu \otimes \eta)$-integrable iff \begin{itemize} \item $x \mapsto D_f(\kappa(x), \eta(x))$ is $\mu$-integrable and \item for $\mu$-almost all $x$, $y \mapsto f \left( \frac{d\kappa(x)}{d\eta(x)}(y) \right)$ is $\eta(x)$-integrable. \end{itemize}
assumptions: Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\mathcal X$ and $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two finite kernels from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$.
conclusions: Then $p \mapsto f \left(\frac{d(\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d(\mu \otimes \eta)}(p)\right)$ is $(\mu \otimes \eta)$-integrable iff \begin{itemize} \item $x \mapsto D_f(\kappa(x), \eta(x))$ is $\mu$-integrable and \item for $\mu$-almost all $x$, $y \mapsto f \left( \frac{d\kappa(x)}{d\eta(x)}(y) \right)$ is $\eta(x)$-integrable.
equivalent_conditions: $x \mapsto D_f(\kappa(x), \eta(x))$ is $\mu$-integrable and \item for $\mu$-almost all $x$, $y \mapsto f \left( \frac{d\kappa(x)}{d\eta(x)}(y) \right)$ is $\eta(x)$-integrable.
nodes.label: lem:integrable_fDiv_compProd_iff

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Since $x \mapsto f \left(\frac{d(\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d(\mu \otimes \eta)} x \right)$ is measurable, the integrability condition w.r.t. $\mu \otimes \eta$ is equivalent to \begin{itemize} \item $x \mapsto \int_y \left\Vert f \left( \frac{d\kappa(x)}{d\eta(x)}(y) \right) \right\Vert \partial \eta(x)$ is $\mu$-integrable and \item for $\mu$-almost all $x$, $y \mapsto f \left( \frac{d\kappa(x)}{d\eta(x)}(y) \right)$ is $\eta(x)$-integrable. \end{itemize} It suffices to use convexity to show that integrability of $x \mapsto \int_y f \left( \frac{d\kappa(x)}{d\eta(x)}(y) \right) \partial \eta(x)$ implies integrability of $x \mapsto \int_y \left\Vert f \left( \frac{d\kappa(x)}{d\eta(x)}(y) \right) \right\Vert \partial \eta(x)$. TODO
nodes.statement_short: Integrability on a product splits into iterated integrability; convexity handles the absolute value (incomplete, TODO).

nodes.name: Finiteness criterion for the conditional f-divergence
nodes.statement: Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two finite kernels, where $\kappa$ is a Markov kernel. Then $D_f(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu) \ne \infty$ if and only if \begin{itemize} \item for $\mu$-almost all $x$, $y \mapsto f \left( \frac{d\kappa(x)}{d\eta(x)}(y) \right)$ is $\eta(x)$-integrable, \item $x \mapsto \int_y f \left( \frac{d\kappa(x)}{d\eta(x)}(y) \right) \partial \eta(x)$ is $\mu$-integrable, \item either $f'(\infty) < \infty$ or for $\mu$-almost all $x$, $\kappa(x) \ll \eta(x)$. \end{itemize}
assumptions: Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two finite kernels, where $\kappa$ is a Markov kernel.
conclusions: Then $D_f(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu) \ne \infty$ if and only if \begin{itemize} \item for $\mu$-almost all $x$, $y \mapsto f \left( \frac{d\kappa(x)}{d\eta(x)}(y) \right)$ is $\eta(x)$-integrable, \item $x \mapsto \int_y f \left( \frac{d\kappa(x)}{d\eta(x)}(y) \right) \partial \eta(x)$ is $\mu$-integrable, \item either $f'(\infty) < \infty$ or for $\mu$-almost all $x$, $\kappa(x) \ll \eta(x)$.
equivalent_conditions: for $\mu$-almost all $x$, $y \mapsto f \left( \frac{d\kappa(x)}{d\eta(x)}(y) \right)$ is $\eta(x)$-integrable, \item $x \mapsto \int_y f \left( \frac{d\kappa(x)}{d\eta(x)}(y) \right) \partial \eta(x)$ is $\mu$-integrable, \item either $f'(\infty) < \infty$ or for $\mu$-almost all $x$, $\kappa(x) \ll \eta(x)$.
nodes.label: lem:condFDiv_ne_top_iff

nodes.name: Finiteness of f-divergence of composition-products
nodes.statement: Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two finite kernels. Then $D_f(\mu \otimes \kappa, \mu \otimes \eta) \ne \infty \iff D_f(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu) \ne \infty$.
assumptions: Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two finite kernels.
nodes.label: lem:fDiv_compProd_ne_top_iff

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Immediate from Lemma~\ref{lem:fDiv_compProd_right}.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the composition-product equality.

nodes.name: f-divergence of composition-products equals conditional f-divergence
nodes.statement: Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two finite kernels. Then $D_f(\mu \otimes \kappa, \mu \otimes \eta) = D_f(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu)$.
assumptions: Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two finite kernels.
nodes.label: lem:fDiv_compProd_right

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The singular part of $\mu \otimes \kappa$ with respect to $\mu \otimes \eta$ is $\mu \otimes \kappa_{\perp \eta}$, hence $(\mu \otimes \kappa)_{\perp (\mu \otimes \eta)}(\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y) = \mu\left[x \mapsto \kappa(x)_{\perp \eta(x)}(\mathcal Y)\right]$. For the integral part, by Lemma~\ref{cor:rnDeriv_compProd_right} and Corollary~\ref{cor:rnDeriv_value}, \begin{align*} \int_{p} f\left(\frac{d (\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d (\mu \otimes \eta)}(p)\right) \partial(\mu \otimes \eta) &= \int_{p} f\left(\frac{d \kappa}{d \eta}(p)\right) \partial(\mu \otimes \eta) \\ &= \int_x \int_y f\left(\frac{d \kappa}{d \eta}(x, y)\right) \partial \eta(x) \partial \mu \\ &= \int_x \int_y f\left(\frac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y)\right) \partial \eta(x) \partial \mu \: . \end{align*} Adding $f'(\infty)$ times the singular parts gives $D_f(\mu \otimes \kappa, \mu \otimes \eta) = \mu\left[D_f(\kappa(x), \eta(x))\right] = D_f(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu)$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the singular part and the integral part separately using kernel Radon-Nikodym derivatives.

nodes.name: Singular part of the composition-product
nodes.statement: The singular part of $\mu \otimes \kappa$ with respect to $\mu \otimes \eta$ is $\mu \otimes \kappa_{\perp \eta}$, hence $(\mu \otimes \kappa)_{\perp (\mu \otimes \eta)}(\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y) = \mu\left[x \mapsto \kappa(x)_{\perp \eta(x)}(\mathcal Y)\right]$.
nodes.statement_short: Singular part of the composition-product.

nodes.name: Integral part via the kernel Radon-Nikodym derivative and Fubini
nodes.statement: For the integral part, by Lemma~\ref{cor:rnDeriv_compProd_right} and Corollary~\ref{cor:rnDeriv_value}, \begin{align*} \int_{p} f\left(\frac{d (\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d (\mu \otimes \eta)}(p)\right) \partial(\mu \otimes \eta) &= \int_{p} f\left(\frac{d \kappa}{d \eta}(p)\right) \partial(\mu \otimes \eta) \\ &= \int_x \int_y f\left(\frac{d \kappa}{d \eta}(x, y)\right) \partial \eta(x) \partial \mu \\ &= \int_x \int_y f\left(\frac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y)\right) \partial \eta(x) \partial \mu \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Integral part via the kernel Radon-Nikodym derivative and Fubini.

nodes.name: Combine the two parts
nodes.statement: Adding $f'(\infty)$ times the singular parts gives $D_f(\mu \otimes \kappa, \mu \otimes \eta) = \mu\left[D_f(\kappa(x), \eta(x))\right] = D_f(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu)$.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the two parts.

nodes.name: Curvature measure
nodes.statement: Let $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a convex function. Then its right derivative $f'_+(x) \coloneqq \lim_{y \downarrow x}\frac{f(y) - f(x)}{y - x}$ is a Stieltjes function (a monotone right continuous function) and it defines a measure $\gamma_f$ on $\mathbb{R}$ by $\gamma_f((x,y]) \coloneqq f'_+(y) - f'_+(x)$~. \cite{liese2012phi} calls $\gamma_f$ the curvature measure of $f$.
nodes.label: def:curvatureMeasure

nodes.name: Curvature measure of a scaled function
nodes.statement: For $a > 0$ and $f$ a convex function, the curvature measure of $af$ is $\gamma_{af} = a \gamma_f$~.
assumptions: For $a > 0$ and $f$ a convex function
conclusions: the curvature measure of $af$ is $\gamma_{af} = a \gamma_f$
nodes.label: lem:curvatureMeasure_mul

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The right derivative of $af$ is $a f'_+$ (with values in $[-\infty, +\infty]$), hence $\gamma_{af}((x,y]) = a f'_+(y) - a f'_+(x) = a \gamma_f((x,y])$. The equality of the measures is obtained at the level of the outer measures, which are built from these interval lengths. For $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, the case $a = 0$ is trivial. It fails in the Lean formalization, where the right derivative is $-\infty$ to the left of the domain of $f$: $0 \cdot f$ is the zero function on $[0, +\infty)$, whose right derivative jumps from $-\infty$ to $0$ at $0$, so that $\gamma_{0 \cdot f}$ has an infinite atom at $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Right derivative scales by $a$, so interval masses scale; extend via outer measures. Remark on the case $a=0$ in Lean.

nodes.name: Interval masses scale by $a$, hence the measures agree
nodes.statement: The right derivative of $af$ is $a f'_+$ (with values in $[-\infty, +\infty]$), hence $\gamma_{af}((x,y]) = a f'_+(y) - a f'_+(x) = a \gamma_f((x,y])$. The equality of the measures is obtained at the level of the outer measures, which are built from these interval lengths.
nodes.statement_short: Interval masses scale by $a$, hence the measures agree.

nodes.name: Remark on the degenerate case $a=0$ in Lean
nodes.statement: For $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, the case $a = 0$ is trivial. It fails in the Lean formalization, where the right derivative is $-\infty$ to the left of the domain of $f$: $0 \cdot f$ is the zero function on $[0, +\infty)$, whose right derivative jumps from $-\infty$ to $0$ at $0$, so that $\gamma_{0 \cdot f}$ has an infinite atom at $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Remark on the degenerate case $a=0$ in Lean.

nodes.name: Curvature measure of a sum
nodes.statement: Let $f,g$ be two convex functions whose effective domains have the same endpoints $a \le b$, and such that the right derivatives $f'_+$ and $g'_+$ either both tend to $-\infty$ at $a$ or both have a finite limit at $a$. Then the curvature measure of $f+g$ is $\gamma_{f+g} = \gamma_f + \gamma_g$~. In particular, this holds for $f,g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ two convex functions.
assumptions: Let $f,g$ be two convex functions whose effective domains have the same endpoints $a \le b$, and such that the right derivatives $f'_+$ and $g'_+$ either both tend to $-\infty$ at $a$ or both have a finite limit at $a$.
conclusions: Then the curvature measure of $f+g$ is $\gamma_{f+g} = \gamma_f + \gamma_g$~.
In particular, this holds for $f,g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ two convex functions.
nodes.label: lem:curvatureMeasure_add

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The right derivative of $f+g$ is $f'_+ + g'_+$, seen as functions with values in $[-\infty, +\infty]$ ($-\infty$ below the domain, $+\infty$ above it). By the assumptions, $f'_+$ and $g'_+$ are equal to $-\infty$ at the same points and equal to $+\infty$ at the same points. On the region where both are finite, $\gamma_{f+g}((x,y]) = \gamma_f((x,y]) + \gamma_g((x,y])$. The region where $f'_+$ and $g'_+$ are $-\infty$, and the region above the first point where they are $+\infty$, are null for the three measures. At $a$ and $b$, the three measures have the same atoms (equal to $0$ or $+\infty$). The assumption at $a$ is needed: if $f'_+(x) \to -\infty$ as $x \downarrow a$ but $g'_+$ has a finite limit at $a$, then $\gamma_g$ has an infinite atom at $a$ but $\gamma_{f+g}$ does not.
nodes.statement_short: Right derivatives add; compare the measures on the finite region, the infinite regions and the endpoint atoms.

nodes.name: Right derivative of the sum, with extended values
nodes.statement: The right derivative of $f+g$ is $f'_+ + g'_+$, seen as functions with values in $[-\infty, +\infty]$ ($-\infty$ below the domain, $+\infty$ above it).
nodes.statement_short: Right derivative of the sum, with extended values.

nodes.name: Infinite values occur at the same points
nodes.statement: By the assumptions, $f'_+$ and $g'_+$ are equal to $-\infty$ at the same points and equal to $+\infty$ at the same points.
nodes.statement_short: Infinite values occur at the same points.

nodes.name: Interval masses add where finite
nodes.statement: On the region where both are finite, $\gamma_{f+g}((x,y]) = \gamma_f((x,y]) + \gamma_g((x,y])$.
nodes.statement_short: Interval masses add where finite.

nodes.name: Infinite regions are null for all three measures
nodes.statement: The region where $f'_+$ and $g'_+$ are $-\infty$, and the region above the first point where they are $+\infty$, are null for the three measures.
nodes.statement_short: Infinite regions are null for all three measures.

nodes.name: Endpoint atoms agree
nodes.statement: At $a$ and $b$, the three measures have the same atoms (equal to $0$ or $+\infty$).
nodes.statement_short: Endpoint atoms agree.

nodes.name: Counterexample showing the assumption at $a$ is needed
nodes.statement: The assumption at $a$ is needed: if $f'_+(x) \to -\infty$ as $x \downarrow a$ but $g'_+$ has a finite limit at $a$, then $\gamma_g$ has an infinite atom at $a$ but $\gamma_{f+g}$ does not.
nodes.statement_short: Counterexample showing the assumption at $a$ is needed.

nodes.name: Integration by parts for Stieltjes functions
nodes.statement: If $f$ and $g$ are two Stieltjes functions with associated measures $\mu_f$ and $\mu_g$ and $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, then \begin{align*} \int_x f(x) \partial\mu_g = f(b)g(b) - f(a)g(a) - \int_x g(x) \partial\mu_f \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: If $f$ and $g$ are two Stieltjes functions with associated measures $\mu_f$ and $\mu_g$ and $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$
nodes.label: thm:integration_by_parts

nodes.name: Taylor formula with integral remainder for convex functions
nodes.statement: (In Lean, this is proved for a \texttt{DivFunction} and $x = 1$, by the fundamental theorem of calculus and Tonelli's theorem, without integration by parts.) For $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ a convex function and $x,y \in \mathbb{R}$, \begin{align*} f(y) - f(x) - (y - x)f'_+(x) &= \int_{z \in (x,y]} (y - z) \partial \gamma_f & \text{ if } x \le y \: , \\ f(y) - f(x) - (y - x)f'_+(x) &= \int_{z \in (y,x]} (z - y) \partial \gamma_f & \text{ if } y \le x \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: For $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ a convex function and $x,y \in \mathbb{R}$
conclusions: f(y) - f(x) - (y - x)f'_+(x) &= \int_{z \in (x,y]} (y - z) \partial \gamma_f & \text{ if } x \le y
f(y) - f(x) - (y - x)f'_+(x) &= \int_{z \in (y,x]} (z - y) \partial \gamma_f & \text{ if } y \le x
nodes.label: lem:convex_taylor

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $\Lambda$ be the Lebesgue measure and let $x < y$. Since $f$ has right derivative $f'_+$ in $(x,y)$ and $f'_+$ is integrable on that interval, \begin{align*} f(y) - f(x) = \int_{z \in (x, y]} f'_+(z) \partial \Lambda \: . \end{align*} We now integrate by parts, using Theorem~\ref{thm:integration_by_parts}. $\Lambda$ is the measure obtained from the Stieltjes function $z \mapsto z - y$. \begin{align*} \int_{z \in (x, y]} f'_+(z) \partial \Lambda &= - \int_{z \in (x,y]} (z - y)\partial \gamma_f + f'_+(y)(y - y) - f'_+(x)(x - y) \\ &= \int_{z \in (x,y]} (y - z)\partial \gamma_f + f'_+(x)(y - x) \: . \end{align*} Putting the two equalities together, we get the result for $x < y$. The proof for $x > y$ is similar, and for $x = y$ both sides of both equations are zero.
nodes.statement_short: Fundamental theorem of calculus for the right derivative, then integration by parts against the curvature measure.

nodes.name: Write $f(y)-f(x)$ as the integral of the right derivative
nodes.statement: Let $\Lambda$ be the Lebesgue measure and let $x < y$. Since $f$ has right derivative $f'_+$ in $(x,y)$ and $f'_+$ is integrable on that interval, \begin{align*} f(y) - f(x) = \int_{z \in (x, y]} f'_+(z) \partial \Lambda \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Write $f(y)-f(x)$ as the integral of the right derivative.

nodes.name: Integrate by parts against the curvature measure
nodes.statement: We now integrate by parts, using Theorem~\ref{thm:integration_by_parts}. $\Lambda$ is the measure obtained from the Stieltjes function $z \mapsto z - y$. \begin{align*} \int_{z \in (x, y]} f'_+(z) \partial \Lambda &= - \int_{z \in (x,y]} (z - y)\partial \gamma_f + f'_+(y)(y - y) - f'_+(x)(x - y) \\ &= \int_{z \in (x,y]} (y - z)\partial \gamma_f + f'_+(x)(y - x) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Integrate by parts against the curvature measure.

nodes.name: Combine; other orderings are similar or trivial
nodes.statement: Putting the two equalities together, we get the result for $x < y$. The proof for $x > y$ is similar, and for $x = y$ both sides of both equations are zero.
nodes.statement_short: Combine; other orderings are similar or trivial.

nodes.name: Statistical information functions phi_{a,b}
nodes.statement: For $a,b \in (0, +\infty)$ let $\phi_{a,b} : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the function defined by \begin{align*} \phi_{a,b}(x) &= \max\left\{0, a x - b \right\} & \text{ for } a \le b \: , \\ \phi_{a,b}(x) &= \max\left\{0, b - a x \right\} & \text{ for } a > b \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:statInfoFun

nodes.name: Integral representation of a convex function
nodes.statement: For $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ a convex function, for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$~, \begin{align*} f(x) &= f(1) + f'_+(1) (x - 1) + \int_{y} \phi_{1,y}(x) \partial\gamma_f \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: For $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ a convex function
for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
nodes.label: cor:convex_taylor_statInfoFun

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:convex_taylor}, for $x > 1$, \begin{align*} f(x) - f(1) - f'_+(1) (x - 1) &= \int_{y \in (1, x]} (x - y) \partial\gamma_f \\ &= \int_{y \in (1, +\infty)} \max\{0, x - y\} \partial\gamma_f \\ &= \int_{y \in (1, +\infty)} \phi_{1,y}(x) \partial\gamma_f \: . \end{align*} That final integral is equal to $\int_y \phi_{1,y}(x) \partial\gamma_f$ (without the restriction to $(1, +\infty)$) because $\phi_{1,y}(x)$ is zero outside of $(1, +\infty)$ for $x \ge 1$. The case of $x < 1$ is similar.
nodes.statement_short: Taylor formula at 1, rewritten with the hockey-stick functions $\phi_{1,y}$.

nodes.name: Apply the convex Taylor formula for $x>1$
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:convex_taylor}, for $x > 1$, \begin{align*} f(x) - f(1) - f'_+(1) (x - 1) &= \int_{y \in (1, x]} (x - y) \partial\gamma_f \\ &= \int_{y \in (1, +\infty)} \max\{0, x - y\} \partial\gamma_f \\ &= \int_{y \in (1, +\infty)} \phi_{1,y}(x) \partial\gamma_f \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the convex Taylor formula for $x>1$.

nodes.name: Remove the restriction of the domain; $x<1$ is similar
nodes.statement: That final integral is equal to $\int_y \phi_{1,y}(x) \partial\gamma_f$ (without the restriction to $(1, +\infty)$) because $\phi_{1,y}(x)$ is zero outside of $(1, +\infty)$ for $x \ge 1$. The case of $x < 1$ is similar.
nodes.statement_short: Remove the restriction of the domain; $x<1$ is similar.

nodes.name: Curvature measure of phi_{a,b}
nodes.statement: The curvature measure of the function $\phi_{a,b}$ is $\gamma_{\phi_{a,b}} = a\delta_{b/a}$~, where $\delta_x$ is the Dirac measure at $x$.
conclusions: The curvature measure of the function $\phi_{a,b}$ is $\gamma_{\phi_{a,b}} = a\delta_{b/a}$~
nodes.label: lem:curvatureMeasure_statInfoFun

nodes.name: f-divergence as integral of hockey-stick divergences
nodes.statement:
For two finite measures $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$,  egin{align*} D_f(\mu, 
u) = f(1) 
u(\mathcal X) + f'_+(1)(\mu(\mathcal X) - 
u(\mathcal X)) + \int_y D_{\phi_{1,y}}(\mu, 
u) \partial\gamma_f \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Any f-divergence is a linear term plus the integral over $\gamma_f$ of the divergences $D_{\phi_{1,y}}$.
assumptions: For two finite measures $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$
conclusions:
D_f(\mu, 
u) = f(1) 
u(\mathcal X) + f'_+(1)(\mu(\mathcal X) - 
u(\mathcal X)) + \int_y D_{\phi_{1,y}}(\mu, 
u) \partial\gamma_f
nodes.label: thm:fDiv_eq_integral_eGamma

nodes.name: D_phi_{1,y} versus E_y
nodes.statement:
For probability measures, $D_{\phi_{1,y}}(\mu, 
u) = E_y(\mu, 
u)$~, but these functions can differ if $\mu$ and $
u$ are finite measures with different masses.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
We prove the result for $f(1) = 0$ and $f'_+(1) = 0$ for simplicity of exposition. From Corollary~ef{cor:convex_taylor_statInfoFun} we get that $f(x) = \int_y \phi_{1,y}(x) \partial\gamma_f$~. From this and the theorem of Fubini,  egin{align*} \int_x f\left(  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) ight) \partial
u = \int_{x} \int_{y} \phi_{1,y} \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) ight) \partial\gamma_f \partial
u = \int_{y} \int_{x} \phi_{1,y} \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) ight) \partial
u \partial\gamma_f \: . \end{align*} For the mutually singular part of the divergence $D_f$,  egin{align*} f'(\infty) = f'_+(\infty) - f'_+(1) = \gamma_f((1,+\infty)) = \int_{y > 1} 1 \partial \gamma_f = \int_{y > 1} \phi_{1,y}'(\infty) \partial \gamma_f \: . \end{align*} The last integral is equal to $\int_{y \in \mathbb{R}} \phi_{1,y}'(\infty) \partial \gamma_f$ since $\phi_{1,y}'(\infty) = 0$ for $y \le 1$. Finally,  egin{align*} D_f(\mu, 
u) &= \int_x f\left(  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) ight) \partial
u + f'(\infty) \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X) \ &= \int_{y} \left(\int_{x} \phi_{1,y} \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) ight) \partial
u + \phi_{1,y}'(\infty) \mu(\mathcal X) ight) \partial\gamma_f \ &= \int_y D_{\phi_{1,y}}(\mu, 
u) \partial \gamma_f \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Integral representation of $f$, Fubini for the absolutely continuous part, and the curvature mass for the singular part.

nodes.name: Reduce to $f(1)=0$, $f'_+(1)=0$
nodes.statement: We prove the result for $f(1) = 0$ and $f'_+(1) = 0$ for simplicity of exposition.

nodes.name: Represent $f$ as an integral of $\phi_{1,y}$
nodes.statement: From Corollary~\ref{cor:convex_taylor_statInfoFun} we get that $f(x) = \int_y \phi_{1,y}(x) \partial\gamma_f$~.
nodes.statement_short: Represent $f$ as an integral of $\phi_{1,y}$.

nodes.name: Swap integrals by Fubini
nodes.statement:
From this and the theorem of Fubini,  egin{align*} \int_x f\left(  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) ight) \partial
u = \int_{x} \int_{y} \phi_{1,y} \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) ight) \partial\gamma_f \partial
u = \int_{y} \int_{x} \phi_{1,y} \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) ight) \partial
u \partial\gamma_f \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Swap integrals by Fubini.

nodes.name: Express $f'(\infty)$ as an integral against $\gamma_f$
nodes.statement: For the mutually singular part of the divergence $D_f$, \begin{align*} f'(\infty) = f'_+(\infty) - f'_+(1) = \gamma_f((1,+\infty)) = \int_{y > 1} 1 \partial \gamma_f = \int_{y > 1} \phi_{1,y}'(\infty) \partial \gamma_f \: . \end{align*} The last integral is equal to $\int_{y \in \mathbb{R}} \phi_{1,y}'(\infty) \partial \gamma_f$ since $\phi_{1,y}'(\infty) = 0$ for $y \le 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Express $f'(\infty)$ as an integral against $\gamma_f$.

nodes.name: Combine both parts
nodes.statement:
Finally,  egin{align*} D_f(\mu, 
u) &= \int_x f\left(  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) ight) \partial
u + f'(\infty) \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X) \ &= \int_{y} \left(\int_{x} \phi_{1,y} \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) ight) \partial
u + \phi_{1,y}'(\infty) \mu(\mathcal X) ight) \partial\gamma_f \ &= \int_y D_{\phi_{1,y}}(\mu, 
u) \partial \gamma_f \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Combine both parts.

nodes.name: Integral representation of f-divergences (Liese-Vajda)
nodes.statement:
egin{align*} D_f(\mu, 
u) = f(1) 
u(\mathcal X) + f'_+(1)(\mu(\mathcal X) - 
u(\mathcal X)) + \int_\pi I_\pi(\mu, 
u) \partial\Gamma_f \: . \end{align*}
conclusions:
D_f(\mu, 
u) = f(1) 
u(\mathcal X) + f'_+(1)(\mu(\mathcal X) - 
u(\mathcal X)) + \int_\pi I_\pi(\mu, 
u) \partial\Gamma_f
nodes.label: thm:fDiv_eq_integral

nodes.name: DPI reduces to the absolutely continuous case
nodes.statement:
Let $\kappa : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be a Markov kernel and $
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ be a finite measure. Suppose that for all finite measures $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ with $\mu \ll 
u$, $D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \le D_f(\mu, 
u)$. Then the same is true without the absolute continuity hypothesis.
assumptions: Let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be a Markov kernel and $\nu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ be a finite measure.

Suppose that for all finite measures $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ with $\mu \ll 
u$, $D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \le D_f(\mu, 
u)$.
conclusions: Then the same is true without the absolute continuity hypothesis.
nodes.label: lem:DPI_of_DPI_ac

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
We use $\kappa \circ \mu = \kappa \circ ( rac{d\mu}{d
u}\cdot 
u) + \kappa \circ \mu_{\perp 
u}$~. By Lemma~ef{lem:fDiv_add_measure_le},  egin{align*} D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \le D_f\left(\kappa \circ ( rac{d\mu}{d
u}\cdot 
u), \kappa \circ 
uight) + (\kappa \circ \mu_{\perp 
u})(\mathcal Y) f'(\infty) \: . \end{align*} Since $\kappa$ is a Markov kernel, $(\kappa \circ \mu_{\perp 
u})(\mathcal Y) = \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal Y)$. By hypothesis, since $ rac{d\mu}{d
u}\cdot 
u \ll 
u$, $D_f\left(\kappa \circ ( rac{d\mu}{d
u}\cdot 
u), \kappa \circ 
uight) \le D_f\left( rac{d\mu}{d
u}\cdot 
u, 
uight)$. We get  egin{align*} D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) &\le D_f\left( rac{d\mu}{d
u}\cdot 
u,
uight) + \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal Y) f'(\infty) \ &= D_f(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Split $\mu$ into absolutely continuous and singular parts, bound with the subadditivity lemma and apply the hypothesis.

nodes.name: Decompose $\kappa\circ\mu$ along the Lebesgue decomposition of $\mu$
nodes.statement:
We use $\kappa \circ \mu = \kappa \circ ( rac{d\mu}{d
u}\cdot 
u) + \kappa \circ \mu_{\perp 
u}$~.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose $\kappa\circ\mu$ along the Lebesgue decomposition of $\mu$.

nodes.name: Bound using the subadditivity lemma
nodes.statement:
By Lemma~ef{lem:fDiv_add_measure_le},  egin{align*} D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \le D_f\left(\kappa \circ ( rac{d\mu}{d
u}\cdot 
u), \kappa \circ 
uight) + (\kappa \circ \mu_{\perp 
u})(\mathcal Y) f'(\infty) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound using the subadditivity lemma.

nodes.name: Markov kernels preserve the singular mass
nodes.statement: Since $\kappa$ is a Markov kernel, $(\kappa \circ \mu_{\perp \nu})(\mathcal Y) = \mu_{\perp \nu}(\mathcal Y)$.
nodes.statement_short: Markov kernels preserve the singular mass.

nodes.name: Apply the hypothesis to the absolutely continuous part
nodes.statement:
By hypothesis, since $ rac{d\mu}{d
u}\cdot 
u \ll 
u$, $D_f\left(\kappa \circ ( rac{d\mu}{d
u}\cdot 
u), \kappa \circ 
uight) \le D_f\left( rac{d\mu}{d
u}\cdot 
u, 
uight)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the hypothesis to the absolutely continuous part.

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement:
We get  egin{align*} D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) &\le D_f\left( rac{d\mu}{d
u}\cdot 
u,
uight) + \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal Y) f'(\infty) \ &= D_f(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Combine.

nodes.name: Composition-product with a kernel
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be a Markov kernel. Then $D_f(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \kappa) = D_f(\mu, 
u)$.
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be a Markov kernel.
nodes.label: thm:fDiv_compProd_left_1

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
By Lemma~ef{cor:rnDeriv_compProd_left} and the fact that $(\mu \otimes \kappa)_{\perp 
u \otimes \kappa} = \mu_{\perp 
u} \otimes \kappa$ (Lemma TODO),  egin{align*} D_f(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \kappa) &= \int_{p} f \left( rac{d (\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d (
u \otimes \kappa)}(p)ight) \partial(
u \otimes \kappa) + f'(\infty) (\mu \otimes \kappa)_{\perp 
u \otimes \kappa}(\mathcal X) \ &= \int_{p} f \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(p_X)ight) \partial(
u \otimes \kappa) + f'(\infty) (\mu_{\perp 
u} \otimes \kappa)(\mathcal X) \ &= \int_x \int_y f \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)ight) \partial \kappa(x) \partial 
u + f'(\infty) \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X) \ &= \int_x f \left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)ight) \partial 
u + f'(\infty) \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X) \ &= D_f(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Radon-Nikodym derivative of the composition-products depends only on the first coordinate; integrate out $\kappa$.

nodes.name: f-divergence of products with a common factor
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\xi$ be a probability measure on $\mathcal Y$. Then $D_f(\mu 	imes \xi, 
u 	imes \xi) = D_f(\mu, 
u)$.
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\xi$ be a probability measure on $\mathcal Y$.
nodes.label: cor:fDiv_prod_left_1

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{thm:fDiv_compProd_left_1} with $\kappa$ the constant kernel with value $\xi$.
nodes.statement_short: Composition-product lemma with a constant kernel.

nodes.name: DPI for measurable maps
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal M (\mathcal X)$ be two finite measures and let $g : \mathcal X 	o \mathcal Y$ be a measurable function. Then $D_f(g_* \mu, g_* 
u) \le D_f(\mu, 
u)$.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.1 DPI: proof using Jensen's inequality for the conditional expectation
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal M (\mathcal X)$ be two finite measures and let $g : \mathcal X \to \mathcal Y$ be a measurable function.
nodes.label: thm:fDiv_map_le

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
By Lemma~ef{lem:DPI_of_DPI_ac}, it is sufficient to prove the inequality with the additional hypothesis $\mu \ll 
u$ (hence also $g_* \mu \ll g_*
u$). In that case,  egin{align*} D_f(g_* \mu, g_* 
u) &= \int_y f \left(  rac{d g_* \mu}{d g_* 
u}(y) ight) \partial(g_* 
u) \ &= \int_{x} f \left(  rac{d g_* \mu}{d g_* 
u}(g(x)) ight) \partial
u \: . \end{align*} By Lemma~ef{lem:rnDeriv_map_eq_condexp}, $
u$-almost everywhere,  egin{align*}  rac{d g_* \mu}{d g_* 
u}(g(x)) &= 
u\left[ rac{d \mu}{d 
u} \mid g^* \mathcal Y ight](x) \: . \end{align*} Using that expression, then Jensen's inequality for the conditional expectation(Theorem~ef{thm:condexp_jensen}), we get  egin{align*} D_f(g_* \mu, g_* 
u) &= \int_{x} f \left( 
u\left[ rac{d \mu}{d 
u} \mid g^* \mathcal Y ight](x) ight) \partial
u \ &\le \int_{x} 
u\left[ f \left(  rac{d \mu}{d 
u} ight) \mid g^* \mathcal Y ight](x) \partial
u \: . \end{align*} The integral of a conditional expectation is equal to the integral of the function, hence  egin{align*} D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) &\le \int_{x} f \left(  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) ight) \partial
u \: . \end{align*} This is equal to $D_f(\mu, 
u)$.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.1 DPI: proof using Jensen's inequality for the conditional expectation
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $\mu \ll \nu$; the pushforward density is a conditional expectation, then apply conditional Jensen.

nodes.name: Reduce to the absolutely continuous case and change variables
nodes.statement:
By Lemma~ef{lem:DPI_of_DPI_ac}, it is sufficient to prove the inequality with the additional hypothesis $\mu \ll 
u$ (hence also $g_* \mu \ll g_*
u$). In that case,  egin{align*} D_f(g_* \mu, g_* 
u) &= \int_y f \left(  rac{d g_* \mu}{d g_* 
u}(y) ight) \partial(g_* 
u) \ &= \int_{x} f \left(  rac{d g_* \mu}{d g_* 
u}(g(x)) ight) \partial
u \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the absolutely continuous case and change variables.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.1 DPI: proof using Jensen's inequality for the conditional expectation

nodes.name: The pushforward density is a conditional expectation
nodes.statement:
By Lemma~ef{lem:rnDeriv_map_eq_condexp}, $
u$-almost everywhere,  egin{align*}  rac{d g_* \mu}{d g_* 
u}(g(x)) &= 
u\left[ rac{d \mu}{d 
u} \mid g^* \mathcal Y ight](x) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: The pushforward density is a conditional expectation.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.1 DPI: proof using Jensen's inequality for the conditional expectation

nodes.name: Apply conditional Jensen
nodes.statement:
Using that expression, then Jensen's inequality for the conditional expectation(Theorem~ef{thm:condexp_jensen}), we get  egin{align*} D_f(g_* \mu, g_* 
u) &= \int_{x} f \left( 
u\left[ rac{d \mu}{d 
u} \mid g^* \mathcal Y ight](x) ight) \partial
u \ &\le \int_{x} 
u\left[ f \left(  rac{d \mu}{d 
u} ight) \mid g^* \mathcal Y ight](x) \partial
u \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply conditional Jensen.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.1 DPI: proof using Jensen's inequality for the conditional expectation

nodes.name: Tower property gives $D_f(\mu,\nu)$
nodes.statement:
The integral of a conditional expectation is equal to the integral of the function, hence  egin{align*} D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) &\le \int_{x} f \left(  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x) ight) \partial
u \: . \end{align*} This is equal to $D_f(\mu, 
u)$.
nodes.statement_short: Tower property gives $D_f(\mu,\nu)$.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.1 DPI: proof using Jensen's inequality for the conditional expectation

nodes.name: Data-processing inequality for f-divergences
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be a Markov kernel. Then $D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \le D_f(\mu, 
u)$.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.1 DPI: proof using Jensen's inequality for the conditional expectation
nodes.statement_short: Markov kernels do not increase f-divergences between finite measures.
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be a Markov kernel.
also_stated_at:
That inequality states that for $\mu, 
u$ two measures on $\mathcal X$ and $\kappa : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ a Markov kernel, $D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \le D_f(\mu, 
u)$.
nodes.label: thm:fDiv_data_proc_3

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
Let $\pi_Y : \mathcal X 	imes \mathcal Y 	o \mathcal Y$ be the projection $\pi_Y((x,y)) = y$. Then $\kappa \circ \mu = \pi_{Y*}(\mu \otimes \kappa)$ and similarly for $
u$. We can use the DPI for that function (Theorem~ef{thm:fDiv_map_le}), then Lemma~ef{thm:fDiv_compProd_left_1},  egin{align*} D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) &= D_f(\pi_{Y*}(\mu \otimes \kappa), \pi_{Y*}(
u \otimes \kappa)) \ &\le D_f(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \kappa) \ &= D_f(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 2.3.4.1 DPI: proof using Jensen's inequality for the conditional expectation
nodes.statement_short: Write $\kappa\circ\mu$ as a pushforward of $\mu\otimes\kappa$, apply the DPI for maps and the composition-product lemma.

nodes.name: Express $\kappa\circ\mu$ as a projection of $\mu\otimes\kappa$
nodes.statement: Let $\pi_Y : \mathcal X \times \mathcal Y \to \mathcal Y$ be the projection $\pi_Y((x,y)) = y$. Then $\kappa \circ \mu = \pi_{Y*}(\mu \otimes \kappa)$ and similarly for $\nu$.
nodes.statement_short: Express $\kappa\circ\mu$ as a projection of $\mu\otimes\kappa$.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.1 DPI: proof using Jensen's inequality for the conditional expectation

nodes.name: DPI for maps, then the composition-product lemma
nodes.statement:
We can use the DPI for that function (Theorem~ef{thm:fDiv_map_le}), then Lemma~ef{thm:fDiv_compProd_left_1},  egin{align*} D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) &= D_f(\pi_{Y*}(\mu \otimes \kappa), \pi_{Y*}(
u \otimes \kappa)) \ &\le D_f(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \kappa) \ &= D_f(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: DPI for maps, then the composition-product lemma.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.1 DPI: proof using Jensen's inequality for the conditional expectation

nodes.name: Sketch: DPI from the composition-product inequality
nodes.statement:
It starts by establishing $D_f(\mu, \nu) \le D_f(\mu \otimes \kappa, \nu \otimes \eta)$ for Markov kernels $\kappa$ and $\eta$, then deduces the DPI.
Indeed, if the measurable spaces are standard Borel, we can write $\mu \otimes \kappa = ((\kappa \circ \mu) \otimes \kappa^\dagger_\mu)_\leftrightarrow$ for a Markov kernel $\kappa^\dagger_\mu$ (see Definition~\ref{def:bayesInv}; $(...)_\leftrightarrow$ is notation for composition with the map that swaps the coordinates) and then use the inequality to get
\begin{align*}
D(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ \nu)
&\le D((\kappa \circ \mu) \otimes \kappa^\dagger_\mu, (\kappa \circ \nu) \otimes \kappa^\dagger_\nu)
\\
&= D(((\kappa \circ \mu) \otimes \kappa^\dagger_\mu)_{\leftrightarrow}, ((\kappa \circ \nu) \otimes \kappa^\dagger_\nu)_{\leftrightarrow})
\\
&= D(\mu \otimes \kappa, \nu \otimes \kappa)
\\
&= D(\mu, \nu)
\: .
\end{align*}
nodes.section: 2.3.4.2 DPI: proof using derivatives of kernels
nodes.statement_short: Write $\mu\otimes\kappa$ via the Bayesian inverse and apply the composition-product inequality.

nodes.name: f-divergence increases under composition-product
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two Markov kernels, with either $\mathcal X$ countable or $\mathcal{Y}$ countably generated. Then $D_f(\mu, 
u) \le D_f(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \eta)$.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.2 DPI: proof using derivatives of kernels
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two Markov kernels, with either $\mathcal X$ countable or $\mathcal{Y}$ countably generated.
nodes.label: thm:fDiv_le_compProd_1

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
TODO: the following proof assumes $\mu \ll 
u$ and $\kappa(x) \ll \eta(x)$ for $
u$-almost all $x$. Describe the general case. Using Lemma~ef{lem:rnDeriv_compProd} and ef{cor:rnDeriv_value},  egin{align*} D(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \eta) &= \int_x \int_y f \left(  rac{\partial \mu}{\partial
u}(x)  rac{\partial \kappa(x)}{\partial\eta(x)}(y) ight) \partial \eta(x) \partial 
u \: . \end{align*} Since $f$ is convex, by Jensen's inequality,  egin{align*} \int_y f \left(  rac{\partial \mu}{\partial
u}(x)  rac{\partial \kappa(x)}{\partial\eta(x)}(y) ight) \partial \eta(x) &\ge f \left( \int_y  rac{\partial \mu}{\partial
u}(x)  rac{\partial \kappa(x)}{\partial\eta(x)}(y) \partial \eta(x) ight) \ &= f \left(  rac{\partial \mu}{\partial
u}(x) \int_y  rac{\partial \kappa(x)}{\partial\eta(x)}(y) \partial \eta(x) ight) \: . \end{align*} Since $\kappa(x) \ll \eta(x)$ for $
u$-almost all $x$, $\int_y  rac{\partial \kappa(x)}{\partial\eta(x)}(y) \partial \eta(x) = \int_y 1 \partial \kappa(x) = 1$ a.e.. We have obtained  egin{align*} D_f(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \eta) \ge \int_x f \left(  rac{\partial \mu}{\partial
u}(x)ight) \partial 
u = D_f(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 2.3.4.2 DPI: proof using derivatives of kernels
nodes.statement_short: Product formula for the kernel Radon-Nikodym derivative, then Jensen's inequality in $y$ (absolutely continuous case only).

nodes.name: Restrict to the absolutely continuous case
nodes.statement: TODO: the following proof assumes $\mu \ll \nu$ and $\kappa(x) \ll \eta(x)$ for $\nu$-almost all $x$. Describe the general case.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to the absolutely continuous case.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.2 DPI: proof using derivatives of kernels

nodes.name: Express the divergence via the product of densities
nodes.statement:
Using Lemma~ef{lem:rnDeriv_compProd} and ef{cor:rnDeriv_value},  egin{align*} D(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \eta) &= \int_x \int_y f \left(  rac{\partial \mu}{\partial
u}(x)  rac{\partial \kappa(x)}{\partial\eta(x)}(y) ight) \partial \eta(x) \partial 
u \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Express the divergence via the product of densities.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.2 DPI: proof using derivatives of kernels

nodes.name: Apply Jensen's inequality in $y$
nodes.statement:
Since $f$ is convex, by Jensen's inequality,  egin{align*} \int_y f \left(  rac{\partial \mu}{\partial
u}(x)  rac{\partial \kappa(x)}{\partial\eta(x)}(y) ight) \partial \eta(x) &\ge f \left( \int_y  rac{\partial \mu}{\partial
u}(x)  rac{\partial \kappa(x)}{\partial\eta(x)}(y) \partial \eta(x) ight) \ &= f \left(  rac{\partial \mu}{\partial
u}(x) \int_y  rac{\partial \kappa(x)}{\partial\eta(x)}(y) \partial \eta(x) ight) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply Jensen's inequality in $y$.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.2 DPI: proof using derivatives of kernels

nodes.name: Inner density integrates to 1
nodes.statement:
Since $\kappa(x) \ll \eta(x)$ for $
u$-almost all $x$, $\int_y  rac{\partial \kappa(x)}{\partial\eta(x)}(y) \partial \eta(x) = \int_y 1 \partial \kappa(x) = 1$ a.e.. We have obtained  egin{align*} D_f(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \eta) \ge \int_x f \left(  rac{\partial \mu}{\partial
u}(x)ight) \partial 
u = D_f(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Inner density integrates to 1.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.2 DPI: proof using derivatives of kernels

nodes.name: Marginals (standard Borel)
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu$ and $
u$ be two measures on $\mathcal X 	imes \mathcal Y$ where $\mathcal Y$ is standard Borel, and let $\mu_X, 
u_X$ be their marginals on $\mathcal X$. Then $D_f(\mu_X, 
u_X) \le D_f(\mu, 
u)$. Similarly, for $\mathcal X$ standard Borel and $\mu_Y, 
u_Y$ the marginals on $\mathcal Y$, $D_f(\mu_Y, 
u_Y) \le D_f(\mu, 
u)$.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.2 DPI: proof using derivatives of kernels
assumptions: Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be two measures on $\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y$ where $\mathcal Y$ is standard Borel, and let $\mu_X, \nu_X$ be their marginals on $\mathcal X$.
conclusions:
Similarly, for $\mathcal X$ standard Borel and $\mu_Y, 
u_Y$ the marginals on $\mathcal Y$, $D_f(\mu_Y, 
u_Y) \le D_f(\mu, 
u)$.
nodes.label: thm:fDiv_fst_le_1

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
We introduce conditional kernels and write $D(\mu, 
u) = D(\mu_X \otimes \mu_{Y|X}, 
u_X \otimes 
u_{Y|X})$. Then apply Theorem~ef{thm:fDiv_le_compProd_1}. For the second statement, we need Lemma~ef{lem:fDiv_map_measurableEmbedding} to swap the role of the two coordinates.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.2 DPI: proof using derivatives of kernels
nodes.statement_short: Disintegrate into marginal and conditional kernel, apply the composition-product inequality; swap coordinates for the second claim.

nodes.name: Disintegrate and apply the composition-product inequality
nodes.statement:
We introduce conditional kernels and write $D(\mu, 
u) = D(\mu_X \otimes \mu_{Y|X}, 
u_X \otimes 
u_{Y|X})$. Then apply Theorem~ef{thm:fDiv_le_compProd_1}.
nodes.statement_short: Disintegrate and apply the composition-product inequality.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.2 DPI: proof using derivatives of kernels

nodes.name: Swap coordinates with a measurable embedding
nodes.statement: For the second statement, we need Lemma~\ref{lem:fDiv_map_measurableEmbedding} to swap the role of the two coordinates.
nodes.statement_short: Swap coordinates with a measurable embedding.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.2 DPI: proof using derivatives of kernels

nodes.name: f-divergence of compositions bounded by composition-products (standard Borel)
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on a standard Borel space $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two finite kernels. $D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \eta \circ 
u) \le D_f(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \eta)$
nodes.section: 2.3.4.2 DPI: proof using derivatives of kernels
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two finite measures on a standard Borel space $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two finite kernels.
nodes.label: lem:fDiv_comp_le_compProd_1

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: By definition, $\kappa \circ \mu$ is the marginal of $\mu \otimes \kappa$ (a measure on $\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y$) on $\mathcal Y$, and similarly for the other measure. Hence by Theorem~\ref{thm:fDiv_fst_le_1}, $D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \eta \circ \nu) \le D_f(\mu \otimes \kappa, \nu \otimes \eta)$.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.2 DPI: proof using derivatives of kernels
nodes.statement_short: Compositions are second marginals of composition-products; apply the marginal theorem.

nodes.name: Conditioning increases f-divergence
nodes.statement: Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two finite kernels. Then $D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \eta \circ \mu) \le D_f(\mu \otimes \kappa, \mu \otimes \eta) = D_f(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu)$
nodes.section: 2.3.4.2 DPI: proof using derivatives of kernels
assumptions: Let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two finite kernels.
nodes.label: thm:fDiv_comp_le_condFDiv_1

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:fDiv_comp_le_compProd_1}, $D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \eta \circ \mu) \le D_f(\mu \otimes \kappa, \mu \otimes \eta)$. This is equal to $D_f(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:fDiv_compProd_right}.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.2 DPI: proof using derivatives of kernels
nodes.statement_short: Composition bound, then the composition-product equality.

nodes.name: Data-processing inequality for f-divergences (standard Borel)
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be a Markov kernel, where both $\mathcal X$ and $\mathcal Y$ are standard Borel. Then $D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \le D_f(\mu, 
u)$.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.2 DPI: proof using derivatives of kernels
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be a Markov kernel, where both $\mathcal X$ and $\mathcal Y$ are standard Borel.
nodes.label: thm:fDiv_data_proc_1

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
By Lemma~ef{lem:fDiv_comp_le_compProd_1}, $D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \le D_f(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \kappa)$. Then the latter is equal to $D_f(\mu, 
u)$ by Lemma~ef{thm:fDiv_compProd_left_1}.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.2 DPI: proof using derivatives of kernels
nodes.statement_short: Composition bound, then the composition-product lemma.

nodes.name: Sketch: DPI via the integral representation
nodes.statement: This proof uses that every $f$-divergence is an integral over $\gamma \ge 0$ of $f$-divergences for the function $\phi_{1,\gamma}$ of Definition~\ref{def:statInfoFun}. It suffices then to prove the DPI for those particular $f$-divergences. Those are equal to the $E_\gamma$ divergence, up to a term that is invariant by composition with a Markov kernel. Finally, we already know that the $E_\gamma$ divergence satisfies the DPI, and that completes the proof.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.3 DPI: proof using the integral representation
nodes.statement_short: Integral representation reduces the DPI to the $\phi_{1,\gamma}$ divergences, which reduce to $E_\gamma$.

nodes.name: f-divergence for phi_{a,b}
nodes.statement:
Let $a,b \in [0, +\infty)$ and let $\mu, 
u$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$.  egin{align*} D_{\phi_{a,b}}(\mu, 
u) &= 	ext{sign}(b-a) rac{1}{2}(a \mu(\mathcal X) - b 
u(\mathcal X)) +  rac{1}{2}
u\left[ \left\vert a  rac{d\mu}{d
u} - b ight\vert ight] +  rac{1}{2}a \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X) \: , \end{align*} in which $	ext{sign}(b-a)$ is $1$ if $b-a > 0$ and $-1$ if $b-a \le 0$.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.3 DPI: proof using the integral representation
assumptions: Let $a,b \in [0, +\infty)$ and let $\mu, \nu$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$.
conclusions:
D_{\phi_{a,b}}(\mu, 
u) &= 	ext{sign}(b-a) rac{1}{2}(a \mu(\mathcal X) - b 
u(\mathcal X)) +  rac{1}{2}
u\left[ \left\vert a  rac{d\mu}{d
u} - b ight\vert ight] +  rac{1}{2}a \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X)
nodes.label: lem:fDiv_statInfoFun_eq

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
If $a \le b$,  egin{align*} D_{\phi_{a,b}}(\mu, 
u) &= 
u\left[ \max\{0, a  rac{d\mu}{d
u} - b\} ight] + a \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X) \ &=  rac{1}{2}(a \mu_{\parallel 
u}(\mathcal X) - b 
u(\mathcal X)) +  rac{1}{2}
u\left[ \left\vert a  rac{d\mu}{d
u} - b ight\vert ight] + a \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X) \ &=  rac{1}{2}(a \mu(\mathcal X) - b 
u(\mathcal X)) +  rac{1}{2}
u\left[ \left\vert a  rac{d\mu}{d
u} - b ight\vert ight] +  rac{1}{2}a \mu_{\perp 
u}(\mathcal X) \: . \end{align*} Similar computations lead to the result for $b \le a$.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.3 DPI: proof using the integral representation
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation using $\max\{0,t\} = \frac12(t+|t|)$; the other case is similar.

nodes.name: f-divergence for phi_{a,b} via statistical information
nodes.statement:
Let $a,b \in [0, +\infty)$ and let $\mu, 
u$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$.  egin{align*} D_{\phi_{a,b}}(\mu, 
u) = \mathcal I_{(a,b)}(\mu, 
u) +  rac{1}{2} \left\vert a \mu(\mathcal X) - b 
u(\mathcal X) ight\vert + 	ext{sign}(b-a) rac{1}{2}(a \mu(\mathcal X) - b 
u(\mathcal X)) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 2.3.4.3 DPI: proof using the integral representation
assumptions: Let $a,b \in [0, +\infty)$ and let $\mu, \nu$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$.
conclusions:
D_{\phi_{a,b}}(\mu, 
u) = \mathcal I_{(a,b)}(\mu, 
u) +  rac{1}{2} \left\vert a \mu(\mathcal X) - b 
u(\mathcal X) ight\vert + 	ext{sign}(b-a) rac{1}{2}(a \mu(\mathcal X) - b 
u(\mathcal X))
nodes.label: cor:fDiv_statInfoFun_eq_statInfo

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Combine Lemma~\ref{lem:fDiv_statInfoFun_eq} and Corollary~\ref{cor:statInfo_eq_integral_abs}.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.3 DPI: proof using the integral representation
nodes.statement_short: Combine the two explicit formulas.

nodes.name: DPI for the phi_{a,b} divergences
nodes.statement:
Let $a,b \in [0, +\infty)$. Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be a Markov kernel. Then $D_{\phi_{a,b}}(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \le D_{\phi_{a,b}}(\mu, 
u)$.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.3 DPI: proof using the integral representation
assumptions: Let $a,b \in [0, +\infty)$.
Let $\mu, \nu$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be a Markov kernel.
nodes.label: lem:fDiv_phi_data_proc

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
By Corollary~ef{cor:fDiv_statInfoFun_eq_statInfo},  egin{align*} D_{\phi_{a,b}}(\mu, 
u) = \mathcal I_{(a,b)}(\mu, 
u) +  rac{1}{2} \left\vert a \mu(\mathcal X) - b 
u(\mathcal X) ight\vert + 	ext{sign}(b-a) rac{1}{2}(a \mu(\mathcal X) - b 
u(\mathcal X)) \: . \end{align*} The statistical information satisfies the data-processing inequality (Theorem~ef{thm:data_proc_statInfo}) and the other terms are invariant by composition with a Markov kernel, hence $D_{\phi_{a,b}}$ also satisfies the data-processing inequality.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.3 DPI: proof using the integral representation
nodes.statement_short: Statistical information satisfies the DPI and the remaining terms are kernel-invariant.

nodes.name: Data-processing inequality for f-divergences (via integral representation)
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be a Markov kernel. Then $D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \le D_f(\mu, 
u)$.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.3 DPI: proof using the integral representation
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be a Markov kernel.
nodes.label: thm:fDiv_data_proc_2

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
By Theorem~ef{thm:fDiv_eq_integral_eGamma},  egin{align*} D_f(\mu, 
u) = f(1) 
u(\mathcal X) + f'_+(1) (\mu(\mathcal X) - 
u (\mathcal X)) + \int_y D_{\phi_{1,y}}(\mu, 
u) \partial\gamma_f \: . \end{align*} The first two terms are unchanged by composition with a Markov kernel. It thus suffices to prove the data processing inequality for the divergences $D_{\phi_{1, \gamma}}$. This was done in Lemma~ef{lem:fDiv_phi_data_proc}.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.3 DPI: proof using the integral representation
nodes.statement_short: Integral representation; linear terms are kernel-invariant and each $\phi_{1,\gamma}$ divergence satisfies the DPI.

nodes.name: Use the integral representation
nodes.statement:
By Theorem~ef{thm:fDiv_eq_integral_eGamma},  egin{align*} D_f(\mu, 
u) = f(1) 
u(\mathcal X) + f'_+(1) (\mu(\mathcal X) - 
u (\mathcal X)) + \int_y D_{\phi_{1,y}}(\mu, 
u) \partial\gamma_f \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Use the integral representation.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.3 DPI: proof using the integral representation

nodes.name: Reduce to the DPI for the $\phi_{1,\gamma}$ divergences
nodes.statement: The first two terms are unchanged by composition with a Markov kernel. It thus suffices to prove the data processing inequality for the divergences $D_{\phi_{1, \gamma}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the DPI for the $\phi_{1,\gamma}$ divergences.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.3 DPI: proof using the integral representation

nodes.name: Apply the DPI for $\phi_{a,b}$ divergences
nodes.statement: This was done in Lemma~\ref{lem:fDiv_phi_data_proc}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the DPI for $\phi_{a,b}$ divergences.
nodes.section: 2.3.4.3 DPI: proof using the integral representation

nodes.name: Restriction of a measure to a sub-sigma-algebra
nodes.statement: For $\mathcal A$ a sub-$\sigma$-algebra and $\mu$ a measure, we write $\mathcal \mu_{| \mathcal A}$ for the measure restricted to the $\sigma$-algebra.

nodes.name: DPI for sub-sigma-algebras
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\mathcal A$ be a sub-$\sigma$-algebra of $\mathcal X$. Then $D_f(\mu_{| \mathcal A}, 
u_{| \mathcal A}) \le D_f(\mu, 
u)$.
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\mathcal A$ be a sub-$\sigma$-algebra of $\mathcal X$.
nodes.label: thm:fDiv_trim_le

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The measure $\mathcal \mu_{| \mathcal A}$ is equal to the map of $\mu$ by the identity, seen as a function to $\mathcal X$ with the $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal A$. That function is measurable since $\mathcal A$ is a sub-sigma-algebra. We can apply Theorem~\ref{thm:fDiv_map_le}.
nodes.statement_short: Restriction is the pushforward by the identity to the coarser sigma-algebra; apply the DPI for maps.

nodes.name: Restriction is a pushforward by a measurable identity map
nodes.statement: The measure $\mathcal \mu_{| \mathcal A}$ is equal to the map of $\mu$ by the identity, seen as a function to $\mathcal X$ with the $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal A$. That function is measurable since $\mathcal A$ is a sub-sigma-algebra.
nodes.statement_short: Restriction is a pushforward by a measurable identity map.

nodes.name: Apply the DPI for maps
nodes.statement: We can apply Theorem~\ref{thm:fDiv_map_le}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the DPI for maps.

nodes.name: f-divergence as supremum over finite sigma-algebras
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$. Then $\sup_{\mathcal A 	ext{ finite}} D_f(\mu_{| \mathcal A}, 
u_{| \mathcal A}) = D_f(\mu, 
u)$.
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$.
conclusions: $\sup_{\mathcal A \text{ finite}} D_f(\mu_{| \mathcal A}, \nu_{| \mathcal A}) = D_f(\mu, \nu)$.
nodes.label: thm:iSup_fDiv_trim

nodes.name: f-divergence of pushforwards equals that of restrictions to the comap
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ be finite measures with $\mu \ll 
u$ and let $g : \mathcal X 	o \mathcal Y$ be a measurable function. Denote by $g^* \mathcal Y$ the comap of the $\sigma$-algebra on $\mathcal Y$ by $g$. Then $D_f(g_* \mu, g_* 
u) = D_f(\mu_{| g^* \mathcal Y}, 
u_{| g^* \mathcal Y})$~.
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ be finite measures with $\mu \ll \nu$ and let $g : \mathcal X \to \mathcal Y$ be a measurable function.
Denote by $g^* \mathcal Y$ the comap of the $\sigma$-algebra on $\mathcal Y$ by $g$.
conclusions: $D_f(g_* \mu, g_* \nu) = D_f(\mu_{| g^* \mathcal Y}, \nu_{| g^* \mathcal Y})$
nodes.label: lem:fDiv_map_eq_fDiv_trim_of_ac

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
Using Lemma~ef{lem:rnDeriv_map_eq_rnDeriv_trim},  egin{align*} D_f(g_* \mu, g_* 
u) &= \int_y f \left(  rac{d g_*\mu}{d g_*
u}(y)ight) \partial(g_*
u) \ &= \int_x f \left(  rac{d g_*\mu}{d g_*
u}(g(x))ight) \partial
u \ &= \int_x f \left( rac{d \mu_{| g^* \mathcal Y}}{d 
u_{| g^* \mathcal Y}}(x) ight) \partial
u \ &= \int_x f \left( rac{d \mu_{| g^* \mathcal Y}}{d 
u_{| g^* \mathcal Y}}(x) ight) \partial
u_{| g^* \mathcal Y} \ &= D_f(\mu_{| g^* \mathcal Y}, 
u_{| g^* \mathcal Y}) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Change of variables and the identification of the pushforward density with the trimmed density.

nodes.name: f-divergence increases under composition-product
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two Markov kernels. Then $D_f(\mu, 
u) \le D_f(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \eta)$.
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two Markov kernels.
nodes.label: thm:fDiv_le_compProd_2

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Since $\kappa$ is a Markov kernel, $\mu$ is the composition of $\mu \otimes \kappa$ and the deterministic kernel for the function $(x,y) \mapsto x$. The same applies for $\nu$ and $\nu \otimes \eta$. The result is then an application of the data-processing inequality, Theorem~\ref{thm:fDiv_data_proc_2}.
nodes.statement_short: First marginal as a deterministic kernel; apply the DPI.

nodes.name: Marginals are compositions with projections
nodes.statement: Since $\kappa$ is a Markov kernel, $\mu$ is the composition of $\mu \otimes \kappa$ and the deterministic kernel for the function $(x,y) \mapsto x$. The same applies for $\nu$ and $\nu \otimes \eta$.
nodes.statement_short: Marginals are compositions with projections.

nodes.name: Apply the DPI
nodes.statement: The result is then an application of the data-processing inequality, Theorem~\ref{thm:fDiv_data_proc_2}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the DPI.

nodes.name: f-divergence of compositions bounded by composition-products
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two finite kernels. Then $D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \eta \circ 
u) \le D_f(\mu \otimes \kappa, 
u \otimes \eta)$.
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two finite kernels.
nodes.label: thm:fDiv_comp_le_compProd_2

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: $\kappa \circ \mu$ is the composition of $\mu \otimes \kappa$ and the deterministic kernel for the function $(x,y) \mapsto y$. The same applies for $\eta \circ \nu$ and $\nu \otimes \eta$. The result is then an application of the data-processing inequality, Theorem~\ref{thm:fDiv_data_proc_2}.
nodes.statement_short: Second marginal as a deterministic kernel; apply the DPI.

nodes.name: Compositions are second marginals
nodes.statement: $\kappa \circ \mu$ is the composition of $\mu \otimes \kappa$ and the deterministic kernel for the function $(x,y) \mapsto y$. The same applies for $\eta \circ \nu$ and $\nu \otimes \eta$.
nodes.statement_short: Compositions are second marginals.

nodes.name: Apply the DPI
nodes.statement: The result is then an application of the data-processing inequality, Theorem~\ref{thm:fDiv_data_proc_2}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the DPI.

nodes.name: Conditioning increases f-divergence (general)
nodes.statement: Let $\mu$ be a finite measure $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two finite kernels. Then $D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \eta \circ \mu) \le D_f(\mu \otimes \kappa, \mu \otimes \eta) = D_f(\kappa, \eta \mid \mu)$~.
assumptions: Let $\mu$ be a finite measure $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two finite kernels.
nodes.label: thm:fDiv_comp_le_condFDiv_2

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: This is a particular case of Theorem~\ref{thm:fDiv_comp_le_compProd_2}.
nodes.statement_short: Special case of the composition-product bound.

nodes.name: Marginals
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu$ and $
u$ be two measures on $\mathcal X 	imes \mathcal Y$, and let $\mu_X, 
u_X$ be their marginals on $\mathcal X$. Then $D_f(\mu_X, 
u_X) \le D_f(\mu, 
u)$. Similarly, for $\mu_Y, 
u_Y$ the marginals on $\mathcal Y$, $D_f(\mu_Y, 
u_Y) \le D_f(\mu, 
u)$.
assumptions: Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be two measures on $\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y$, and let $\mu_X, \nu_X$ be their marginals on $\mathcal X$.
conclusions:
Similarly, for $\mu_Y, 
u_Y$ the marginals on $\mathcal Y$, $D_f(\mu_Y, 
u_Y) \le D_f(\mu, 
u)$.
nodes.label: thm:fDiv_fst_le_2

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The measure $\mu_X$ is the composition of $\mu$ and the deterministic kernel for the function $(x,y) \mapsto x$, and similarly $\mu_Y$ is the composition of $\mu$ and a deterministic kernel. The results are both applications of the data-processing inequality, Theorem~\ref{thm:fDiv_data_proc_2}.
nodes.statement_short: Marginals are compositions with deterministic kernels; apply the DPI.

nodes.name: f-divergence invariant under kernels that keep the first coordinate
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow (\mathcal X 	imes \mathcal Y)$ be a Markov kernel such that for all $x$, $(\kappa(x))_X = \delta_x$. Then $D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) = D_f(\mu, 
u)$.
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow (\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y)$ be a Markov kernel such that for all $x$, $(\kappa(x))_X = \delta_x$.
nodes.label: lem:fDiv_compProd_prod_eq

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
$D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u) \le D_f(\mu, 
u)$ by Theorem~ef{thm:fDiv_data_proc_2}. For the other inequality, remark that $\mu = (\kappa \circ \mu)_X$ (and similarly for $
u$). Hence by Theorem~ef{thm:fDiv_fst_le_2} $D_f(\mu, 
u) \le D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u)$.
nodes.statement_short: DPI in one direction, the marginal inequality in the other.

nodes.name: One inequality is the DPI
nodes.statement: $D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ \nu) \le D_f(\mu, \nu)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:fDiv_data_proc_2}.
nodes.statement_short: One inequality is the DPI.

nodes.name: The other is the marginal inequality
nodes.statement:
For the other inequality, remark that $\mu = (\kappa \circ \mu)_X$ (and similarly for $
u$). Hence by Theorem~ef{thm:fDiv_fst_le_2} $D_f(\mu, 
u) \le D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ 
u)$.
nodes.statement_short: The other is the marginal inequality.

nodes.name: Binary f-divergence d_f
nodes.statement: In this section $d_f(p, q)$ denotes the $f$-divergence between two Bernoulli distributions with means $p$ and $q$.

nodes.name: DPI for events
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $E$ be an event. Then $D_f(\mu, 
u) \ge d_f(\mu(E), 
u(E))$.
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $E$ be an event.
nodes.label: cor:data_proc_event

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Use the deterministic kernel $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \{0, 1\}$ with $\kappa(x) = \delta_1 \mathbb{I}\{x \in E\} + \delta_0 \mathbb{I}\{x \notin E\}$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:fDiv_data_proc_2}.
nodes.statement_short: DPI for the indicator kernel of $E$.

nodes.name: Binary f-divergence is convex with minimum at the diagonal
nodes.statement: For all $y \in [0,1]$, $x \mapsto d_f(x, y)$ is convex and attains a minimum at $x = y$.
assumptions: For all $y \in [0,1]$
conclusions: $x \mapsto d_f(x, y)$ is convex and attains a minimum at $x = y$
nodes.label: lem:fDiv_bernoulli_convex

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} d_f(x, y) &= y f(\frac{x}{y}) + (1 - y) f(\frac{1 - x}{1 - y}) \: , \\ (x \mapsto d_f(x, y))'_+(x) &= f'_+(\frac{x}{y}) - f'_+(\frac{1 - x}{1 - y}) \: . \end{align*} $f'_+$ is non-decreasing, hence we get that $(x \mapsto d_f(x, y))'_+$ is also non-decreasing and $x \mapsto d_f(x, y)$ is convex. For $x \le y$, $x/y \le 1 \le (1-x)/(1-y)$, hence $f'_+(\frac{x}{y}) \le f'_+(\frac{1 - x}{1 - y})$ and $(x \mapsto d_f(x, y))'_+(x) \le 0$. The opposite holds for $x \ge y$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the right derivative of $x\mapsto d_f(x,y)$; it is non-decreasing and changes sign at $y$.

nodes.name: Right derivative is non-decreasing, hence convexity
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} d_f(x, y) &= y f(\frac{x}{y}) + (1 - y) f(\frac{1 - x}{1 - y}) \: , \\ (x \mapsto d_f(x, y))'_+(x) &= f'_+(\frac{x}{y}) - f'_+(\frac{1 - x}{1 - y}) \: . \end{align*} $f'_+$ is non-decreasing, hence we get that $(x \mapsto d_f(x, y))'_+$ is also non-decreasing and $x \mapsto d_f(x, y)$ is convex.
nodes.statement_short: Right derivative is non-decreasing, hence convexity.

nodes.name: Sign of the derivative gives the minimum at $y$
nodes.statement: For $x \le y$, $x/y \le 1 \le (1-x)/(1-y)$, hence $f'_+(\frac{x}{y}) \le f'_+(\frac{1 - x}{1 - y})$ and $(x \mapsto d_f(x, y))'_+(x) \le 0$. The opposite holds for $x \ge y$.
nodes.statement_short: Sign of the derivative gives the minimum at $y$.

nodes.name: f-divergence bounded below by binary divergence of means
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal P([0,1])$. Then  egin{align*} D_f(\mu, 
u) \ge d_f(\mu[X], 
u[X]) \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal P([0,1])$.
nodes.label: lem:fDiv_bounded_ge_fDiv_mean

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
Let $u$ be the uniform distribution on $[0,1]$. Then $D_f(\mu, 
u) = D_f(\mu 	imes u, 
u 	imes u)$ (by Lemma~ef{lem:fDiv_compProd_prod_eq}). Let $g : [0,1] 	imes [0,1] 	o \{0,1\}$ be the measurable function with $g(x, y) = \mathbb{I}\{y \le x\}$. We also write $g$ for the corresponding deterministic kernel. By the data-processing inequality (Theorem~ef{thm:fDiv_data_proc_2}),  egin{align*} D_f(\mu 	imes u, 
u 	imes u) \ge D_f(g \circ (\mu 	imes u), g \circ (
u 	imes u)) \: . \end{align*} Those two last measures are Bernoulli distributions with means $\mu[X]$ and $
u[X]$.
nodes.statement_short: Add an independent uniform variable and threshold to get Bernoulli variables with the same means; apply the DPI.

nodes.name: Tensor with a uniform variable without changing the divergence
nodes.statement: Let $u$ be the uniform distribution on $[0,1]$. Then $D_f(\mu, \nu) = D_f(\mu \times u, \nu \times u)$ (by Lemma~\ref{lem:fDiv_compProd_prod_eq}).
nodes.statement_short: Tensor with a uniform variable without changing the divergence.

nodes.name: Apply the DPI with the threshold map
nodes.statement: Let $g : [0,1] \times [0,1] \to \{0,1\}$ be the measurable function with $g(x, y) = \mathbb{I}\{y \le x\}$. We also write $g$ for the corresponding deterministic kernel. By the data-processing inequality (Theorem~\ref{thm:fDiv_data_proc_2}), \begin{align*} D_f(\mu \times u, \nu \times u) \ge D_f(g \circ (\mu \times u), g \circ (\nu \times u)) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the DPI with the threshold map.

nodes.name: The images are Bernoulli with the right means
nodes.statement: Those two last measures are Bernoulli distributions with means $\mu[X]$ and $\nu[X]$.
nodes.statement_short: The images are Bernoulli with the right means.

nodes.name: f-divergence bounded below by binary divergence of kernel means
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and let $\kappa : \mathcal X ightsquigarrow [0,1]$. Then  egin{align*} D_f(\mu, 
u) \ge d_f((\kappa \circ \mu)[X], (\kappa \circ 
u)[X]) \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow [0,1]$.
nodes.label: cor:fDiv_ge_fDiv_mean_comp

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: First, by the data-processing inequality (Theorem~\ref{thm:fDiv_data_proc_2}), $D_f(\mu, \nu) \ge D_f(\kappa \circ \mu, \kappa \circ \nu)$~. Then use Lemma~\ref{lem:fDiv_bounded_ge_fDiv_mean}.
nodes.statement_short: DPI, then the bound for measures on $[0,1]$.

nodes.name: f-divergence lower bound on Bayes risks
nodes.statement: Let $\pi, \xi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ and $P, Q : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$. Suppose that the loss $\ell'$ takes values in $[0,1]$. Then \begin{align*} D_f(\pi \otimes Q, \xi \otimes P) &\ge d_f(\mathcal R_\pi^Q, \mathcal R_\xi^P) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: The f-divergence between joint laws bounds the binary f-divergence between the two Bayes risks.
assumptions: Let $\pi, \xi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ and $P, Q : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$.
Suppose that the loss $\ell'$ takes values in $[0,1]$.
conclusions: D_f(\pi \otimes Q, \xi \otimes P) &\ge d_f(\mathcal R_\pi^Q, \mathcal R_\xi^P)
nodes.label: lem:fDiv_estimation_ge

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $\mathcal R_\pi^Q \ge \mathcal R_\xi^P$. Let $\hat{y}_B$ be a Bayes estimator for the estimation task $(P, y, \ell')$ with prior $\xi$. If it does not exist, the proof can be adapted by taking an estimator with risk $\varepsilon$-close to the Bayes risk for any $\varepsilon > 0$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:fDiv_ge_fDiv_mean_comp}, \begin{align*} D_f(\pi \otimes Q, \xi \otimes P) &\ge d_f(\ell' \circ (y \parallel \hat{y}_B) \circ (\pi \otimes Q) [X], \ell' \circ (y \parallel \hat{y}_B) \circ (\xi \otimes P) [X]) \\ &= d_f(\ell' \circ (y \parallel \hat{y}_B) \circ (\pi \otimes Q) [X], \mathcal R_\xi^P) \: . \end{align*} By definition of the Bayes risk as an infimum, \begin{align*} \ell' \circ (y \parallel \hat{y}_B) \circ (\pi \otimes Q) [X] \ge \mathcal R_\pi^Q \ge \mathcal R_\xi^P \: . \end{align*} Since $x \mapsto d_f(x, y)$ is monotone on $[y, 1]$, \begin{align*} D_f(\pi \otimes Q, \xi \otimes P) &\ge d_f(\ell' \circ (y \parallel \hat{y}_B) \circ (\pi \otimes Q) [X], \mathcal R_\xi^P) \\ &\ge d_f(\mathcal R_\pi^Q, \mathcal R_\xi^P) \: . \end{align*} This concludes the proof for $\mathcal R_\pi^Q \ge \mathcal R_\xi^P$. If that inequality is reversed, we proceed similarly but take the Bayes estimator for $Q$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the mean bound to the loss of a Bayes estimator and use monotonicity of $d_f(\cdot,y)$ on $[y,1]$; symmetric case similar.

nodes.name: Case $\mathcal R_\pi^Q \ge \mathcal R_\xi^P$
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $\mathcal R_\pi^Q \ge \mathcal R_\xi^P$. Let $\hat{y}_B$ be a Bayes estimator for the estimation task $(P, y, \ell')$ with prior $\xi$. If it does not exist, the proof can be adapted by taking an estimator with risk $\varepsilon$-close to the Bayes risk for any $\varepsilon > 0$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:fDiv_ge_fDiv_mean_comp}, \begin{align*} D_f(\pi \otimes Q, \xi \otimes P) &\ge d_f(\ell' \circ (y \parallel \hat{y}_B) \circ (\pi \otimes Q) [X], \ell' \circ (y \parallel \hat{y}_B) \circ (\xi \otimes P) [X]) \\ &= d_f(\ell' \circ (y \parallel \hat{y}_B) \circ (\pi \otimes Q) [X], \mathcal R_\xi^P) \: . \end{align*} By definition of the Bayes risk as an infimum, \begin{align*} \ell' \circ (y \parallel \hat{y}_B) \circ (\pi \otimes Q) [X] \ge \mathcal R_\pi^Q \ge \mathcal R_\xi^P \: . \end{align*} Since $x \mapsto d_f(x, y)$ is monotone on $[y, 1]$, \begin{align*} D_f(\pi \otimes Q, \xi \otimes P) &\ge d_f(\ell' \circ (y \parallel \hat{y}_B) \circ (\pi \otimes Q) [X], \mathcal R_\xi^P) \\ &\ge d_f(\mathcal R_\pi^Q, \mathcal R_\xi^P) \: . \end{align*} This concludes the proof for $\mathcal R_\pi^Q \ge \mathcal R_\xi^P$.
nodes.statement_short: Case $\mathcal R_\pi^Q \ge \mathcal R_\xi^P$.

nodes.name: Take a (near-)Bayes estimator for $P$
nodes.statement: Let $\hat{y}_B$ be a Bayes estimator for the estimation task $(P, y, \ell')$ with prior $\xi$. If it does not exist, the proof can be adapted by taking an estimator with risk $\varepsilon$-close to the Bayes risk for any $\varepsilon > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a (near-)Bayes estimator for $P$.

nodes.name: Bound by $d_f$ of the mean losses
nodes.statement: By Corollary~\ref{cor:fDiv_ge_fDiv_mean_comp}, \begin{align*} D_f(\pi \otimes Q, \xi \otimes P) &\ge d_f(\ell' \circ (y \parallel \hat{y}_B) \circ (\pi \otimes Q) [X], \ell' \circ (y \parallel \hat{y}_B) \circ (\xi \otimes P) [X]) \\ &= d_f(\ell' \circ (y \parallel \hat{y}_B) \circ (\pi \otimes Q) [X], \mathcal R_\xi^P) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound by $d_f$ of the mean losses.

nodes.name: Its risk under $Q$ is at least the Bayes risk
nodes.statement: By definition of the Bayes risk as an infimum, \begin{align*} \ell' \circ (y \parallel \hat{y}_B) \circ (\pi \otimes Q) [X] \ge \mathcal R_\pi^Q \ge \mathcal R_\xi^P \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Its risk under $Q$ is at least the Bayes risk.

nodes.name: Monotonicity of $d_f(\cdot, y)$ concludes
nodes.statement: Since $x \mapsto d_f(x, y)$ is monotone on $[y, 1]$, \begin{align*} D_f(\pi \otimes Q, \xi \otimes P) &\ge d_f(\ell' \circ (y \parallel \hat{y}_B) \circ (\pi \otimes Q) [X], \mathcal R_\xi^P) \\ &\ge d_f(\mathcal R_\pi^Q, \mathcal R_\xi^P) \: . \end{align*} This concludes the proof for $\mathcal R_\pi^Q \ge \mathcal R_\xi^P$.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity of $d_f(\cdot, y)$ concludes.

nodes.name: Symmetric case with the Bayes estimator for $Q$
nodes.statement: If that inequality is reversed, we proceed similarly but take the Bayes estimator for $Q$.
nodes.statement_short: Symmetric case with the Bayes estimator for $Q$.

nodes.name: Joint convexity of f-divergences
nodes.statement: The function $(\mu, \nu) \mapsto D_f(\mu, \nu)$ is convex.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu_0, \mu_1, 
u_0, 
u_1$ be four measures. Let $\lambda \in [0,1]$. Let $\xi$ be the probability measure on $\{0,1\}$ with $\xi(\{1\}) = \lambda$. Let $\kappa$ be the kernel $\{0,1\} ightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ defined by $\kappa(0) = \mu_0$ and $\kappa(1) = \mu_1$. Let $\eta$ be the kernel $\{0,1\} ightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ defined by $\eta(0) = 
u_0$ and $\eta(1) = 
u_1$.  egin{align*} D_f(\xi \otimes \kappa, \xi \otimes \eta) &= D_f(\kappa, \eta \mid \xi) = (1 - \lambda) D_f(\mu_0, 
u_0) + \lambda D_f(\mu_1,

u_0 + \lambda

Let $\mu_0, \mu_1, 
u_0, 
u_1$ be four measures. Let $\lambda \in [0,1]$. Let $\xi$ be the probability measure on $\{0,1\}$ with $\xi(\{1\}) = \lambda$. Let $\eta$ be the kernel $\{0,1\} ightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ defined by $\eta(0) = 
u_0$ and $\eta(1) = 
u_1$.  egin{align*} D_f(\xi \otimes \kappa, \xi \otimes \eta) &= D_f(\kappa, \eta \mid \xi) = (1 - \lambda) D_f(\mu_0, 
u_0) + \lambda D_f(\mu_1, 
u_1) \: , \ D_f(\kappa \circ \xi, \eta \circ \xi) &= D_f((1 - \lambda)\mu_0 + \lambda \mu_1, (1 - \lambda)
u_0 + \lambda 
u_1) \: . \end{align*}

nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{thm:fDiv_comp_le_condFDiv_2}, $D_f(\kappa \circ \xi, \eta \circ \xi) \le D_f(\xi \otimes \kappa, \xi \otimes \eta)$.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: By Taylor with integral remainder, if $f'' \le \beta g''$, \begin{align*} f(x) = \int_1^x f''(t) (x - t) dt \le \beta \int_1^x g''(t) (x - t) dt = \beta g(x) \: . \end{align*} Then use Lemma~\ref{lem:fDiv_mono_fun}.
nodes.statement_short: Taylor with integral remainder gives $f \le \beta g$, then monotonicity in $f$.

u)}{D_g(\mu,

nodes.name: Two-point measures and their divergence
nodes.statement: Let $x$ and $y$ be two points in disjoint non-empty measurable sets. For $t \in (0,1) \cup (1, +\infty)$ and $\varepsilon \in (0, 1/t]$ let $\mu_{t, \varepsilon} = t \varepsilon \delta_x + (1 - t \varepsilon) \delta_y$ and $\nu_\varepsilon = \varepsilon \delta_x + (1 - \varepsilon) \delta_y$~. \begin{align*} D_f(\mu_{t, \varepsilon}, \nu_\varepsilon) &= \varepsilon f(t) + (1 - \varepsilon) f(\frac{1 - t \varepsilon}{1 - \varepsilon}) \\ &= \varepsilon f(t) + \varepsilon (1 - t) \frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon (1 - t)} f(1 + \frac{\varepsilon(1 - t)}{1 - \varepsilon}) \end{align*}

u \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$,  egin{align*} \KL(\mu, 
u) &\ge - \log(1 - \TV^2(\mu, 
u)) \: , \ 	ext{or equivalently, } \TV(\mu, 
u) &\le \sqrt{1 - \exp\left(-\KL(\mu, 
u) ight)} \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: For $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$
nodes.label: cor:bh_kl

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Use the second inequality of Theorem~\ref{thm:bh_fDiv}, for $f: x \mapsto x \log x$~.
nodes.statement_short: Second Bretagnolle-Huber bound with $f(x) = x\log x$.

nodes.name: Bretagnolle-Huber inequality for Hellinger divergences
nodes.statement:
TODO: move this somewhere after the definition of $\He_\alpha$. Let $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$. For $\alpha > 0$,  egin{align*} \He_{1+\alpha}(\mu, 
u) &\ge  rac{1}{\alpha} \left( (1 - \TV(\mu, 
u))^{-\alpha} - 2 ight) \: , \ 	ext{or equivalently, } 1 - \TV(\mu, 
u) &\ge \exp\left(- rac{1}{\alpha} \log \left( 2 + \alpha \He_{1+\alpha}(\mu, 
u) ight)ight) \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$.
For $\alpha > 0$
nodes.label: cor:cor:bh_hellingerAlpha

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
Use the second inequality of Theorem~ef{thm:bh_fDiv}, for $f: x \mapsto  rac{x^{1+\alpha} - 1}{\alpha}$ to get  egin{align*} \He_{1+\alpha}(\mu, 
u) \ge  rac{1}{\alpha} \left((1 + \TV(\mu, 
u))^{-\alpha} + (1 - \TV(\mu, 
u))^{-\alpha} - 2 ight) \: . \end{align*} We then neglect one term: $(1 + \TV(\mu, 
u))^{-\alpha} \ge 0$.
