nodes.statement: The left mutual information $I_D^L(\pi, P)$ is an infimum: $I_D^L(\pi, P) = \inf_{\xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)} D(\pi \times \xi, \pi \otimes P)$. For all $\xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:fDiv_estimation_ge}, \begin{align*} D_f(\pi \times \xi, \pi \otimes P) &\ge d_f(\mathcal R_\pi^{\theta \mapsto \xi}, \mathcal R_\pi^P) \: . \end{align*} The risk of a constant Markov kernel is equal to the risk of the discard kernel $d_\Theta$ (TODO ref). The proof for the right mutual information is similar.

nodes.statement_short: Bound each term of the infimum with the f-divergence estimation bound; constant kernels have the risk of the discard kernel.

nodes.name: Unfold the left mutual information as an infimum
nodes.statement: The left mutual information $I_D^L(\pi, P)$ is an infimum: $I_D^L(\pi, P) = \inf_{\xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)} D(\pi \times \xi, \pi \otimes P)$.
nodes.statement_short: Unfold the left mutual information as an infimum.

nodes.name: Bound each term with the estimation lemma
nodes.statement: For all $\xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:fDiv_estimation_ge}, \begin{align*} D_f(\pi \times \xi, \pi \otimes P) &\ge d_f(\mathcal R_\pi^{\theta \mapsto \xi}, \mathcal R_\pi^P) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound each term with the estimation lemma.

nodes.statement: The risk of a constant Markov kernel is equal to the risk of the discard kernel $d_\Theta$ (TODO ref). The proof for the right mutual information is similar.

nodes.name: Bayes binary risk via the tilted measure
nodes.statement:
Let $\zeta$ be a measure such that $\mu \ll \zeta$ and $
u \ll \zeta$. Let $p =  rac{d \mu}{d\zeta}$ and $q =  rac{d 
u}{d\zeta}$. For $\alpha \in (0,1)$, for $g_\alpha(x) = \min\{(\alpha-1)x, \alpha x\}$,  egin{align*} \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u) = e^{-(1 - \alpha) R_\alpha(\xi_0\mu, \xi_1
u)} \int_x \exp \left(g_\alpha\left( \log  rac{\xi_1 q(x)}{\xi_0 p(x)} ight)ight) \partial(\xi_0\mu)^{(\alpha, \xi_1
u)} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1.1 Upper bound with the Chernoff information
assumptions: Let $\zeta$ be a measure such that $\mu \ll \zeta$ and $\nu \ll \zeta$.
Let $p = \frac{d \mu}{d\zeta}$ and $q = \frac{d \nu}{d\zeta}$.
For $\alpha \in (0,1)$, for $g_\alpha(x) = \min\{(\alpha-1)x, \alpha x\}$
nodes.label: lem:bayesBinaryRisk_eq_exp_renyi_mul_integral

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
egin{align*} \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u) &= \int_x \min \left\{\xi_0 p(x), \xi_1 q(x)ight\} \partial\zeta \ &= \int_x (\xi_0 p(x))^\alpha (\xi_1 q(x))^{1-\alpha} \min \left\{ \left( rac{\xi_0p(x)}{\xi_1q(x)}ight)^{1 - \alpha}, \left( rac{\xi_1q(x)}{\xi_0p(x)}ight)^\alphaight\} \partial\zeta \ &= e^{-(1 - \alpha) R_\alpha(\xi_0\mu, \xi_1
u)} \int_x \min \left\{ \left( rac{\xi_1q(x)}{\xi_0p(x)}ight)^{\alpha - 1}, \left( rac{\xi_1q(x)}{\xi_0p(x)}ight)^\alphaight\} \partial(\xi_0\mu)^{(\alpha, \xi_1
u)} \: . \end{align*}

nodes.statement_short: Factor $(\xi_0p)^\alpha(\xi_1q)^{1-\alpha}$ out of the minimum and recognize the tilted measure.

For $\alpha \in (0,1)$,  egin{align*} \mathcal B_\xi(\mu, 
u) \le e^{-(1 - \alpha) R_\alpha(\xi_0\mu, \xi_1
u)} = \xi_0^\alpha \xi_1^{1-\alpha} e^{-(1 - \alpha) R_\alpha(\mu, 
u)} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1.1 Upper bound with the Chernoff information
assumptions: For $\alpha \in (0,1)$
nodes.label: cor:bayesBinaryRisk_le_exp_renyi

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Use $g_\alpha(x) \le 0$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesBinaryRisk_eq_exp_renyi_mul_integral}.

nodes.statement_short: Optimize the Rényi bound over $\alpha$.

nodes.name: One minus TV bounded by exponential of Chernoff information
nodes.statement: For probability measures, \begin{align*} 1 - \TV(\mu, \nu) \le e^{- C_1(\mu, \nu)} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1.1 Upper bound with the Chernoff information
assumptions: For probability measures
nodes.label: lem:one_sub_tv_le_exp_chernoff

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
By definition, since $\mu$ and $
u$ are probability measures, $1 - \TV(\mu, 
u) = \mathcal B_{(1,1)}(\mu, 
u)$. Then apply Lemma~ef{lem:bayesBinaryRisk_le_exp_chernoff}.
nodes.section: 4.1.1 Upper bound with the Chernoff information
nodes.statement_short: $1-\TV$ is the Bayes binary risk with prior $(1,1)$; apply the Chernoff bound.

nodes.name: KL lower bound on Bayes risks
nodes.statement: Let $\pi, \xi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ and $P, Q : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$. Suppose that the loss $\ell'$ takes values in $[0,1]$. Then \begin{align*} \KL(\pi \otimes Q, \xi \otimes P) &\ge \kl(\mathcal R_\pi^Q, \mathcal R_\xi^P) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Lower bounds using the data-processing inequality
assumptions: Let $\pi, \xi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ and $P, Q : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$.
Suppose that the loss $\ell'$ takes values in $[0,1]$.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: This is Lemma~\ref{lem:fDiv_estimation_ge} specialized to the Kullback-Leibler divergence.

nodes.statement_short: Specialize the f-divergence estimation bound to KL.

nodes.name: Conditional KL lower bound on Bayes risks
nodes.statement: Let $\pi, \xi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ and $P, Q : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$. Suppose that the loss $\ell'$ takes values in $[0,1]$. Then \begin{align*} \KL(\pi \otimes Q, \pi \otimes P) &\ge \kl(\mathcal R_\pi^Q, \mathcal R_\xi^P) - \KL(\pi, \xi) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Lower bounds using the data-processing inequality
assumptions: Let $\pi, \xi \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ and $P, Q : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$.
Suppose that the loss $\ell'$ takes values in $[0,1]$.
nodes.label: cor:kl_estimation_ge_sub_kl'

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Use $\KL(\pi \otimes Q, \xi \otimes P) = \KL(\pi, \xi) + \KL(\pi \otimes Q, \pi \otimes P)$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:kl_estimation_ge}.
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Lower bounds using the data-processing inequality
nodes.statement_short: Chain rule for KL in the estimation bound.

nodes.name: KL lower bound on binary Bayes risks
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha, \beta \in (0, 1)$. Let $P, Q : \{0,1\} \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$. We write $\pi_\alpha$ for the probability measure on $\{0,1\}$ with $\pi_\alpha(\{0\}) = \alpha$. Then \begin{align*} \KL(\pi_\beta \otimes Q, \pi_\alpha \otimes P) &\ge \kl(B_\beta(Q(0), Q(1)), B_\alpha(P(0), P(1))) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Lower bounds using the data-processing inequality
assumptions: Let $\alpha, \beta \in (0, 1)$.
Let $P, Q : \{0,1\} \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$.
We write $\pi_\alpha$ for the probability measure on $\{0,1\}$ with $\pi_\alpha(\{0\}) = \alpha$.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:kl_estimation_ge}.
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Lower bounds using the data-processing inequality
nodes.statement_short: Special case of the KL estimation bound.

nodes.name: Conditional KL lower bound on binary Bayes risks
nodes.statement: Let $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and let $\alpha, \beta \in (0, 1)$. Let $P, Q : \{0,1\} \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$. We write $\pi_\alpha$ for the probability measure on $\{0,1\}$ with $\pi_\alpha(\{0\}) = \alpha$. Then \begin{align*} \KL(\pi_\beta \otimes Q, \pi_\beta \otimes P) &\ge \kl(B_\beta(Q(0), Q(1)), B_\alpha(P(0), P(1))) - \kl(\beta, \alpha) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Lower bounds using the data-processing inequality
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and let $\alpha, \beta \in (0, 1)$.
Let $P, Q : \{0,1\} \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$.
We write $\pi_\alpha$ for the probability measure on $\{0,1\}$ with $\pi_\alpha(\{0\}) = \alpha$.

nodes.name: Proof

nodes.statement_short: Special case of the conditional KL estimation bound.

nodes.name: KL to product measures lower bound on binary Bayes risk
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u, \xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and let $\alpha,  eta \in (0, 1)$. Let $P : \{0,1\} ightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ be the kernel with $P(0) = \mu$ and $P(1) = 
u$. We write $\pi_\alpha$ for the probability measure on $\{0,1\}$ with $\pi_\alpha(\{0\}) = \alpha$. Let $ ar{ eta} = \min\{ eta, 1 -  eta\}$. Then  egin{align*} \KL(\pi_\alpha \otimes P, \pi_\alpha 	imes \xi) &\ge \kl(B_\alpha(\mu, 
u),  ar{ eta}) - \kl(\alpha,  ar{ eta}) \: , \ \KL(\pi_ eta 	imes \xi, \pi_ eta \otimes P) &\ge \kl( ar{ eta}, B_\alpha(\mu, 
u)) - \kl( ar{ eta}, \alpha) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Lower bounds using the data-processing inequality
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu, \xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and let $\alpha, \beta \in (0, 1)$.
Let $P : \{0,1\} \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ be the kernel with $P(0) = \mu$ and $P(1) = \nu$.
We write $\pi_\alpha$ for the probability measure on $\{0,1\}$ with $\pi_\alpha(\{0\}) = \alpha$.
Let $\bar{\beta} = \min\{\beta, 1 - \beta\}$.
nodes.label: lem:kl_estimation_ge_prod

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: We apply Corollary~\ref{cor:kl_estimation_ge_sub_kl} for the constant kernel with value $\xi$ and use Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesBinaryRisk_self}.
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Lower bounds using the data-processing inequality
nodes.statement_short: Conditional KL bound with a constant kernel, plus the Bayes risk of identical measures.

nodes.name: Fano's inequality, binary case
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and let $\alpha \in (0, 1)$.  egin{align*} h_2(\alpha) - h_2(B_\alpha(\mu, 
u)) \le \JS_\alpha(\mu, 
u) \: , \end{align*} in which $h_2: x \mapsto x\log rac{1}{x} + (1 - x)\log rac{1}{1 - x}$ is the binary entropy function.
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Lower bounds using the data-processing inequality
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and let $\alpha \in (0, 1)$.
nodes.label: thm:sub_bayesBinaryRisk_le_jensenShannon

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
Apply Lemma~ef{lem:jensenShannon_eq_inf_kl} and then Lemma~ef{lem:kl_estimation_ge_prod} with $ eta = 1/2$ to get  egin{align*} \JS_\alpha(\mu, 
u) &= \inf_{\xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)}\KL(\pi_\alpha \otimes P, \pi_\alpha 	imes \xi) \ &\ge \kl(B_\alpha(\mu, 
u), 1/2) - \kl(\alpha, 1/2) \ &= h_2(\alpha) - h_2(B_\alpha(\mu, 
u)) \: . \end{align*} Note that $ eta = 1/2$ is the value that results in the best bound: the lower bound on $\JS_\alpha(\mu, 
u)$ from some $ eta \le 1/2$ would be  egin{align*} \kl(B_\alpha(\mu, 
u),  eta) - \kl(\alpha,  eta) &= h_2(\alpha) - h_2(B_\alpha(\mu, 
u)) - (\alpha - B_\alpha(\mu, 
u)) \log  rac{1 -  eta}{ eta} \ &\le h_2(\alpha) - h_2(B_\alpha(\mu, 
u)) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Lower bounds using the data-processing inequality
nodes.statement_short: Variational formula for JS and the product lower bound with $\beta=1/2$, which is optimal.

nodes.name: Bayes binary risk lower bound via Rényi divergence
nodes.statement:
For $\alpha,  eta \in (0, 1/2)$,  egin{align*}  eta \log rac{\alpha}{B_\alpha(\mu, 
u)} + (1 -  eta) \log rac{1 - \alpha}{1 - B_\alpha(\mu, 
u)} &\le (1 -  eta) R_{ eta}(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*} As a consequence,  egin{align*}  eta \log rac{\alpha}{B_\alpha(\mu, 
u)} &\le (1 -  eta) (R_{ eta}(\mu, 
u) + \log 2) \: . \end{align*} In particular, $\log rac{\alpha}{B_\alpha(\mu, 
u)} \le R_{1/2}(\mu, 
u) + \log 2$~.
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Lower bounds using the data-processing inequality
assumptions: For $\alpha, \beta \in (0, 1/2)$
nodes.label: thm:log_inv_bayesBinaryRisk_le_renyi

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
By Lemma~ef{lem:renyi_eq_inf_kl} and then Lemma~ef{lem:kl_estimation_ge_prod},  egin{align*} (1 -  eta) R_{ eta}(\mu, 
u) &= \inf_{\xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)} \KL(\pi_ eta 	imes \xi, \pi_ eta \otimes P) \ &\ge \kl( eta, B_\alpha(\mu, 
u)) - \kl( eta, \alpha) \ &=  eta \log rac{\alpha}{B_\alpha(\mu, 
u)} + (1 -  eta)\log rac{1 - \alpha}{1 - B_\alpha(\mu, 
u)} \: . \end{align*} The first particular case is obtained by using $\alpha \le 1/2$ and $B_\pi(\mu, 
u) \ge 0$. The second one further sets $ eta = 1/2$.
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Lower bounds using the data-processing inequality
nodes.statement_short: Variational formula for Rényi and the product lower bound, then simplify.

nodes.name: Variational formula plus the product lower bound
nodes.statement:
By Lemma~ef{lem:renyi_eq_inf_kl} and then Lemma~ef{lem:kl_estimation_ge_prod},  egin{align*} (1 -  eta) R_{ eta}(\mu, 
u) &= \inf_{\xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)} \KL(\pi_ eta 	imes \xi, \pi_ eta \otimes P) \ &\ge \kl( eta, B_\alpha(\mu, 
u)) - \kl( eta, \alpha) \ &=  eta \log rac{\alpha}{B_\alpha(\mu, 
u)} + (1 -  eta)\log rac{1 - \alpha}{1 - B_\alpha(\mu, 
u)} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Variational formula plus the product lower bound.
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Lower bounds using the data-processing inequality

nodes.name: Specialize to obtain the consequences
nodes.statement: The first particular case is obtained by using $\alpha \le 1/2$ and $B_\pi(\mu, \nu) \ge 0$. The second one further sets $\beta = 1/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize to obtain the consequences.

nodes.name: Testing bound via Rényi divergence on events
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two probability measures on $\mathcal X$ and $E$ an event. Let $\alpha \in (0,1)$. Then  egin{align*} \mu(E)^\alpha + 
u(E^c)^{1 - \alpha} \ge \exp\left(-(1 - \alpha) R_{\alpha}(\mu, 
u)ight) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Lower bounds using the data-processing inequality
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two probability measures on $\mathcal X$ and $E$ an event.
Let $\alpha \in (0,1)$.
nodes.label: lem:testing_bound_renyi_mean

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu_E$ and $
u_E$ be the two Bernoulli distributions with respective means $\mu(E)$ and $
u(E)$. By Lemma~ef{lem:renyi_data_proc_event}, $R_\alpha(\mu, 
u) \ge R_\alpha(\mu_E, 
u_E)$. That divergence is  egin{align*} R_\alpha(\mu_E, 
u_E) &=  rac{1}{\alpha - 1}\log \left(\mu(E)^\alpha 
u(E)^{1 - \alpha} + \mu(E^c)^\alpha 
u(E^c)^{1 - \alpha}ight) \ &\ge  rac{1}{\alpha - 1}\log \left(\mu(E)^\alpha + 
u(E^c)^{1 - \alpha}ight) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Lower bounds using the data-processing inequality
nodes.statement_short: Rényi DPI for the event, then drop terms in the Bernoulli Rényi divergence.

nodes.name: Reduce to Bernoulli laws via the event DPI
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu_E$ and $
u_E$ be the two Bernoulli distributions with respective means $\mu(E)$ and $
u(E)$. By Lemma~ef{lem:renyi_data_proc_event}, $R_\alpha(\mu, 
u) \ge R_\alpha(\mu_E, 
u_E)$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to Bernoulli laws via the event DPI.
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Lower bounds using the data-processing inequality

nodes.name: Compute and bound the Bernoulli Rényi divergence
nodes.statement:
That divergence is  egin{align*} R_\alpha(\mu_E, 
u_E) &=  rac{1}{\alpha - 1}\log \left(\mu(E)^\alpha 
u(E)^{1 - \alpha} + \mu(E^c)^\alpha 
u(E^c)^{1 - \alpha}ight) \ &\ge  rac{1}{\alpha - 1}\log \left(\mu(E)^\alpha + 
u(E^c)^{1 - \alpha}ight) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Compute and bound the Bernoulli Rényi divergence.
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Lower bounds using the data-processing inequality

nodes.name: Testing bound via Hellinger distance
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Lower bounds using the data-processing inequality
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two probability measures on $\mathcal X$ and $E$ an event.
nodes.label: cor:testing_bound_hellinger

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The inequality is an application of Lemma~\ref{lem:testing_bound_renyi_mean} for $\alpha = 1/2$. The equality is Lemma~\ref{lem:renyi_half_eq_log_hellinger}.
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Lower bounds using the data-processing inequality
nodes.statement_short: Rényi testing bound at $\alpha=1/2$ and the Hellinger-Rényi identity.

nodes.name: Change of measure lemma
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$ with $\mu \ll \nu$ and let $E$ be an event on $\mathcal X$.
Let $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$.
nodes.label: lem:llr_change_measure

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
egin{align*} 
u(E) \ge \mu\left[\mathbb{I}(E) e^{- \log rac{d \mu}{d 
u} }ight] &\ge \mu\left[\mathbb{I}\left(E \cap \left\{\log rac{d \mu}{d 
u} \le  etaight\}ight) e^{- \log rac{d \mu}{d 
u} }ight] \ &\ge e^{-  eta}\mu\left(E \cap \left\{\log rac{d \mu}{d 
u} \le  etaight\}ight) \ &\ge e^{-  eta}\left( \mu(E) - \mu\left\{ \log rac{d \mu}{d 
u} >  eta ight\} ight) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma
nodes.statement_short: Lower-bound $\nu(E)$ by restricting to where the log-likelihood ratio is at most $\beta$.

nodes.name: Change of measure - functions
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$ with $\mu \ll \nu$ and let $f : \mathcal X \to [0,1]$ be a measurable function.
Let $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$.
nodes.label: lem:llr_change_measure_fun

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
egin{align*} 
u[f] \ge \mu\left[f e^{- \log rac{d \mu}{d 
u} }ight] &\ge \mu\left[f \mathbb{I}\left\{\log rac{d \mu}{d 
u} \le  etaight\} e^{- \log rac{d \mu}{d 
u} }ight] \ &\ge e^{-  eta}\mu\left[f \mathbb{I}\left\{\log rac{d \mu}{d 
u} \le  etaight\} ight] \ &\ge e^{-  eta}\left( \mu[f] - \mu\left[f \mathbb{I}\left\{ \log rac{d \mu}{d 
u} >  eta ight\}ight] ight) \ &\ge e^{-  eta}\left( \mu[f] - \mu \left\{ \log rac{d \mu}{d 
u} >  eta ight\}ight) \: . \end{align*} The first and second inequalities use $f \ge 0$ and the last inequality uses $f \le 1$~.
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma
nodes.statement_short: Same chain of inequalities as for events, using $0\le f\le 1$.

nodes.name: Change of measure for Bayes risks
nodes.statement: Consider an estimation problem with loss $\ell' : \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z \to [0,1]$. Let $\pi, \zeta \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ and $P, Q : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ be such that $\zeta \otimes Q \ll \pi \otimes P$. Then for all $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$, \begin{align*} \mathcal R_\pi^P e^{\beta} \ge \mathcal R_\zeta^Q - (\zeta \otimes Q)\left\{ \log\frac{d (\zeta \otimes Q)}{d (\pi \otimes P)} > \beta \right\} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma
assumptions: Consider an estimation problem with loss $\ell' : \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z \to [0,1]$.
Let $\pi, \zeta \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ and $P, Q : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ be such that $\zeta \otimes Q \ll \pi \otimes P$.
for all $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$
conclusions: \mathcal R_\pi^P e^{\beta} \ge \mathcal R_\zeta^Q - (\zeta \otimes Q)\left\{ \log\frac{d (\zeta \otimes Q)}{d (\pi \otimes P)} > \beta \right\}
nodes.label: lem:change_measure_risk

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $\hat{y}_B$ be a Bayes estimator for $(P, y, \ell')$. If no such estimator exists, the proof can be adapted by taking an estimator with risk $\varepsilon$-close to the Bayes risk and then minimizing over $\varepsilon > 0$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:llr_change_measure_fun} to the function $(\theta, x) \mapsto \hat{y}_B(x)\left[ z \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z) \right]$~, which takes values in $[0,1]$ and to the measures $\pi \otimes P$ and $\zeta \otimes Q$. \begin{align*} \mathcal R_\pi^P e^{\beta} &\ge (\zeta \otimes Q)\left[ (\theta, x) \mapsto \hat{y}_B(x)\left[ z \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z) \right] \right] - (\zeta \otimes Q)\left\{ \log\frac{d (\zeta \otimes Q)}{d (\pi \otimes P)} > \beta \right\} \\ &\ge \mathcal R_\zeta^Q - (\zeta \otimes Q)\left\{ \log\frac{d (\zeta \otimes Q)}{d (\pi \otimes P)} > \beta \right\} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma
nodes.statement_short: Apply the functional change of measure to the expected loss of a (near-)Bayes estimator.

nodes.name: Take a (near-)Bayes estimator
nodes.statement: Let $\hat{y}_B$ be a Bayes estimator for $(P, y, \ell')$. If no such estimator exists, the proof can be adapted by taking an estimator with risk $\varepsilon$-close to the Bayes risk and then minimizing over $\varepsilon > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a (near-)Bayes estimator.
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma

nodes.name: Apply the functional change of measure to its loss
nodes.statement: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:llr_change_measure_fun} to the function $(\theta, x) \mapsto \hat{y}_B(x)\left[ z \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z) \right]$~, which takes values in $[0,1]$ and to the measures $\pi \otimes P$ and $\zeta \otimes Q$. \begin{align*} \mathcal R_\pi^P e^{\beta} &\ge (\zeta \otimes Q)\left[ (\theta, x) \mapsto \hat{y}_B(x)\left[ z \mapsto \ell'(y(\theta), z) \right] \right] - (\zeta \otimes Q)\left\{ \log\frac{d (\zeta \otimes Q)}{d (\pi \otimes P)} > \beta \right\} \\ &\ge \mathcal R_\zeta^Q - (\zeta \otimes Q)\left\{ \log\frac{d (\zeta \otimes Q)}{d (\pi \otimes P)} > \beta \right\} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the functional change of measure to its loss.
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma

nodes.name: Change of measure for Bayes risks against product measures
nodes.statement: Consider an estimation problem with loss $\ell' : \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z \to [0,1]$. Let $\pi, \zeta \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ and $P : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$. Then for all $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$, \begin{align*} \mathcal R_\pi^P e^{\beta} \ge \mathcal R_\zeta^{d_{\mathcal X}} - \inf_{\xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)}(\zeta \times \xi)\left\{ \log\frac{d (\zeta \times \xi)}{d (\pi \otimes P)} > \beta \right\} \: , \end{align*} in which the infimum over $\xi$ is restricted to probability measures such that $\zeta \times \xi \ll \pi \otimes P$ and $d_{\mathcal X} : \Theta \rightsquigarrow *$ is the discard kernel.
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma
assumptions: Consider an estimation problem with loss $\ell' : \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z \to [0,1]$.
Let $\pi, \zeta \in \mathcal P(\Theta)$ and $P : \Theta \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$.
for all $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$
conclusions: \mathcal R_\pi^P e^{\beta} \ge \mathcal R_\zeta^{d_{\mathcal X}} - \inf_{\xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)}(\zeta \times \xi)\left\{ \log\frac{d (\zeta \times \xi)}{d (\pi \otimes P)} > \beta \right\}
nodes.label: lem:change_measure_risk_inf

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: For any $\xi$, we apply Lemma~\ref{lem:change_measure_risk} to $\zeta \times \xi$ and $\pi \otimes P$ and remark that by Lemma~\ref{lem:bayesRisk_const} the risk for a constant kernel with value $\xi$ is independent of $\xi$ and equal to $\mathcal R_\zeta^{d_{\mathcal X}}$.
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma
nodes.statement_short: Apply the risk change of measure to product measures; constant kernels have the discard-kernel risk.

nodes.name: 3 points change of measure
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u, \xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and let $E$ be an event on $\mathcal X$. Let $ eta_1,  eta_2 \in \mathbb{R}$. Then  egin{align*} \mu(E) e^{ eta_1} + 
u(E^c) e^{ eta_2} \ge 1 - \xi\left\{ \log rac{d \xi}{d \mu} >  eta_1 ight\} - \xi\left\{ \log rac{d \xi}{d 
u} >  eta_2 ight\} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu, \xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and let $E$ be an event on $\mathcal X$.
Let $\beta_1, \beta_2 \in \mathbb{R}$.
nodes.label: lem:llr_change_measure_add

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Two applications of Lemma~\ref{lem:llr_change_measure}, then sum them and use $\xi(E)+\xi(E^c) = 1$.
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma
nodes.statement_short: Two applications of the change of measure lemma, summed.

nodes.name: Change of measure - mean
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $E$ be an event on $\mathcal X$.
Let $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: Proof

nodes.name: Change of measure bound on the Bayes binary risk via the tilted measure
nodes.statement:
For $\alpha \in (0,1)$, let $\pi_\alpha \in \mathcal P(\{0,1\})$ be the measure $(\alpha, 1 - \alpha)$. Let $\alpha, \gamma \in (0,1)$, $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and let $P : \{0,1\} ightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ be the kernel with $P(0) = \mu$ and $P(1) = 
u$~. Then for all $ eta \in \mathbb{R}$~,  egin{align*} &\mathcal B_{\pi_\alpha}(\mu, 
u) e^{\kl(\gamma, \alpha) + (1 - \gamma) R_\gamma(\mu, 
u) +  eta} \ &\ge \min\{\gamma, 1 - \gamma\} - (\pi_\gamma 	imes \mu^{(\gamma, 
u)})\left\{ \log rac{d (\pi_\gamma 	imes \mu^{(\gamma, 
u)})}{d (\pi_\alpha \otimes P)} > \KL(\pi_\gamma 	imes \mu^{(\gamma, 
u)}, \pi_\alpha \otimes P) +  eta ight\} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma
assumptions: For $\alpha \in (0,1)$, let $\pi_\alpha \in \mathcal P(\{0,1\})$ be the measure $(\alpha, 1 - \alpha)$.
Let $\alpha, \gamma \in (0,1)$, $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and let $P : \{0,1\} \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ be the kernel with $P(0) = \mu$ and $P(1) = \nu$~.
for all $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$
nodes.label: lem:change_measure_risk_mean

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
An application of Lemma~ef{lem:change_measure_risk_inf} gives  egin{align*} \mathcal B_{\pi_\alpha}(\mu, 
u) e^{ eta} \ge \min\{\gamma, 1 - \gamma\} - \inf_{\xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)}(\pi_\gamma 	imes \xi)\left\{ \log rac{d (\pi_\gamma 	imes \xi)}{d (\pi_\alpha \otimes P)} >  eta ight\} \: . \end{align*} Take $\xi = \mu^{(\gamma, 
u)}$ and  egin{align*}  eta &= \KL(\pi_\gamma 	imes \xi, \pi_\alpha \otimes P) +  eta' \ &= \kl(\gamma, \alpha) + \KL(\pi_\gamma 	imes \xi, \pi_\gamma \otimes P) +  eta' \ &= \kl(\gamma, \alpha) + (1 - \gamma) R_\gamma(\mu, 
u) +  eta' \: . \end{align*} We obtain  egin{align*} &\mathcal B_{\pi_\alpha}(\mu, 
u) e^{\kl(\gamma, \alpha) + (1 - \gamma) R_\gamma(\mu, 
u) +  eta'} \ &\ge \min\{\gamma, 1 - \gamma\} - (\pi_\gamma 	imes \xi)\left\{ \log rac{d (\pi_\gamma 	imes \xi)}{d (\pi_\alpha \otimes P)} > \KL(\pi_\gamma 	imes \xi, \pi_\alpha \otimes P) +  eta' ight\} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma
nodes.statement_short: Risk change of measure against products, choosing the tilted measure and a threshold shifted by the KL.

nodes.name: Change of measure against product measures
nodes.statement: An application of Lemma~\ref{lem:change_measure_risk_inf} gives \begin{align*} \mathcal B_{\pi_\alpha}(\mu, \nu) e^{\beta} \ge \min\{\gamma, 1 - \gamma\} - \inf_{\xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)}(\pi_\gamma \times \xi)\left\{ \log\frac{d (\pi_\gamma \times \xi)}{d (\pi_\alpha \otimes P)} > \beta \right\} \: . \end{align*}

nodes.name: Choose the tilted measure and shift the threshold by the KL
nodes.statement: Take $\xi = \mu^{(\gamma, \nu)}$ and \begin{align*} \beta &= \KL(\pi_\gamma \times \xi, \pi_\alpha \otimes P) + \beta' \\ &= \kl(\gamma, \alpha) + \KL(\pi_\gamma \times \xi, \pi_\gamma \otimes P) + \beta' \\ &= \kl(\gamma, \alpha) + (1 - \gamma) R_\gamma(\mu, \nu) + \beta' \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Choose the tilted measure and shift the threshold by the KL.
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma

nodes.name: Substitute
nodes.statement: We obtain \begin{align*} &\mathcal B_{\pi_\alpha}(\mu, \nu) e^{\kl(\gamma, \alpha) + (1 - \gamma) R_\gamma(\mu, \nu) + \beta'} \\ &\ge \min\{\gamma, 1 - \gamma\} - (\pi_\gamma \times \xi)\left\{ \log\frac{d (\pi_\gamma \times \xi)}{d (\pi_\alpha \otimes P)} > \KL(\pi_\gamma \times \xi, \pi_\alpha \otimes P) + \beta' \right\} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Substitute.

Let $E$ be an event on $\mathcal X$ and let $\beta > 0$.

For $\mu, 
u$ finite measures and $\alpha,  eta > 0$,  egin{align*} \mu\left\{ \log rac{d \mu}{d 
u} > R_{1+\alpha}(\mu,

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
This is a Chernoff bound, using that the cumulant generating function of $\log rac{d\mu}{d
u}$ under $\mu$ has value $\alpha R_{1+\alpha}(\mu, 
u)$ at $\alpha$ by Lemma~ef{lem:renyi_cgf_2}.  egin{align*} \mu\left\{ \log rac{d \mu}{d 
u} > R_{1+\alpha}(\mu, 
u) +  eta ight\} &= \mu\left\{ \exp\left(\alpha\log rac{d \mu}{d 
u}ight) > \exp\left(\alpha R_{1+\alpha}(\mu, 
u) + \alpha  etaight) ight\} \ &\le e^{-\alpha R_{1+\alpha}(\mu, 
u) - \alpha  eta} \mu\left[\left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}ight)^\alpha ight] \end{align*} Then $\mu\left[\left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}ight)^\alpha ight] = 
u\left[\left( rac{d \mu}{d 
u}ight)^{1+\alpha} ight] = e^{\alpha R_{1+\alpha}(\mu, 
u)}$.

Let $\alpha,\beta > 0$.

nodes.name: Proof

nodes.name: Change of measure bound on the Bayes binary risk via Rényi divergence
nodes.statement:
For $\alpha \in (0,1)$, let $\pi_\alpha \in \mathcal P(\{0,1\})$ be the measure $(\alpha, 1 - \alpha)$. Let $\alpha, \gamma \in (0,1)$, $\mu, 
u \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and let $P : \{0,1\} ightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ be the kernel with $P(0) = \mu$ and $P(1) = 
u$~. Then for all $ eta > 0$ and $\varepsilon>0$~,  egin{align*} \mathcal B_{\pi_\alpha}(\mu, 
u) e^{\inf_{\xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)} R_{1 + \varepsilon}(\pi_\gamma 	imes \xi, \pi_\alpha \otimes P) +  eta} &\ge \min\{\gamma, 1 - \gamma\} - e^{-\varepsilon  eta} \: . \end{align*}

Let $\alpha, \gamma \in (0,1)$, $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and let $P : \{0,1\} \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ be the kernel with $P(0) = \mu$ and $P(1) = \nu$~.
for all $\beta > 0$ and $\varepsilon>0$
conclusions: \mathcal B_{\pi_\alpha}(\mu, \nu) e^{\inf_{\xi \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)} R_{1 + \varepsilon}(\pi_\gamma \times \xi, \pi_\alpha \otimes P) + \beta} &\ge \min\{\gamma, 1 - \gamma\} - e^{-\varepsilon \beta}
nodes.label: lem:change_measure_risk_cgf

nodes.name: 3 points change of measure with variance
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u, \xi$ be three probability measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $E$ be an event on $\mathcal X$. For $ eta > 0$~,  egin{align*} \mu(E) e^{\KL(\xi, \mu) + \sqrt{ eta \Var_{\xi}\left[\log rac{d\xi}{d\mu}ight]}} + 
u(E^c) e^{\KL(\xi, 
u) + \sqrt{ eta \Var_{\xi}\left[\log rac{d\xi}{d
u}ight]}} \ge 1 -  rac{2}{ eta} \: . \end{align*}

assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu, \xi$ be three probability measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $E$ be an event on $\mathcal X$.
For $\beta > 0$

nodes.name: Proof

Then use Chebyshev's inequality to bound the probabilities of deviation of the log-likelihood ratios.

nodes.name: 3 points change of measure with Rényi divergence
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u, \xi$ be three probability measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $E$ be an event on $\mathcal X$. Let $\alpha,  eta \ge 0$. Then  egin{align*} \mu(E) e^{R_{1+\alpha}(\xi, \mu) +  eta} + 
u(E^c) e^{R_{1+\alpha}(\xi, 
u) +  eta} \ge 1 - 2 e^{-\alpha  eta} \: . \end{align*}

assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu, \xi$ be three probability measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $E$ be an event on $\mathcal X$.
Let $\alpha, \beta \ge 0$.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Use Lemma~\ref{lem:llr_change_measure_add} with the choices $R_{1+\alpha}(\xi, \mu) + \beta$ and $R_{1+\alpha}(\xi, \nu) + \beta$ for $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$. Then apply Lemma~\ref{lem:renyi_chernoff_bound}.
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma
nodes.statement_short: Three-point change of measure with Rényi thresholds and the Rényi Chernoff bound.

nodes.name: Testing lower bound via Chernoff divergence of order 1+alpha
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two probability measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $E$ be an event on $\mathcal X$. Let $\alpha > 0$. Then  egin{align*} \mu(E) + 
u(E^c) \ge  rac{1}{2}\exp\left( - C_{1+\alpha}(\mu, 
u) -  rac{\log 4}{\alpha}ight) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two probability measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $E$ be an event on $\mathcal X$.
Let $\alpha > 0$.
nodes.label: lem:testing_bound_renyi_one_add

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
Use Lemma~ef{lem:renyi_change_measure_add} with $ eta = \log(4)/\alpha$ and use that  egin{align*} \mu(E) e^{R_{1+\alpha}(\xi, \mu) +  eta} + 
u(E^c) e^{R_{1+\alpha}(\xi, 
u) +  eta} \le (\mu(E) + 
u(E^c)) e^{\max \{R_{1+\alpha}(\xi, \mu), R_{1+\alpha}(\xi, 
u)\} +  eta} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma
nodes.statement_short: Three-point Rényi bound with $\beta=\log 4/\alpha$, bounding both exponents by their max.

nodes.name: Testing lower bound for i.i.d. products via Chernoff divergence
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two probability measures on $\mathcal X$, let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $E$ be an event on $\mathcal X^n$. For all $\alpha > 0$,  egin{align*} \mu^{\otimes n}(E) + 
u^{\otimes n}(E^c) \ge  rac{1}{2}\exp\left( - n C_{1+ rac{\alpha}{\sqrt{n}}}(\mu, 
u) -  rac{\log 4}{\alpha}\sqrt{n}ight) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two probability measures on $\mathcal X$, let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $E$ be an event on $\mathcal X^n$.
For all $\alpha > 0$
nodes.label: lem:testing_bound_renyi_one_add_n

nodes.name: Proof

nodes.statement_short: Tensorization of Rényi divergences in the single-sample testing bound.

nodes.name: Asymptotic testing lower bound via Chernoff information
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu, 
u$ be two probability measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $(E_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be events on $\mathcal X^n$. For all $\gamma \in (0,1)$,  egin{align*} \limsup_{n 	o +\infty}  rac{1}{n}\log  rac{1}{\gamma \mu^{\otimes n}(E_n) + (1 - \gamma)
u^{\otimes n}(E_n^c)} \le C_1(\mu, 
u) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma
nodes.statement_short: The exponential decay rate of any sequence of tests is at most the Chernoff information.
assumptions: Let $\mu, \nu$ be two probability measures on $\mathcal X$ and let $(E_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be events on $\mathcal X^n$.
For all $\gamma \in (0,1)$
nodes.label: thm:testing_bound_chernoff

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
Let $\xi$ be a probability measure on $\mathcal X$ and $ eta > 0$. By Corollary~ef{cor:kl_change_measure},  egin{align*} \mu^{\otimes n}(E_n) e^{\KL(\xi^{\otimes n}, \mu^{\otimes n}) + n eta} &\ge \xi^{\otimes n}(E_n) - \xi^{\otimes n}\left\{ \log rac{d \xi^{\otimes n}}{d \mu^{\otimes n}} - \KL(\xi^{\otimes n}, \mu^{\otimes n}) > n eta ight\} \: , \ 
u^{\otimes n}(E_n^c) e^{\KL(\xi^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n}) + n eta} &\ge \xi^{\otimes n}(E_n^c) - \xi^{\otimes n}\left\{ \log rac{d \xi^{\otimes n}}{d 
u^{\otimes n}} - \KL(\xi^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n}) > n eta ight\} \: . \end{align*} We sum both inequalities with weights $\gamma$ and $1-\gamma$ respectively and use that each $\KL$ on the left is less than their max, as well as $\xi^{\otimes n}(E_n) + \xi^{\otimes n}(E_n^c) = 1$.  egin{align*} &e^{n eta} (\gamma\mu^{\otimes n}(E_n) + (1-\gamma)
u^{\otimes n}(E_n^c)) e^{\max\{\KL(\xi^{\otimes n}, \mu^{\otimes n}), \KL(\xi^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n})\}} \ &\ge \min\{\gamma, 1-\gamma\} - \gamma\xi^{\otimes n}\left\{ \log rac{d \xi^{\otimes n}}{d \mu^{\otimes n}} - \KL(\xi^{\otimes n}, \mu^{\otimes n}) > n eta ight\} - (1 - \gamma)\xi^{\otimes n}\left\{ \log rac{d \xi^{\otimes n}}{d 
u^{\otimes n}} - \KL(\xi^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n}) > n eta ight\} \: . \end{align*} Let $p_{n,\mu}( eta)$ and $p_{n, 
u}( eta)$ be the two probabilities on the right hand side. By the law of large numbers, both tend to 0 when $n$ tends to $+\infty$. In particular, for $n$ large enough, the right hand side is positive and we can take logarithms on both sides. We also use the tensorization of $\KL$ (Theorem~ef{thm:kl_pi}).  egin{align*} & n \max\{\KL(\xi, \mu), \KL(\xi, 
u)\} \ &\ge \log  rac{1}{\gamma \mu^{\otimes n}(E_n) + (1 - \gamma)
u^{\otimes n}(E_n^c)} + \log (\min\{\gamma, 1-\gamma\} - \gamma p_{n, \mu}( eta) - (1 - \gamma) p_{n, 
u}( eta)) - n eta \end{align*} For $n 	o +\infty$,  egin{align*} \max\{\KL(\xi, \mu), \KL(\xi, 
u)\} \ge \limsup_{n 	o + \infty} rac{1}{n}\log  rac{1}{\gamma \mu^{\otimes n}(E_n) + (1 - \gamma)
u^{\otimes n}(E_n^c)} -  eta \end{align*} Since $ eta > 0$ is arbitrary, we can take a supremum over $ eta$ on the right.
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma
nodes.statement_short: Change of measure towards $\xi^{\otimes n}$ for both hypotheses, law of large numbers for the deviations, and KL tensorization; then optimize.

nodes.name: Mean change of measure towards $\xi^{\otimes n}$ for both hypotheses
nodes.statement:
Let $\xi$ be a probability measure on $\mathcal X$ and $ eta > 0$. By Corollary~ef{cor:kl_change_measure},  egin{align*} \mu^{\otimes n}(E_n) e^{\KL(\xi^{\otimes n}, \mu^{\otimes n}) + n eta} &\ge \xi^{\otimes n}(E_n) - \xi^{\otimes n}\left\{ \log rac{d \xi^{\otimes n}}{d \mu^{\otimes n}} - \KL(\xi^{\otimes n}, \mu^{\otimes n}) > n eta ight\} \: , \ 
u^{\otimes n}(E_n^c) e^{\KL(\xi^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n}) + n eta} &\ge \xi^{\otimes n}(E_n^c) - \xi^{\otimes n}\left\{ \log rac{d \xi^{\otimes n}}{d 
u^{\otimes n}} - \KL(\xi^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n}) > n eta ight\} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Mean change of measure towards $\xi^{\otimes n}$ for both hypotheses.
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma

nodes.name: Weighted sum, bounding both KLs by their max
nodes.statement:
We sum both inequalities with weights $\gamma$ and $1-\gamma$ respectively and use that each $\KL$ on the left is less than their max, as well as $\xi^{\otimes n}(E_n) + \xi^{\otimes n}(E_n^c) = 1$.  egin{align*} &e^{n eta} (\gamma\mu^{\otimes n}(E_n) + (1-\gamma)
u^{\otimes n}(E_n^c)) e^{\max\{\KL(\xi^{\otimes n}, \mu^{\otimes n}), \KL(\xi^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n})\}} \ &\ge \min\{\gamma, 1-\gamma\} - \gamma\xi^{\otimes n}\left\{ \log rac{d \xi^{\otimes n}}{d \mu^{\otimes n}} - \KL(\xi^{\otimes n}, \mu^{\otimes n}) > n eta ight\} - (1 - \gamma)\xi^{\otimes n}\left\{ \log rac{d \xi^{\otimes n}}{d 
u^{\otimes n}} - \KL(\xi^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n}) > n eta ight\} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Weighted sum, bounding both KLs by their max.
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma

nodes.name: Deviation probabilities vanish by the law of large numbers
nodes.statement: Let $p_{n,\mu}(\beta)$ and $p_{n, \nu}(\beta)$ be the two probabilities on the right hand side. By the law of large numbers, both tend to 0 when $n$ tends to $+\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Deviation probabilities vanish by the law of large numbers.
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma

nodes.name: Take logarithms and tensorize KL
nodes.statement:
In particular, for $n$ large enough, the right hand side is positive and we can take logarithms on both sides. We also use the tensorization of $\KL$ (Theorem~ef{thm:kl_pi}).  egin{align*} & n \max\{\KL(\xi, \mu), \KL(\xi, 
u)\} \ &\ge \log  rac{1}{\gamma \mu^{\otimes n}(E_n) + (1 - \gamma)
u^{\otimes n}(E_n^c)} + \log (\min\{\gamma, 1-\gamma\} - \gamma p_{n, \mu}( eta) - (1 - \gamma) p_{n, 
u}( eta)) - n eta \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Take logarithms and tensorize KL.
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma

nodes.name: Pass to the limit and let $\beta \to 0$
nodes.statement: For $n \to +\infty$, \begin{align*} \max\{\KL(\xi, \mu), \KL(\xi, \nu)\} \ge \limsup_{n \to + \infty}\frac{1}{n}\log \frac{1}{\gamma \mu^{\otimes n}(E_n) + (1 - \gamma)\nu^{\otimes n}(E_n^c)} - \beta \end{align*} Since $\beta > 0$ is arbitrary, we can take a supremum over $\beta$ on the right.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to the limit and let $\beta \to 0$.
nodes.section: 4.1.3 Lower bounds using the change of measure lemma

nodes.name: Sample complexity of simple binary hypothesis testing
nodes.statement: The sample complexity of simple binary hypothesis testing with prior $(\pi, 1 - \pi) \in \mathcal P(\{0, 1\})$ at risk level $\delta \in \mathbb{R}_{+, \infty}$ is \begin{align*} n(\mu, \nu, \pi, \delta) = \min\{n \in \mathbb{N} \mid B_\pi(\mu^{\otimes n}, \nu^{\otimes n}) \le \delta\} \: . \end{align*} This is the sample complexity $n_\xi^P(\delta)$ of Definition~\ref{def:priorSampleComplexity} specialized to simple binary hypothesis testing.
nodes.label: def:binaryPriorSampleComplexity

nodes.name: Sample complexity is zero for large risk level
nodes.statement: For $\delta \ge \min\{\pi, 1 - \pi\}$, the sample complexity of simple binary hypothesis testing is $n(\mu, \nu, \pi, \delta) = 0$~.
assumptions: For $\delta \ge \min\{\pi, 1 - \pi\}$
nodes.label: lem:binaryPriorSampleComplexity_eq_zero

nodes.name: Upper bound on the binary sample complexity via Rényi divergences
nodes.statement: The sample complexity of simple binary hypothesis testing satisfies $n(\mu, \nu, \pi, \delta) \le n_0$~, with $n_0$ the smallest natural number such that \begin{align*} \log\frac{1}{\delta} \le \sup_{\alpha \in (0,1)} \left( n_0 (1 - \alpha)R_\alpha(\mu, \nu) + \alpha\log\frac{1}{\pi} + (1 - \alpha)\log\frac{1}{1 - \pi} \right) \end{align*}
conclusions: $n(\mu, \nu, \pi, \delta) \le n_0$~, with $n_0$ the smallest natural number such that \begin{align*} \log\frac{1}{\delta} \le \sup_{\alpha \in (0,1)} \left( n_0 (1 - \alpha)R_\alpha(\mu, \nu) + \alpha\log\frac{1}{\pi} + (1 - \alpha)\log\frac{1}{1 - \pi} \right)
nodes.label: lem:binaryPriorSampleComplexity_le_renyi

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
It suffices to show that $B_\pi(\mu^{\otimes n_0}, 
u^{\otimes n_0}) \le \delta$~. By Corollary~ef{cor:bayesBinaryRisk_le_exp_renyi}, for all $\alpha \in (0,1)$,  egin{align*} B_\pi(\mu^{\otimes n_0}, 
u^{\otimes n_0}) &\le \pi^{\alpha} (1 - \pi)^{1 - \alpha}e^{- (1 - \alpha)R_\alpha(\mu^{\otimes n_0}, 
u^{\otimes n_0})} \: . \end{align*} The Rényi divergence tensorizes: $R_\alpha(\mu^{\otimes n_0}, 
u^{\otimes n_0}) = n_0 R_\alpha(\mu, 
u)$~.  egin{align*} B_\pi(\mu^{\otimes n_0}, 
u^{\otimes n_0}) &\le \exp\left(- \left( n_0 (1 - \alpha)R_\alpha(\mu, 
u) + \alpha\log rac{1}{\pi} + (1 - \alpha)\log rac{1}{1 - \pi} ight) ight) \: . \end{align*} By definition, $n_0$ is such that the infimum over $\alpha$ of the right hand side is less than $\delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the Bayes risk of $n_0$ samples by the Rényi bound and tensorize.

nodes.name: Reduce to bounding the Bayes risk at $n_0$
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that $B_\pi(\mu^{\otimes n_0}, \nu^{\otimes n_0}) \le \delta$~.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to bounding the Bayes risk at $n_0$.

nodes.name: Rényi upper bound on the Bayes binary risk
nodes.statement: By Corollary~\ref{cor:bayesBinaryRisk_le_exp_renyi}, for all $\alpha \in (0,1)$, \begin{align*} B_\pi(\mu^{\otimes n_0}, \nu^{\otimes n_0}) &\le \pi^{\alpha} (1 - \pi)^{1 - \alpha}e^{- (1 - \alpha)R_\alpha(\mu^{\otimes n_0}, \nu^{\otimes n_0})} \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Rényi upper bound on the Bayes binary risk.

nodes.name: Tensorize the Rényi divergence
nodes.statement:
The Rényi divergence tensorizes: $R_\alpha(\mu^{\otimes n_0}, 
u^{\otimes n_0}) = n_0 R_\alpha(\mu, 
u)$~.  egin{align*} B_\pi(\mu^{\otimes n_0}, 
u^{\otimes n_0}) &\le \exp\left(- \left( n_0 (1 - \alpha)R_\alpha(\mu, 
u) + \alpha\log rac{1}{\pi} + (1 - \alpha)\log rac{1}{1 - \pi} ight) ight) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Tensorize the Rényi divergence.

nodes.name: Conclude from the definition of $n_0$
nodes.statement: By definition, $n_0$ is such that the infimum over $\alpha$ of the right hand side is less than $\delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude from the definition of $n_0$.

nodes.name: Lower bound on the binary sample complexity via Rényi divergence of order 1/2
nodes.statement: For $\delta \le \pi \le 1/2$, the sample complexity of simple binary hypothesis testing satisfies \begin{align*} n(\mu, \nu, \pi, \delta) \ge \frac{\log\frac{\pi}{2\delta}}{R_{1/2}(\mu, \nu)} \: . \end{align*}
assumptions: For $\delta \le \pi \le 1/2$
nodes.label: lem:binaryPriorSampleComplexity_ge_renyi

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
By Theorem~ef{thm:log_inv_bayesBinaryRisk_le_renyi},  egin{align*} \log rac{\pi}{B_\pi(\mu^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n})} \le R_{1/2}(\mu^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n}) + \log 2 \: . \end{align*} The Rényi divergence tensorizes (Theorem~ef{lem:renyi_prod_n}): $R_{1/2}(\mu^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n}) = n R_{1/2}(\mu, 
u)$~. We finally use that $B_\pi(\mu^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n}) \le \delta$ for $n = n(\mu, 
u, \pi, \delta)$~.
nodes.statement_short: Rényi lower bound on the Bayes risk with tensorization of $R_{1/2}$.

nodes.name: Rényi lower bound on the Bayes risk of $n$ samples
nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{thm:log_inv_bayesBinaryRisk_le_renyi}, \begin{align*} \log\frac{\pi}{B_\pi(\mu^{\otimes n}, \nu^{\otimes n})} \le R_{1/2}(\mu^{\otimes n}, \nu^{\otimes n}) + \log 2 \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Rényi lower bound on the Bayes risk of $n$ samples.

nodes.name: Tensorize $R_{1/2}$
nodes.statement: The Rényi divergence tensorizes (Theorem~\ref{lem:renyi_prod_n}): $R_{1/2}(\mu^{\otimes n}, \nu^{\otimes n}) = n R_{1/2}(\mu, \nu)$~.
nodes.statement_short: Tensorize $R_{1/2}$.

nodes.name: Use the risk level at the sample complexity
nodes.statement: We finally use that $B_\pi(\mu^{\otimes n}, \nu^{\otimes n}) \le \delta$ for $n = n(\mu, \nu, \pi, \delta)$~.
nodes.statement_short: Use the risk level at the sample complexity.

nodes.name: Lower bound on the binary sample complexity via Jensen-Shannon divergence
nodes.statement: For $\delta \le \min\{\pi, 1 - \pi\}$, the sample complexity of simple binary hypothesis testing satisfies \begin{align*} n(\mu, \nu, \pi, \delta) \ge \frac{h_2(\pi) - h_2(\delta)}{\JS_\pi(\mu, \nu)} \: , \end{align*} in which $h_2: x \mapsto x\log\frac{1}{x} + (1 - x)\log\frac{1}{1 - x}$ is the binary entropy function.
assumptions: For $\delta \le \min\{\pi, 1 - \pi\}$
nodes.label: lem:binaryPriorSampleComplexity_ge_jensenShannon

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
We start from Theorem~ef{thm:sub_bayesBinaryRisk_le_jensenShannon}.  egin{align*} \JS_\pi(\mu^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n}) \ge h_2(\pi) - h_2(B_\pi(\mu^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n})) \: . \end{align*} By Lemma~ef{lem:jensenShannon_prod_n}, $\JS_\pi(\mu^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n}) \le n \JS_\pi(\mu, 
u)$. The final result is obtained by using that $B_\pi(\mu^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n}) \le \delta$ for $n = n(\mu, 
u, \pi, \delta)$.
nodes.statement_short: Binary Fano inequality plus subadditivity of JS over products.

nodes.name: Apply binary Fano to the product measures
nodes.statement: We start from Theorem~\ref{thm:sub_bayesBinaryRisk_le_jensenShannon}. \begin{align*} \JS_\pi(\mu^{\otimes n}, \nu^{\otimes n}) \ge h_2(\pi) - h_2(B_\pi(\mu^{\otimes n}, \nu^{\otimes n})) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply binary Fano to the product measures.

nodes.name: Subadditivity of JS and the risk level conclude
nodes.statement:
By Lemma~ef{lem:jensenShannon_prod_n}, $\JS_\pi(\mu^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n}) \le n \JS_\pi(\mu, 
u)$. The final result is obtained by using that $B_\pi(\mu^{\otimes n}, 
u^{\otimes n}) \le \delta$ for $n = n(\mu,

nodes.statement_short: Subadditivity of JS and the risk level conclude.

nodes.name: Wald's equation
nodes.statement: Let $\mu \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ and let $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be $\mu$-integrable real random variables. Let $\tau$ be a random variable with value in $\mathbb{N}$. Suppose that $\mu[X_n \mathbb{I}\{\tau \ge n\}] = \mu[X_n]\mu\{\tau \ge n\}$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and that $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu[|X_n| \mathbb{I}\{\tau \ge n\}] < \infty$. Then the sums $S_\tau = \sum_{n=1}^\tau X_n$ and $T_\tau = \sum_{n=1}^\tau \mu[X_n]$ are integrable and $\mu[S_\tau] = \mu[T_\tau]$.

nodes.name: Measurable space of measures
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal B$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$. Let $\mathcal X$ be a measurable space. For a measurable set $s$ of $\mathcal X$, let $(\mu \mapsto \mu(s))^* \mathcal B$ be the $\sigma$-algebra on $\mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ defined by the comap of the evaluation function at $s$. Then $\mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ is a measurable space with $\sigma$-algebra $\bigsqcup_{s} (\mu \mapsto \mu(s))^* \mathcal B$ where the supremum is over all measurable sets $s$.
nodes.label: def:measure_measurableSpace

nodes.name: Measurability of measure-valued functions
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal X, \mathcal Y$ be measurable spaces, and let $f : \mathcal X \to \mathcal M(\mathcal Y)$ such that for all measurable sets $s$ of $\mathcal X$, the function $x \mapsto f(x)(s)$ is measurable. Then $f$ is measurable.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal X, \mathcal Y$ be measurable spaces, and let $f : \mathcal X \to \mathcal M(\mathcal Y)$ such that for all measurable sets $s$ of $\mathcal X$, the function $x \mapsto f(x)(s)$ is measurable.
nodes.label: lem:measurable_measure_fun

nodes.name: Kernel
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal X, \mathcal Y$ be two measurable spaces. A probability transition kernel (or simply kernel) from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$ is a measurable map from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal M (\mathcal Y)$, the measurable space of measures on $\mathcal Y$. We write $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ for a kernel $\kappa$ from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$.
also_stated_at: $\kappa, \eta$ are used to refer to transition kernels, and we write $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ to indicate that $\kappa$ is a transition kernel from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$. That is, $\kappa$ is a measurable map from $\mathcal X$ to the measures on $\mathcal Y$.
nodes.label: def:kernel

nodes.name: Deterministic kernel
nodes.statement: The deterministic kernel defined by a measurable function $f : \mathcal X \to \mathcal Y$ is the kernel $d_f: \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ defined by $d_f(x) = \delta_{f(x)}$, where for any $y \in \mathcal Y$, $\delta_y$ is the Dirac probability measure at $y$.
nodes.label: def:deterministic_kernel

nodes.name: Copy kernel
nodes.statement: The copy kernel $c_{\mathcal X} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X \times \mathcal X$, from the function $x \mapsto (x, x)$.

nodes.name: Kernel extensionality
nodes.statement: Two kernels $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ are equal iff for all measurable functions $f : \mathcal Y \to \mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$ and all $x \in \mathcal X$, \begin{align*} \int_y f(y) \partial \kappa(x) = \int_y f(y) \partial \eta(x) \: . \end{align*}
conclusions: Two kernels $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ are equal iff for all measurable functions $f : \mathcal Y \to \mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$ and all $x \in \mathcal X$, \begin{align*} \int_y f(y) \partial \kappa(x) = \int_y f(y) \partial \eta(x)
equivalent_conditions: Two kernels $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ are equal
for all measurable functions $f : \mathcal Y \to \mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$ and all $x \in \mathcal X$, \begin{align*} \int_y f(y) \partial \kappa(x) = \int_y f(y) \partial \eta(x)
nodes.label: thm:kernel_ext

nodes.name: Finite kernel
nodes.statement: A kernel $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ is said to be finite if there exists $C < +\infty$ such that for all $x \in \mathcal X$, $\kappa(x)(\mathcal Y) \le C$.
also_stated_at: A kernel is finite if there exists $C < + \infty$ such that $\kappa(x, \mathcal Y) \le C$ for all $x \in \mathcal X$ (note that this is stronger than the condition that all $\kappa(x)$ are finite since it requires a uniform bound).
nodes.label: def:finite_kernel

nodes.name: Markov kernel
nodes.statement: A kernel $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ is said to be a Markov kernel if for all $x \in \mathcal X$, $\kappa(x)$ is a probability measure.
also_stated_at: It is s-finite if it can be written as a countable sum of finite kernels, and is called a Markov kernel if $\kappa(x)$ is a probability measure for all $x \in \mathcal X$.
nodes.label: def:markov_kernel

nodes.name: Markov kernels are finite
nodes.statement: A Markov kernel is finite, with constant $C = 1$.

nodes.name: s-finite kernel
nodes.statement: A kernel $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ is said to be a s-finite if it is equal to a countable sum of finite kernels.
nodes.label: def:sFinite_kernel

nodes.name: Composition-product
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ and $\eta : (\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y) \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ be two s-finite kernels. The composition-product of $\kappa$ and $\eta$ is a kernel $\kappa \otimes \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow (\mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z)$ such that for all measurable functions $f : \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z \to \mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$ and $x \in \mathcal X$~, \begin{align*} \int_{y,z} f(y,z) \partial(\kappa \otimes \eta)(x) = \int_y \int_z f(y,z) \partial\eta(x,y) \partial\kappa(x) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:kernel_compProd

nodes.name: Composition-product with a kernel independent of the first coordinate
nodes.statement: The composition-product is defined for $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ and $\eta : \mathcal X \times \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$, but since a kernel $\mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ can be seen as a kernel $\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ independent of the first coordinate, we abuse notation and also write $\kappa \otimes \xi$ for $\xi : \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$.

nodes.name: Composition-product of a measure and a kernel
nodes.statement: Let $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ be an s-finite measure and $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be an s-finite kernel. Let $\mathcal U$ be a measurable space with a unique element $u$. Let $\mu_k : \mathcal U \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ be the constant kernel with value $\mu$. The composition-product of $\mu$ and $\kappa$ is the measure on $\mathcal M(\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y)$ defined by $(\mu_k \otimes \kappa) (u)$~.
nodes.label: def:measure_compProd

nodes.name: Composition
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ and $\eta : \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ be two kernels. The composition of $\kappa$ and $\eta$ is the kernel $\eta \circ \kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ such that for all measurable functions $f : \mathcal Z \to \mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$ and all $x \in \mathcal X$, \begin{align*} \int_z f(z) \partial(\eta \circ \kappa)(x) = \int_y \int_z f(z) \partial\eta(y) \partial\kappa(x) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:kernel_comp

nodes.name: Composition of a measure and a kernel
nodes.statement: We can also define the composition of a measure and a kernel, by $\kappa \circ \mu = (\kappa \circ \mu_k) (u)$, where $\mathcal U$ is a measurable space with a unique element $u$ and $\mu_k : \mathcal U \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ is the constant kernel with value $\mu$.

nodes.name: Product
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ and $\eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ be two s-finite kernels. The product of $\kappa$ and $\eta$ is the kernel $\kappa \times \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z$ such that for all measurable functions $f : \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z \to \mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$ and all $x \in \mathcal X$, \begin{align*} \int_{y,z} f(y,z) \partial(\kappa \times \eta)(x) = \int_y \int_z f(y,z) \partial\eta(x) \partial\kappa(x) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:kernel_prod

nodes.name: Composition-product as a composition
nodes.statement:
For $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ and $\eta : \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ (independent of $\mathcal X$), the composition-product can be written as a composition: $\kappa \otimes \eta = (d_{\text{id}} \times \eta) \circ \kappa$ where $d_{\text{id}}$ is the deterministic kernel for the identity.
In particular, the composition-product of a measure and a kernel $\kappa$ is the composition of that measure with the kernel $d_{\text{id}} \times \kappa$.

nodes.name: Parallel product
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ and $\eta : \mathcal X' \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y'$ be two s-finite kernels. The parallel product of $\kappa$ and $\eta$ is the kernel $\kappa \parallel \eta : \mathcal X \times \mathcal X' \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Y'$ such that for all measurable functions $f : \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Y' \to \mathbb{R}_{+,\infty}$ and all $x \in \mathcal X \times \mathcal X'$, \begin{align*} \int_{y,y'} f(y,y') \partial(\kappa \parallel \eta)(x,x') = \int_y \int_{y'} f(y,y') \partial\eta(x') \partial\kappa(x) \: . \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:kernel_parallel_prod

nodes.name: Kernels form a copy-discard category
nodes.statement:
Measurable spaces and s-finite kernels are a copy-discard category (and in particular a symmetric monoidal category) with the following data:
\begin{itemize}
  \item Objects: measurable spaces
  \item Morphisms: s-finite kernels, with identity kernels and composition of kernels
  \item Tensor product of objects: product of measurable spaces $\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y$
  \item Tensor product of morphisms: parallel product $\kappa \parallel \eta$ 
  \item Unit: measurable space with one element (denoted by $*$)
  \item The associator, left and right unitors and braiding are given by the deterministic kernels of the corresponding equivalences between measurable spaces
  \item Copy morphism: $c_{\mathcal X}: \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X \times \mathcal X$
  \item Delete morphism: $d_{\mathcal X} : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow *$
\end{itemize}

nodes.name: Markov category
nodes.statement: If we restrict the morphisms to Markov kernels, we get a Markov category (TODO ref), which is a copy-discard category in which for every morphism $\kappa$, $d_{\mathcal Y} \circ \kappa = d_{\mathcal X}$.

nodes.name: Blackwell sufficiency
nodes.statement: We define a partial order on kernels by the following. Let $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ and $\eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ (with same domain as $\kappa$). Then $\kappa$ is Blackwell sufficient for $\eta$, denoted by $\eta \le_B \kappa$, if there exists a Markov kernel $\xi : \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ such that $\eta = \xi \circ \kappa$.
nodes.label: def:blackwellOrder

nodes.name: Disintegrating kernel
nodes.statement: A kernel $\eta : \mathcal X \times \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ is said to disintegrate a kernel $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z$ if $\kappa = \kappa_{Y} \otimes \eta$.

nodes.name: Disintegration in standard Borel spaces
nodes.statement: If either $\mathcal X$ is countable of $\mathcal Y$ has a countably generated $\sigma$-algebra, and $\mathcal Z$ is standard Borel, then for every s-finite kernel $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z$, there exists a Markov kernel $\kappa_{Z \mid Y} : \mathcal X \times \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ that disintegrates $\kappa$.
assumptions: If either $\mathcal X$ is countable of $\mathcal Y$ has a countably generated $\sigma$-algebra, and $\mathcal Z$ is standard Borel
conclusions: for every s-finite kernel $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y \times \mathcal Z$, there exists a Markov kernel $\kappa_{Z \mid Y} : \mathcal X \times \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Z$ that disintegrates $\kappa$
nodes.label: thm:disintegration

nodes.name: Bayesian inverse
nodes.statement: For $\mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ and $\kappa : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$, a Bayesian inverse of $\kappa$ is a Markov kernel $\kappa_\mu^\dagger : \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$ such that $\mu \otimes \kappa = ((\kappa \circ \mu) \otimes \kappa_\mu^\dagger)_\leftrightarrow$ in which $(\cdot)_\leftrightarrow$ denotes swapping the two coordinates. If such an inverse exists it is unique up to a $(\kappa \circ \mu)$-null set, and we talk about \emph{the} Bayesian inverse of $\kappa$ with respect to $\mu$.
nodes.section: A.7 Bayesian inverse of a kernel
nodes.label: def:bayesInv

nodes.name: Existence of the Bayesian inverse
nodes.statement: For $\mathcal X$ standard Borel, $\mu$ and $\kappa$ s-finite, the Bayesian inverse of $\kappa$ with respect to $\mu$ exists and is obtained by disintegration of the measure $\mu \otimes \kappa$ on $\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y$ into a measure $\kappa \circ \mu \in \mathcal M(\mathcal Y)$ and a Markov kernel $\kappa_\mu^\dagger : \mathcal Y \rightsquigarrow \mathcal X$.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: $\mu$-almost all $x$ and $(\kappa \circ \mu)$-almost all $y$ is the same as $(\mu \times (\kappa \circ \mu))$-almost all $(x, y)$. It suffices to show that for all measurable sets of $\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y$, the integrals with respect to that product measure of the two sides of the equality on the set are equal. Furthermore, it is sufficient to show it for sets of the form $s \times t$ since those are a $\pi$-system. Since $\kappa(x) \ll \kappa \circ \mu$ almost surely, we have $\mu \otimes \kappa \ll \mu \times (\kappa \circ \mu)$, hence $(\kappa \circ \mu) \otimes \kappa_\mu^\dagger \ll (\kappa \circ \mu) \times \mu$. We get that $\kappa_\mu^\dagger(y) \ll \mu$ almost surely. \begin{align*} \int_{x \in s, y \in t} \frac{d \kappa_\mu^\dagger(y)}{d \mu}(x) \partial (\mu \times (\kappa \circ \mu)) &= \int_{y \in t} \int_{x \in s} \frac{d \kappa_\mu^\dagger(y)}{d \mu}(x) \partial \mu \partial (\kappa \circ \mu) \\ &= \int_{y \in t} \kappa_\mu^\dagger(y)(s) \partial (\kappa \circ \mu) \\ &= ((\kappa \circ \mu) \otimes \kappa_\mu^\dagger) (t \times s) \: . \end{align*} \begin{align*} \int_{x \in s, y \in t} \frac{d \kappa(x)}{d(\kappa \circ \mu)}(y) \partial (\mu \times (\kappa \circ \mu)) &= \int_{x \in s} \int_{y \in t} \frac{d \kappa(x)}{d(\kappa \circ \mu)}(y) \partial (\kappa \circ \mu) \partial \mu \\ &= \int_{x \in s} \kappa(x)(t) \partial \mu \\ &= (\mu \otimes \kappa) (s \times t) \: . \end{align*} By the defining property of the Bayesian inverse, those two quantities are equal.

nodes.statement_short: Compare integrals of both sides over product rectangles, a $\pi$-system, using the defining property of the Bayesian inverse.

nodes.name: Radon-Nikodym derivative of kernels
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two finite kernels, with either $\mathcal X$ countable or $\mathcal{Y}$ countably generated. The Radon-Nikodym derivative of $\kappa$ with respect to $\eta$, denoted by $\frac{d \kappa}{d \eta}$, is a measurable function $\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y \to \mathbb{R}_{+, \infty}$ with $\kappa = \frac{d \kappa}{d \eta} \cdot \eta + \kappa_{\perp \eta}$, where for all $x$, $\kappa_{\perp \eta}(x) \perp \eta(x)$.
also_stated_at: This is a measurable function $\frac{d \kappa}{d \eta} : \mathcal X \times \mathcal Y \to \mathbb{R}_{+, \infty}$ with $\kappa = \frac{d \kappa}{d \eta} \cdot \eta + \kappa_{\perp \eta}$, where for all $x$, $\kappa_{\perp \eta}(x) \perp \eta(x)$.
nodes.label: def:kernel_rnDeriv

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the kernel Radon-Nikodym derivative
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa, \eta : \mathcal X \rightsquigarrow \mathcal Y$ be two finite kernels, with either $\mathcal X$ countable or $\mathcal{Y}$ countably generated. If for some $f$ and $\xi$, $\kappa = f \cdot \eta + \xi$ with $\xi(x) \perp \eta(x)$ for all $x$, then for all $x$, $f(x, y) = \frac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}(y)$ for $\eta(x)$-almost all $y \in \mathcal Y$.

nodes.label: lem:rnDeriv_unique

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $f$ and $\xi$ be such that $\kappa = f \cdot \eta + \xi$ with $\xi(x) \perp \eta(x)$ for all $x$. Then for all $x \in \mathcal X$, $\kappa(x) = f(x, \cdot) \cdot \eta(x) + \xi(x)$ with $\xi(x) \perp \eta(x)$. By the uniqueness result for the Radon-Nikodym derivative of measures, $f(x, \cdot) = \frac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}$ almost everywhere.
nodes.statement_short: Apply uniqueness of the Radon-Nikodym derivative of measures pointwise in $x$.

nodes.statement: By the uniqueness result for the Radon-Nikodym derivative of measures, $f(x, \cdot) = \frac{d \kappa(x)}{d \eta(x)}$ almost everywhere.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
First, by Theorem~ef{thm:rnDeriv_chain_compProd}, for $(
u \otimes \eta)$-almost all $(x,y)$,  egin{align*}  rac{d(\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d(
u \otimes \eta)}(x, y) =  rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)  rac{d(\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d(\mu \otimes \eta)}(x, y) \: . \end{align*} It remains to show that $ rac{d \mu}{d 
u}(x)  rac{d(\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d(\mu \otimes \eta)}(x, y)$ is $(
u \otimes \eta)$-almost everywhere equal to $ rac{d\mu}{d
u}(x) rac{d \kappa}{d \eta}(x,y)$. By Lemma~ef{cor:rnDeriv_compProd_right}, $(\mu \otimes \eta)$-almost surely,  egin{align*}  rac{d \kappa}{d \eta} =  rac{d (\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d (\mu \otimes \eta)} \: . \end{align*} We then use Lemma~ef{lem:ae_rnDeriv_ne_zero} to turn that into a $(
u \otimes \eta)$-almost sure equality:  egin{align*}  rac{d(\mu \otimes \eta)}{d(
u \otimes \eta)} rac{d \kappa}{d \eta} =  rac{d(\mu \otimes \eta)}{d(
u \otimes \eta)} rac{d (\mu \otimes \kappa)}{d (\mu \otimes \eta)} \: . \end{align*} Finally, by Lemma~ef{cor:rnDeriv_compProd_left}, $ rac{d(\mu \otimes \eta)}{d(
u \otimes \eta)} =  rac{d\mu}{d
u}$ almost surely.

nodes.label: lem:integrable_f_rnDeriv_of_derivAtTop_ne_top

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: By convexity and $f(0) < \infty$, $f'(\infty)<\infty$, we can sandwich $f$ between two affine functions of $\frac{d\mu}{d\nu}$. Those functions are integrable since the measures are finite.
nodes.section: C Convex functions of Radon-Nikodym derivatives
nodes.statement_short: Sandwich $f$ between two affine functions of the density.

nodes.name: Jensen's inequality for conditional expectations
nodes.statement: For $f$ convex, $f\left(\mu [g \mid m]\right) \le \mu [f \circ g \mid m]$.
nodes.section: C Convex functions of Radon-Nikodym derivatives
assumptions: For $f$ convex
nodes.label: thm:condexp_jensen
